News.title: Fugitive accused of murder arrested after hiding in Britain as a refugee for 27 years
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

KEEPING LOW Fugitive accused of murder arrested after hiding in Britain as a refugee for 27 years

A FUGITIVE accused of murder before fleeing to Britain and posing as a refugee has been arrested after 27 years on the run.

Sabri Sopoti, 60, faces extradition to serve a 24-year jail sentence for shooting a man dead with a machine gun in Albania in 1999.

Prosecutors allege Sopoti got asylum here by pretending to be Kosovo war refugee Zenel Bytyqi.

At Westminster magistrates’ court, he was remanded in custody before a full extradition hearing in December.





Prosecutors say someone rang him in 1999 and told him to “sort out that garbage playing with you and your family”.

His wife later told investigators he became visibly agitated after the call and left home carrying both a machine gun and a pistol.

Sopoti took a Scorpion sub-machine gun and pistol to kill the man in a café.

He vanished and was convicted in his absence.

Albanian authorities allege he fled to Britain using a different identity, claiming to be a refugee from war-torn Kosovo.

They say he was allowed to remain in the UK and lived under the assumed identity for almost three decades before being traced.

His extradition hearing is due to take place in December.

Sopoti was caught in an operation involving Interpol Manchester.

News.title: Warning to fishermen to immediately kill sinister ‘round’ fish carrying dark ‘disease’
News.content:
ANGLERS have received urgent warnings to kill an invasive fish species in one part of North America.

The fish are known to carry a disease that can harm fish and other wildlife in the area.



In the Hilton Beach village of Ontario, Canada, fishermen are encouraged to immediately kill the invasive round goby fish when they catch them.

The Invasive Species Centre in Sault Ste. Marie in Canada considers the fish to be invasive as it “aggressively feeds on small aquatic organisms and can spawn several times each year.”



“Round goby decrease the levels of native fish by eating eggs and competing for food,” the centre states.

“It is also suggested that round goby pass a strain of botulism to the birds and fish that eat them; this toxin comes from the zebra mussels that the goby eat and causes fish and bird death.”

Across Canada, it is illegal for anglers to possess these fish or use them as bait for other fish.

In Hilton Beach, resident Karen Godson recently caught a round goby and immediately killed it, after googling the fish to determine that it was an invasive species.

Lauren Rogers, a communications coordinator with the Invasive Species Centre told SooToday that the fish “can carry a disease that impacts Great Lakes fish and fish-eating birds.”

“They are problematic because they can outcompete native fish, consume fish eggs and young, and disrupt aquatic food webs,” Rogers said.



“They are also linked to botulism outbreaks in the Great Lakes. By feeding on invasive mussels that can accumulate the botulism toxin, gobies can transfer that toxin to larger fish and fish-eating birds, contributing to fish and bird die-offs.”

The fish mostly eat zebra mussels, which no other fish in the region consume.

This allows the round goby fish to “uniquely exploit a resource that could fuel a population explosion,” the centre states.

News.title: Labour’s Freeview switch-off plan could leave more than eight million homes without live TV, Ofcom report warns
News.content:
LABOUR’S plan to switch off Freeview television could hit more than eight million households.

Regulator Ofcom’s annual media report found 28 per cent of homes do not have a TV connected to the internet.



Ministers are looking at 2034 and 2044 as potential dates to only broadcast telly over the internet.

Older generations are overwhelmingly reliant on Freeview.



Dennis Reed, of campaign group Silver Voices, said: “Ministers learned with winter fuel what happens when older people are taken for granted.

“This report is the warning

“Free TV through an aerial must be guaranteed until 2044.”

MPs across the political divide have thrown their weight behind The Sun’s Save Our Sets campaign to protect Freeview TV.

Labour MP Sarah Champion said: “Free TV is still relied on by over eight million homes.

“It is important we get this transition right and extend free terrestrial television to 2044.”



The Government is consulting on the plans.

A spokesman said: “Any future transition would only proceed once we are confident the right safeguards, infrastructure and support are in place.”

News.title: ‘Psychic’ IT worker sacked after telling colleague he’d seen her in his dreams & claimed powers were ‘protected belief’
News.content:
MYSTIC FIRED ‘Psychic’ IT worker sacked after telling colleague he’d seen her in his dreams & claimed powers were ‘protected belief’

A “PSYCHIC” IT worker who was sacked after telling a female employee they had already met “in his dreams” has lost a battle for compensation.

Elrich Daudet claimed his new colleague had appeared to him months beforehand, as a muse for his poetry and songwriting.



The woman sent an email to another colleague, saying the senior computer analyst – who claimed he was born with prophetic powers – was “doing her head in”.

He was fired for gross misconduct, after sending her love poems and likening her scent to “flowers in the Garden of Eden”, making her feel “panicky” and “uncomfortable”.



He insisted that he had known that the two of them would cross paths and that she had been “haunting” his dreams.

Daudet claimed damages for unfair dismissal, harassment and discrimination on the basis of being a black man and his “protected beliefs”.

However, the UK’s top employment judge Lord Fairley rejected his appeal, saying: “She thought he was coming on to her and that made her feel uncomfortable.”

“It doesn’t matter whether he touches her or if it’s in an email.”

He added that there was no legal error in concluding that Daudet’s belief in the power of dreams was not a “protected belief” under equality law.

The messages he sent were also not a “manifestation” of beliefs, he argued, given there was no need to disclose them and doing so amounted to “harassment”.



The Employment Appeal Tribunal heard that Daudet had been providing IT equipment and services to public authorities since 2008.

After the woman reported his messages, Daudet faced an internal disciplinary enquiry which led to his eventual sacking for “gross misconduct” in December 2022.

His lawyers argued that the belief that dreams can predict the future should in fact be protected under equality laws.

But the claim was ultimately denied, with Lord Fairley arguing that there was “ample evidence” of “distress or alarm” caused to the woman by Daudet’s correspondence.

“She thought he was coming on to her and that made her feel uncomfortable,” he said.



“It doesn’t matter whether he touches her or if it’s in an email.”

News.title: Tens of thousands of migrants poised to make beeline for Britain after storming Spanish enclave
News.content:
MANY of the 60,000 migrants who stormed Ceuta will head for Britain once they are in mainland Europe, Reform UK said.

Madrid will have to move tens of thousands from the tiny Spanish enclave, which borders Morocco, as it is now swamped.



Officials will take them across the Strait of Gibraltar.

At which point many are expected to try to head for Britain.



The Sun has uncovered examples of illegal migrants using Morocco as a launchpad.

Some have posted on TikTok to show the route they plan to take.

In one photo, a man is seen ­pointing to the Union Jack.

The Arabic caption reads: “Search in progress.”



A video post by another seemingly shows him in northern France.

On it, he writes: “The Kingdom is only a matter of time.”

Reform’s Robert Jenrick said: “Ceuta is our future if we don’t secure our border.

“These men are on their way to Calais.”

News.title: ‘Sorry, she died’ – Strange language in Nancy Guthrie ransom notes holds key to help snare suspects Unabomber-style
News.content:
THE chilling ransom notes sent by Nancy Guthrie’s kidnappers – demanding up to $6 million in bitcoin before claiming she died of natural causes – feature bizarre language which could offer crucial clues.

Guthrie, the 84-year-old mother of Today host Savannah Guthrie, was taken from her home in Tuscan, Arizona on February 1.



Despite a massive multi-agency investigation involving local police and the FBI, Guthrie has never been seen again — and no suspects have been named, despite authorities sifting through thousands of tips.

Investigators previously released surveillance footage showing a masked subject arriving at Guthrie’s home in the middle of the night and walking toward her front door.



Now, officials from Pima County Sheriff’s Department have released two haunting ransom notes allegedly sent to the Guthrie family after her disappearance.

The second message contained bizarre claims about Nancy’s fate, stating: “She perished shortly after she was taken” and “she is buried in nature now.”



The writer claimed, “We did not fully grasp the seriousness of her physical condition.

“We never intended to hurt her, that was not our intention.

“She perished shortly after she was taken. We believe it was heart related.

“She is buried in nature now. Nothing you could have done could have changed the outcome.



“We want your family to know this and hope you all can find peace. We are truly sorry.”

Nancy lived with chronic pain, and had fragile health including a heart condition requiring a pacemaker and vital daily medications, officials previously confirmed.

The unusual wording in the messages could offer investigators potential clues about the person or people behind the alleged kidnapping — in a similar way that language helped expose the identity of the infamous Unabomber.

Ted Kaczynski, who carried out a decades-long bombing campaign across the US, was eventually identified in part because of his distinctive writing style, word choices and ideas outlined in his manifesto.

After Kaczynski demanded newspapers publish the document, his brother recognized similarities between the writing and his own views, helping investigators connect him to the crimes.



The first ransom email sent to the Guthrie family claimed Nancy was being held captive and laid out strict payment deadlines, while including details from inside her home that appeared intended to prove the sender had access to the property.

Read the full ransom notes The subject of an email sent to KOLD read “News Tip” and one line after “o not play games, law enforcement will not be able to help you,” was blurred out by officials. First ransom note sent on February 2: Hello Savannah,

We have your mother Nancy. She is safe but scared. She will be held for ransom and once payment is received she will be released unharmed. We will be holding her for a maximum of 7 days. You will need to send bitcoin in the amount of $4 million USD before 5PM on Thursday the 5th. If payment is not received, the ransom will be increased to 6 million USD which will need to be paid by 5PM on Monday the 9th. Once payment is received to the bitcoin

address below she will be released within 12 hours of deposit to a safe drop off location back in Tucson. If payment is not recieved by the last deadline on Monday the 9th at 5PM, she will be killed. Your mother is aware of this and her life is in your hands. It is in the best interest of everyone to have this completed as soon as possible. You will not be able to contact me from here on out, there will be no negotiation. Do not play games, law enforcement will

not be able to help you. *ANOTHER LINE BLURRED OUT BY OFFICIALS* She had a white smart watch on the floor of the foot of her bed and the white flood light in backyard was destroyed. Second ransom note sent on February 6: Guthrie Family,

We did not fully grasp the seriousness of her physical condition. We never intended to hurt her, that was not our intention. She perished shortly after she was taken. We believe it was heart related. She is buried in nature now. Nothing you could have done could have changed the outcome. We want your family to know this and hope you all can find peace. We are truly sorry. *ANOTHER LINE BLURRED OUT BY OFFICIALS*

The chilling message began, “Hello Savannah, We have your mother Nancy. She is safe but scared.”

It claimed Nancy would be held “for ransom” for “a maximum of 7 days” and demanded “bitcoin in the amount of $4 million USD before 5 pm on Thursday the 5th.”

The sender threatened that if payment was not received, “the ransom will be increased to 6 million USD,” with a final deadline of “5 pm on Monday the 9th.”

The email claimed that once the bitcoin payment was made, Nancy “will be released within 12 hours” at “a safe drop off location back in Tucson.”



It ended with a threat, “If payment is not received by the last deadline… she will be killed,” adding, “Your mother is aware of this and her life is in your hands.”

The message warned, “There will be no negotiation. Do not play games, law enforcement will not be able to help you.”

The sender also appeared to prove they had been inside Nancy’s home by revealing details that had not been made public, claiming a white smartwatch had been left on the floor at the foot of her bed and that a white floodlight in the backyard had been destroyed.

The note was first sent to the local CBS affiliate on February 2, and a second note was sent on February 6.



While law enforcement tested the Bitcoin account with a small transfer, the funds were never accessed or paid out by the family.

In Friday’s update, officials also referenced the footage recovered from Nancy’s home that showed an “an unidentified male who knows what happened to Nancy.”



“Two videos recovered from Nancy’s doorbell camera may be from two separate days,” they said.

“These videos are critical to our understanding of the unidentified male’s behaviors and choices.”

Officials said the videos show how the man prepared for the events that unfolded on the night Nancy’s vanished.

Meanwhile, heartbroken Savannah issued another plea this month while on air hosting The Today Show, asking for anyone with information to speak out.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I just want to take the opportunity to ask people, to really to beg people to come forward. Somebody knows something,” she said.



“This is a news story today that is on your radar but this is the life that my sister lives, that I live, my brother lives, our extended families live, our children live every day. We are in agony.”

News.title: There’s nowhere I’d rather be over hot summer than slaving away on my farm. But there is a fly in the ointment…
News.content:
YOU might think that one of the (many) downsides about farming is that you can’t ever book a summer holiday.

It’s impossible because you don’t know when the harvest will be.





This year it began in the middle of July but sometimes you don’t get cracking until the end of September.

This means the farmer is forced to stay at home for the summer, looking at Instagram pictures of all his non-farming friends as they frolic on boats and in bars in the sun-drenched Mediterranean.

Sounds terrible, yes?

Well it isn’t. Some jobs on the farm are unpleasant. Sexing rabbits is annoyingly difficult, and disposing of dead piglets is heartbreaking.

But I’ve been harvesting all week, and this job is an absolute joy.

I boing out of bed before dawn, knowing the moisture in the crops will be dead right, and then, from the ­tractor’s lofty seat, I watch the sun rise through the dust cloud being left in the ­combine’s wake. It’s a stunning sight.

When the combine’s hopper is full, I have to position my trailer under its spout, making sure that none of the grain coming out of it is spilled.

This requires the sort of concentration that would normally only be deployed by a surgeon who’s been called upon to operate on his own daughter’s eyes.





And then, when the trailer is full, I must race back to the farmyard to tip the grain into the shed, and use my JCB to push the 12-tonne pile up against the back wall before racing back to the field to get the next load.

Speed and power is important here, and I like that.

At lunchtime, Lisa — guided by the plume of dust that rises over whatever field we happen to be harvesting at that moment — will arrive on the scene and drop off some sandwiches.

Good ones, made from stuff she picked that morning.

And we eat these on the move because there’s no time to lose.

The moisture levels are changing by the hour and if they go above 15 per cent, you have to stop.

It’s hot and it’s dirty out there, and you work non-stop for 15 or 20 hours at a stretch.

But then, finally, you turn off the engines and in the golden-hour silence that results, you crack open an ice cold bottle of beer and gulp at it as the sun goes down. I’ve drunk beers in many exotic and beautiful locations over the years, but none of them match the beer you treat yourself to after a hard day’s harvesting.

And not just because, in my case, the beer in question is a Hawkstone, made from the barley I harvested last year.

Having decided that beer is the best invention of all time, you trundle home and hit the sack.



Because you’ll be up at 4am to go through the whole process again.

And you cannot wait because you absolutely love it and there’s no job you’d rather do. And nowhere you’d rather be.

The only slight fly in the ointment is that thanks to the hot summer and this Government’s strange hatred of farmers, you don’t actually get paid for the wheat and the barley you’ve harvested.

In fact, I worked out this morning that it’d be cheaper to go on an expensive holiday.

A LOAD OF HOG WASH... A SURVEY has found that cars are responsible for 40 per cent of hedgehog deaths in this country. Well yes, but I notice the survey was, in part, funded by something called the People’s Trust For Endangered Species. And in my experience, any organisation with the word “people’s” in its title tends to be run by woolly-headed Thunbergites who see the car as being responsible for every one of the world’s ills. It’s possibly true, of course, that 40 per cent of hedgehogs die after being run over. But that leaves 60 per cent that die of what? Is Donald Trump killing them? Or the IDF? Or the ghost of Margaret Thatcher? Nope. A huge number are killed by badgers – but we can rely on the People’s Hedgehog Party or whatever they’re called to keep that quiet.

Couldn’t Hillary have thought of summit else?

I READ the other day that when explorer Edmund ­Hillary and Sherpa Tenzing reached the top of Mount Everest, they transmitted news of their achievement to the Times newspaper in London using the pre-arranged code, “snow conditions bad”. I think this might be the worst code ever.

Because what if the snow conditions really had been bad?

The reporters at the Times would have got Hillary’s message, breathed a sigh of relief that their exclusive story was safe, and then not sent help.

It’d be like the captain of a submarine agreeing with his bosses before attempting to get to the bottom of the ocean’s deepest trench that the code for success would be “sub filling with water”.

LOTS of pictures this week of people flooding across the English ­Channel in small boats.



And, having examined them closely, I have a question.

If these people really are refugees, fleeing from some awful atrocity in their own country, then where are the women?

Where are the children? Where are the elderly ­people?

Are we expected to believe that this atrocity, whatever it is, only affects young men?

PROF'S ADVICE STINGS EXPERTS have announced – and I’ve noticed this – that we are being plagued by far fewer wasps than usual this summer. We are told they don’t like the heat, which I find unlikely because the damn things seem to manage just fine in ­places like Corfu. But whatever the ­reason, Professor Seirian Sumner, a behavioural ecologist at University College London, recommends that when we have a picnic, we cut off a morsel of meat or fruit and push it to the side of the plate so the wasps have something to eat as well. Hmmm. Ms Sumner may be excellent at understanding what goes on in an animal’s head, but I fear she isn’t quite as good at understanding humans. Because frankly, no one is going to do that unless they are completely mad.

LABOUR NEVER LEARN

LAST year, Diane Abbott apologised for being antisemitic and was then ejected from the Labour Party for saying she didn’t regret it at all.

And guess what? She’s back.

I guess Diane must have apologised for retracting her previous apology but, whatever, Labour has decided it can’t manage without this intellectual powerhouse and has welcomed her back into the fold.

Of course, there will be those who say that West-minster should be full of people from all walks of life and with varying levels of intelligence.

But I disagree. I want to be governed by people who are ferociously bright – really properly clever with analytical minds and tremendous knowledge accrued from many years of reading and travel and work.



Not someone who dresses like a daytime TV host, someone who left school pregnant and with no qualifications at 16, and someone who can’t add up.

SO, let’s see if I’ve got this straight. Having shared a social media post suggesting Nigel Farage should have his head cut off, the leader of the Green Party, Zack Polanski, says he won’t apologise because it was a mistake.

Right. So according to this increasingly annoying idiot, if you knock an old lady over, there’s no need to say sorry if it was an accident.

News.title: Remains of missing boy, 14, pulled from River Taw after weeks of searching
News.content:
Remains of missing boy, 14, pulled from River Taw after weeks of searching

Taylor Charlton was 14 when he disappeared from Barnstaple in Devon on May 8, sparking a massive search and rescue effort from the local community and emergency services

View Image Taylor Charlton was 14 when he went missing in February (Image: Karl Grafton <karlgrafton@hotmail.com>)

Police have confirmed that human remains found in a river in Devon are missing teenager Taylor Charlton.

Taylor, 14 at the time of his disappearance, went missing on the night of Friday May 8 in Barnstaple, sparking an extensive operation to find him.

Police said the support shown by the local community since Taylor was reported missing had been "tremendous".

Volunteers and members of the police searched tirelessly to find Taylor. Tragically, Devon and Cornwall Police confirmed today that remains found in the River Taw on June 24 belonged to Taylor, Devon Live reports.

Police arrested a 20-year-old man on suspicion of murder on June 12. He was later released on bail while investigations continued.

On July 2, a woman in her 40s was also arrested on suspicion of murder. She has since been released on bail pending further enquiries.

Police say there is an ongoing investigation into the circumstances of Taylor's death, and detectives will "continue to establish the full facts".

Devon and Cornwall Police said: “Taylor’s family have been updated of this development and our thoughts and condolences are with them, Taylor’s friends and the local community.

“Taylor’s loved-ones continue to be supported by specialist officers at this incredibly difficult and distressing time.

“We respectfully ask that the family’s privacy is respected as they come to terms with this tragic news.

“This is not the outcome that anyone hoped for and we know how deeply this will affect the local community who have shown tremendous support throughout the search.

“An investigation into the circumstances surrounding Taylor’s death remains ongoing and detectives will continue to establish the full facts.”

Article continues below

Police have asked people not to speculate about the case or share unconfirmed information online while enquiries continue.

Anyone with information that could help the investigation has been asked to contact police.

News.title: Naples earthquake live: Italy struck by 4.7 magnitude quake as rocks crush cars
News.content:
Residents in Naples have been left terrified after a powerful earthquake caused damage to the Italian city - it registered at 4.7 magnitude

A powerful earthquake has struck southern Italy, causing damage in the city of Naples.

The 4.7 magnitude quake has left neighbourhoods without power, and residents are taking to the streets in fear. It occurred just before 8pm (local time).

According to data released by the INGV (National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology), the magnitude was 4.7. Power outages have been reported from Pizzofalcone to Fuorigrotta, and there has been a massive landslide in Pozzuoli.

Images show buildings have crumbled, with debris crushing cars,

News.title: Faces of victims betrayed by 'monster' funeral director Robert Bush as families fume at 'atrocious' sentence
News.content:
Faces of victims betrayed by 'monster' funeral director Robert Bush as families fume at 'atrocious' sentence

Families of dozens of Robert Bush's victims have condemned the sentence he received after bodies were left to rot and the wrong ashes handed out at his Legacy funeral parlour

View 9 Images Dozens of people were victimised by Bush after their deaths (Image: Humberside Police/PA Wire)

These are the faces of the victims betrayed by "monster" Legacy funeral director Robert Bush, whose families have been left furious after he was handed a "joke" 20 year sentence for crimes.

‌



Bush, 48, the owner of Legacy Independent Funeral Services in Hull, East Yorkshire, left bodies to rot - including the remains of a miscarried baby - in his mortuary, and gave the wrong ashes to bereaving families, while conning other clients to fund a life of luxury. He pleaded guilty to 67 offences spanning 12 years, including 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial - which affected hundreds of families - and was today sentenced to 20 years behind bars after he abused their trust "on an industrial scale".

‌



Furious family members condemned the sentence as "atrocious" and a "joke" after 35 bodies and half a tonne of ashes were recovered from the home - with more victims feared.

‌



'Monster' funeral director Robert Bush jailed for 20 years as heartbroken families demand public inquiry READ MORE :

View 9 Images Bush victimised 300 people (Image: Humberside Police/PA Wire)

Hull Crown Court heard that Bush had defrauded nearly 200 families out of £500,000, and acted out of "financial greed" while mishandling victims' remains and handing out the wrong ashes to their loved ones. Sentencing today, Judge Mr Justice Hilliard said he had "caused anguish and pain on a scale beyond comprehension".

View 9 Images Bush was sentenced to 20 years behind bars today (Image: Elizabeth Cook/PA Wire)

‌



He said in his remarks that, unless a body was among those recovered and identified by police following a raid on Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull in 2024, people who used the service can't be "absolutely certain they received the ashes of their loved one".

Police have been able to identify the remains recovered during that raid, with their family members - up to 300 people - among Bush's many victims.

The court was told relatives of 46 people who were cremated between 2017 and 2024 were given the wrong ashes and the loved ones of another 11 deceased never received any. The court also heard from some of the 226 pensioners who said they had been “conned” out of what little savings they had after being sold fake funeral plans by Bush.

‌



He pleaded guilty to 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial and 30 counts of fraud by false representation relating to bodies found at the site, four “foetus allegations” of fraud, where he presented ashes to women falsely saying that they were “the remains of their unborn”, a further charge of fraud covering the ashes of 57 people between 2017 and 2024, fraudulent trading relating to funeral plans between 2012 and 2024 and theft from 12 charities.

The judge said following Bush's sentencing today that he had “never known offences affect so many people so deeply”, adding that the ex-mortician "must have a heartless side to him - which allowed him to treat the living and the dead in the way he did, and he was very confident he would get away with what he was doing".

View 9 Images Stephen Perrins was also identified as a victim of Bush's (Image: PA)

‌



The judge said: "How betrayed they now feel." Families remained silent and hugged as he was jailed while Bush simply stood up with his hands clasped in front while leaving the dock.

They hugged and wept after leaving the court, and told the Mirror of their anguish as they reacted to the sentence Bush received. One woman said: "He should never come out again for what he’s done." Another added: “He’s only going to be 58 when he comes out. It’s a joke.”

Tristan Essex, 26, said: “We’ve been failed again! We’ve waited two and a half years for this!” Michaela Baldwin, whose stepfather Danny Middleton’s body was found at Legacy, said the sheer number of people victimised by him should have warranted at least another decade behind bars for Bush.

‌



View 9 Images One of Danny Middleton's family members said Bush should have gotten 30 years behind bars (Image: PA)

She said: “I understand that no matter what the judge would have given him, it wouldn’t be long enough for us, but still 20 years is still… If you think there’s bodies that was involved in this, and that’s less than a year for each."

“[He should have got] at least 30 – one year for each, at least. I hate him, I’ll always hate him, there’s just so much greed in why he’s done this.” Joanne Moody, whose father Peter Moody was one of the bodies found at Legacy, said Robert Bush’s sentence was “atrocious”.

‌



She said: “It’s a joke, he’s going to be out in 10 years. There’s no justice for any of us, we’re all still going to be kicking around when he gets out. We’re not going to get closure.”

View 9 Images The Legacy case has moved the Government into action on regulating funeral providers (Image: Danny Lawson/PA Wire)

Phil and Jackie Groizard believe they were given the wrong ashes for Mr Groizard’s mother-in-law Carol, and said Bush appeared to have simply scooped some random remains into a bag for them when they inquired. Mrs Groizard said Bush’s sentence was “not long enough.” She said: “He’ll only be 58 when he comes out. He’s got away with it – it should have been life."

Article continues below

The Government pledged to formally regulate the funeral sector following Bush's sentencing, with the Department for Health and Social Care issuing a statement announcing the move. A spokesperson said regulation would be a priority “following the harrowing case in Hull”.

Health and Social Care Secretary Yvette Cooper said: “In the wake of this horrific case, we will now bring forward comprehensive proposals to ensure respect and dignity for the deceased in every setting, including proper regulation of the funeral sector.”

News.title: Manchester mayoral election results LIVE: Labour and Reform go to second round of votes after major delays
News.content:
Results for Britain's biggest-ever by-election are expected at any moment, with Labour confident Bev Craig will be named Mayor of Greater Manchester at some point this evening

Manchester mayoral election results LIVE: Labour and Reform go to second round of votes after major delays

The Mayor of Greater Manchester race will progress to a second round of votes, it has been confirmed, as Labour's Bev Craig hopes to succeed Andy Burnham.

Following a long night of counting across Greater Manchester, Craig and Reform UK's Sian Astley will be going through to the second round. Tom Stannard, Manchester returning officer, told counters at Manchester's Co-op Live arena that a second preference count will take place.

He has told counters to "focus on accuracy over speed" after several hours of waiting in the room. Ms Craig is the favourite to succeed Andy Burnham, who vacated the post when he became MP for Makerfield last month. The new Prime Minister has since set up a No10 in the North in the heart of Manchester.

Reform UK were initially tipped to be a strong challenger for the coveted post, which is set to become more powerful as Mr Burnham devolves power from Westminster.

News.title: Fire and 'explosions' at Washington factory as 'close windows' warning issued
News.content:
Thick black smoke coming from the scene of the fire

Emergency services rushed to the incident at a factory in the Crowther Industrial Estate, Washington, in Tyne and Wear, with witnesses telling of 'several explosions'

Massive plumes of smoke can be seen coming from a raging fire at a factory after reports of "several explosions" in the North East.

Emergency services rushed to the incident in the Crowther Industrial Estate, Washington, in Tyne and Wear, with witnesses saying that there's no signs of the fire easing.

Northumbria Police says officers are on the scene to support the Tyne and Wear Fire and Rescue Service in responding to the fire in Washington, with a 'cordon currently in place'.

Pictures from the scene show five fire brigade appliances and an aerial ladder platform dispatched. Thick black smoke is billowing into the sky which can be seen for miles.

News.title: CEO accused of murdering daughter, 9, had 'condoms and confession' in car
News.content:
CEO accused of murdering daughter, 9, had 'condoms and confession' in car

Prosecutors allege Luciano Frattolin, 45, murdered his nine-year-old daughter Melina in New York on the day she was due to return home to his ex-wife in Canada

View 5 Images Melina Frattolin, 9, was found dead in a pond in New York (Image: NYS Police)

A coffee CEO accused of murdering his nine-year-old daughter had condoms and a series of disturbing notes in his car, including one titled "confession", a trial heard.

Luciano Frattolin, 45, told police the youngster had been kidnapped by men in a white van before she was found dead in the shallow water of a pond in Ticonderoga, New York, last July.

Prosecutors allege the businessman, who is the head of Canadian coffee company Gambella, dumped Melina Frattolin's body in a muddy swamp in the Adirondacks before detectives found inconsistencies in his account.

Authorities previously said the father and daughter travelled through Connecticut and New York before Melina was scheduled to return home to her mum in Quebec.

View 5 Images Luciano Frattolin, 45, is accused of murdering his daughter Melina (Image: AP)

A court heard the father had multiple condoms stashed inside bags in a rental car he was using on the trip.

State police investigator Jacalyn Sommer told Essex County Court jurors on Thursday that two stained pairs of underpants belonging to Melina showed signs of "seminal fluid".

A shirt and shorts belonging to Frattolin allegedly had signs of the same fluid, the court heard.

Prosecutors allege that on the day Melina was supposed to return home, Frattolin staged her disappearance to cover up her death.

He has been charged with second-degree murder and concealing a human corpse in connection to the death.

View 5 Images Frattolin at Essex County Court, NY (Image: Canadian Press/Shutterstock)

A document titled "closure/confession" was found in the grey Toyota Prius that Frattolin had rented, jurors were told on Thursday.

The note appeared to be a draft press release directed at Canadian media in which Frattolin labelled his ex-wife Kali Galanis "the queen of evil".

"You were not supposed to be a mother for a reason," Frattolin said in the letter, which was reportedly written in the case that he was able to secure custody of Melina.

"Death is better than living with you," he wrote. "Your Dad is the only one who can control you."

Frattolin added: "The problem was never me [...] It was always your mental illness".

View 5 Images Melina vanished on the day she was supposed to return to Canada (Image: NYS Police)

Prosecutors claim the businessman also penned a "father's report" with details spanning 10 years.

The document, which was discovered in the vehicle's glovebox, included notes for a "Plan A" and "Plan B". Frattolin also had photos of his ex-wife, Galanis, as well as baby pictures of Melina.

Among his belongings were user manuals for a Porsche, authorities said.

New York State police said Frattolin's smartphone had recorded more than 200,000 location data points as part of their investigation into Melina's death.

‌



View 5 Images Frattolin is the head of Canada-based coffee company Gambella (Image: Canadian Press/Shutterstock)

Galanis previously told the court that Frattolin wanted to take Melina to his native Ethiopia for two weeks in January 2025, but that the child " didn't want to go".

The mum said she had grown worried about these plans as her lawyer had mentioned cases involving estranged spouses who took their children to other countries and failed to return.

Article continues below

Galanis noted that Melina had revealed "other troubling and alarming things" about her father.

"I became uncomfortable," Galanis testified. "I was not OK with that anymore."

The trial continues.

News.title: F-35B fighter jet crashes at Miramar Air Base as US Marines address 'mishap'
News.content:
F-35B fighter jet crashes at Miramar Air Base as US Marines address 'mishap'

The jet went down near the Miramar Air Base in San Diego, California, following what the US Marines called a 'Class A mishap' - the pilot has been rushed to a medical facility

View 2 Images The wreckage near Miramar Air Base in California (Image: Sky10)

An F-35B fighter jet has crashed near a California air base, with the pilot rushed to a medical facility following what the US Marines called a "Class A mishap".

‌



The jet went down Friday afternoon near the Miramar Air Base in San Diego.

‌



The US Marines described the incident as a "Class A mishap" - the most severe mishap category used to describe incidents where the damage totals more than $2million, a military aircraft is destroyed, or a service member has died.

‌



The pilot ejected, was recovered and then taken to a medical facility, the statement added.

"We can confirm a Class A mishap involving a Marine Corps F-35B in the vicinity of MCAS Miramar," a spokesperson said.

View 2 Images The US Marines said the pilot ejected (Image: Sky10)

‌



"The pilot ejected and has been recovered. More information will be made available shortly."

Aerial footage from a news helicopter showed smoke billowing from the wreckage in a dirt field, with multiple military and firefighting vehicles and people standing nearby.

Flame retardant material appeared to be placed on the ground, and at least one person was seen spraying the wreckage with a fire hose.

Article continues below

Candace Hadley, a spokesperson for San Diego Fire, said firefighters were on scene to respond to a vegetation fire that sparked near the crash site. She referred additional questions to Miramar.

The F-35B comes from a family of advanced stealth fighter jets flown by the Marine Corps, Navy and Air Force.

The "B" version is capable of vertical landings and has an engine designed for short take-offs.

News.title: Drone images show Suffolk wildfire devastation as helicopters scrambled
News.content:
A wildfire ravaging Dunwich Heath in Suffolk is still 'unstable' according to the local council with the number of firefighters at the scene increasing

A wildfire that has destroyed an area the size of 200 football pitches in Suffolk remains "unstable".

The blaze at Dunwich Heath has devastated wildlife habitats, which could now take up to 25 years to recover, after it went up in flames at about 5pm on Wednesday.

Hundreds of people were evacuated from caravan sites, and they have now been given a short window to collect their belongings.

National Trust director-general Hilary McGrady described the “heartbreaking” loss of important habitat - which was home to rare species such as nightjars, skylarks and the rare Dartford warbler - due to the blaze.

The land was also home to adders, lizards and slow worms, as well as butterflies including the rare silver-studded blue.

The lowland heath habitat is one of the UK’s rarest, and an estimated 92% of it has been lost in England over the last 120 years, the charity said.

News.title: Watch: Moroccan police clash with migrants near border with Spain's Ceuta
News.content:
Tens of thousands of migrants have entered Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta, with many swimming and using inflatables to travel from Morocco.

Others ran through a gate in the border fence.

The territory's leader, Juan JesÃºs Vivas, said the number of arrivals has been overwhelming resources and urged the Spanish government to intervene.

Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez described the situation as an "attack" and said all illegal migrants would be returned to Morocco "as soon as possible".

Ceuta, on Morocco's northern coast, has long been a focal point for migrants attempting to reach Europe.

More than 25,000 have returned to Morocco voluntarily so far, officials said.

More on this story.

News.title: Fifa executive says staff 'deceived' by Infantino plans
News.content:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino's position came under further scrutiny on Friday as the governing body's chief operating officer strongly criticised his plan to sell stakes in competitions to private investors.

In a statement released to the Associated Press, Kevin Lamour described the controversial plans as "the project of one person" and said "the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions".

He added Fifa's own administration was "deceived" about the project. BBC Sport has approached Fifa for comment.

The lengthy statement did not mention Infantino by name.

It came on the same day a third confederation spoke out against the plans, a senior adviser to Infantino resigned, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the Swiss was "the wrong man" to lead Fifa.

US President Donald Trump - addressing the proposals for the first time - said he had not spoken to Infantino about the plans.

The two have developed a close relationship since Trump assumed office for a second time in 2025.

Lamour said in his statement: "Our mission - the mission of the hundreds of passionate, dedicated, and exemplary Fifa employees - is to serve football.

"A president must bring people together, unite them, and inspire them. Today, we are experiencing the opposite."

Lamour acknowledged he had a duty of loyalty to his employer but also to "certain values" and supporting his colleagues.

"If that means I lose my job, then so be it," he added. "I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."

News.title: No sentence long enough for jailed funeral director Robert Bush, say families
News.content:
Karen Dry, who organised monthly vigils for the victims' families when the investigation began, said: "No sentence was ever going to be enough."

She said families were hoping Bush would be sentenced to more than 30 years, but what was "really messing with people's heads" was the prospect of him only serving half of his sentence.

When asked does it feel fair? She replied: "No, it really doesn't.

"For some people, I totally get that today is the end of it for them.

"But I'm my mam and dad's daughter, and we are a bit more determined than just letting these things lie."

She said without regulation of the industry, "in five or 10 years' time there will be another funeral director with another 300 families in a courtroom somewhere".

"We've got to put a stop to it and it's got to stop now."

News.title: Israeli official says troops won't pull back in Gaza without 'genuine' Hamas disarmament
News.content:
A senior Israeli official has said troops will not pull back from their current positions in Gaza without the "genuine disarmament" of Palestinian armed group Hamas in the territory.

Hamas meanwhile said handing over its heavy weapons was contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.

It comes after Donald Trump said the Board of Peace had reached an agreement for the "complete disarmament" of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza.

On Friday Trump insisted that Israel was "very happy" with the proposed agreement, describing it as a "big step for the Middle East". However far-right Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir dismissed the draft as "not acceptable".

It is part of the second phase of a US-brokered Gaza ceasefire plan that aims to end the war in Gaza.

The 20-point plan, unveiled in September last year, included the creation of the Board of Peace to oversee the agreement's implementation, as well as the disarmament of Hamas, withdrawal of Israeli troops and reconstruction of Gaza.

Speaking at a cabinet meeting at Camp David on Friday, Trump said he had an "understanding" with Israel over the latest disarmament proposal agreed with Hamas, adding that "Israel's very happy about it".

Asked whether Hamas would disarm before Israeli forces withdrew from Gaza or vice versa, Trump did not answer directly but said Gaza remained "a very complex situation".

Hamas weapons would be handed over to the Board of Peace, he added.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has not yet commented on the latest proposal.

News.title: How Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's Rein Me In broke the UK's singles chart record
News.content:
This reworking of Rein Me In, from Fender's third studio album, the Mercury Prize-winning People Watching, features an extra verse about the breakdown of a relationship from a female perspective, from Dean.

"[It's] very personal and reminded us of home, but when Olivia put her touch on it, it became a much more universal track," he told Radio 1, adding "that's what made it so huge and so beautiful".

He said he wanted to "personally thank" Dean, who helped him achieve his first ever number one single, adding: "It wouldn't have happened without Olivia obviously, but now I feel like it belongs to the fans, they've made it what it is".

When asked how he'd be celebrating the achievement, Fender joked "I think I'm just gonna have a really big sandwich".

It hasn't been a straightforward ascent to the top for Rein Me In - originally released as a solo Fender track and repurposed as a duet in June 2025, it took eight months to reach number one in February this year.

Dean said when the track came out, external that the original version of Rein Me In was her "favourite song on Sam's album" and it was "a pleasure to write a new verse from a female perspective".

A lot of the song's success as a duet comes from its authenticity, with the lyrics exploring the fallout from the end of a relationship and the difficulties faced by both parties as they try to move on from each other.

Whilst Fender's verses feel full of anger and regret at not being able to open up and be the partner he wanted to be, they are complimented by the softer and more reflective tone of Dean's, in which she encourages him to try again to make it work.

It has been described by Blunt Magazine's Jake Fitzpatrick, external as "stormy, tender and anthemic" and a "love letter to the kind of songwriting that knows when to burn slow".

The song has also received praise amongst many critics and bloggers, including Cult Following's Ewan Gleadow, external, who says that Dean's addition helps it to find "a new depth", noting "charm is a big part of it too, with all those reflections on where you come from and where you're headed".

News.title: Two more small boat pilots jailed for Channel crossings
News.content:
Two men who piloted overcrowded small boats have been jailed for endangering others while crossing the Channel.

Omar Heidari, a 34-year-old Afghan national who steered a dinghy carrying 95 people to the UK in June, has been jailed for two years.

Manas Yuk, an 18-year-old Sudanese national, was sentenced to 18 months in youth detention after piloting a boat carrying 81 people - including a number of children - just days prior.

The men were sentenced at Canterbury Crown Court on Friday having earlier pleaded guilty to endangerment.

It means 10 people have now been sentenced under a law targeting those who risk the safety of others by piloting small boats since it came into force in January.

The Home Office said Heidari had endangered the largest number of lives of anyone so far sentenced for the offence.

The boat was overcrowded during the crossing on 23 June, with some passengers hanging their legs over the sides of the vessel, it said. A number of the passengers were not wearing life jackets.

He was jailed for endangering others as well as arriving in the UK without valid entry clearance.

News.title: Parents sue school over 'inhumane' calming rooms after BBC report
News.content:
Parents are suing a special school after a BBC investigation uncovered CCTV footage showing autistic children being locked inside calming rooms and abused.

Ten families are claiming that their children â all of whom had learning disabilities or several mental disorders - were amongst those harmed by their treatment in the rooms.

A police investigation into the abuse, recorded inside the rooms at Whitefield special school in north London, ended two years ago without any charges.

The school is now run by a new trust which says the failings have led to "important learning".

Many special schools use seclusion spaces such as calming rooms outside of classrooms to address sensory needs or challenging behaviour.

But the leaked footage obtained by the BBC showed children being shoved into padded rooms, thrown to the floor, restrained by the neck - or left alone, sitting in vomit.

One 12-year-old boy appeared in over 55 hours of CCTV footage filmed inside the rooms.

At the time, the Children's Commissioner for England, Dame Rachel de Souza, said the use of the rooms was "horrifying".

Leigh Day is now bringing a civil legal claim on behalf of 10 families against the trust which ran the school and the London borough of Waltham Forest.

The law firm says the use of the rooms was "barbaric", according to its clients. The claim alleges that children were falsely imprisoned and their human rights were breached.

"What was done to these children was profoundly harmful, and its impact continues to be felt by families every day", says Alison Millar, who is leading the case.

The CCTV obtained by the BBC had been recorded between 2014 and 2017 but only emerged in 2021.

Last month, a long-delayed review commissioned by Waltham Forest found that restraint and seclusion became "normalised" and a culture developed that allowed "pejorative views of non-compliant children".

It added that parents were clear that the practices were "unimaginable" and "inhumane".

The BBC has also found evidence of mistreatment in seclusion rooms at other schools across the UK.

CCTV from a different school showed a boy being "brutally" and "unlawfully" restrained, while elsewhere an autistic child was kept inside a cage.

News.title: Massive Attack banned from Singapore after pro-Palestine display at show
News.content:
Massive Attack have been banned from Singapore after the British band reportedly expressed pro-Palestinian sentiments during a performance in the city-state.

The band's two members held up a Palestinian flag at the show on Wednesday and shouted "free Palestine", authorities said, with some in the audience reportedly joining them.

Singapore's police force has now banned Massive Attack from future entry into the country, while its media regulator simultaneously said it would not grant future applications for them to perform there.

The Asian nation has strict rules on public speech and what it deems as demonstrations, arguing that it is necessary to regulate them to protect social harmony.

Authorities have previously investigated public events related to the Israel-Gaza war. Earlier this year, they fined several people for organising an unauthorised walk in support of the Palestinian cause.

A police spokeswoman told the BBC that following an investigation the two band members had been issued "stern warnings" concerning alleged offences under Section 3 of the Foreign National Emblems (Control of Display) Act 1949 and Section 16 of the Public Order Act.

The two laws ban the display of foreign flags in public in most cases and set conditions on public events of a political nature, respectively.

The spokeswoman said Singapore's police "take a serious view of acts which could potentially harm the racial and religious harmony in Singapore".

"The peace and harmony between different races and religions in Singapore should not be taken for granted, and we must not let external events affect our society," she added.

Massive Attack is currently on a world tour, with Wednesday's performance their only date in Singapore. Their next show is due to be held in Seoul on Saturday.

The band, which pioneered the trip-hop genre, has long been known for its openly political stance on a number of issues, including the war in Gaza.

Massive Attack's frontman Robert Del Naja was arrested earlier this year when he took part in a demonstration in London. He was accused of showing support for Palestine Action, which is a proscribed organisation in the UK.

News.title: Disgraced funeral boss who failed to bury bodies jailed for 20 years
News.content:
This story contains details some might find distressing.

The court heard Bush defrauded nearly 200 families out of Â£562,117 and had acted out of "financial greed".

Hilliard warned that unless a body was one of those recovered by police in 2024 and properly identified, no-one who had used Legacy's cremations services "at any time can be absolutely certain they received the ashes of their loved one".

"He must have a heartless side to him - which allowed him to treat the living and the dead in the way he did, and he was very confident he would get away with what he was doing."

The judge added: "I don't think I have ever known offences affecting so many people and so deeply."

The court was told relatives of 46 people who were cremated between 2017 and 2024 were given the wrong ashes and the loved ones of another 11 never received any.

"How betrayed they now feel," said the judge.

"Husbands and wives, partners, parents, children, grandchildren, now discovering that they are left with nothing, or in some cases we heard, an empty plastic bag or a teaspoonful of ash which the police managed to recover for them."

News.title: Southport killer charged with prison attacks and possessing weapon
News.content:
Southport killer Axel Rudakubana has been charged with three attacks while in prison and possessing a weapon.

Police say the offences took place at HMP Belmarsh over six months from May to October 2025.

The 19-year-old murdered Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, Bebe King, six, and Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, and injured eight other children and two adults in an attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in July 2024.

He was given a 52-year sentence in January 2025. Earlier this month he was moved to a secure psychiatric hospital.

Rudakubana is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court remotely on 11 September.

He has been charged with the following four offences:

Assault on an emergency worker on 6 May 2025

Attempted grievous bodily harm on 8 May 2025

Unauthorised possession of an offensive weapon in prison on 26 June 2025

Assault on an emergency worker on 28 October 2025

In May 2025, it was reported boiling water had been thrown on a prison officer at Belmarsh. They were taken to hospital and discharged on the same day.

When Rudakubana was jailed, the judge was unable to impose a whole life order due to him being under-18 when he carried out the attack. He will likely never be released.

On 23 July, the MoJ confirmed Rudakubana was transferred from HMP Belmarsh to Broadmoor, a high-security psychiatric hospital in Berkshire.

Under the Mental Health Act, the MoJ is likely to have had no choice but to accept doctors' recommendations about whether Rudakubana could be held safely in prison.

The decision to transfer him was criticised by a lawyer representing the families of victims.

News.title: Puberty blockers trial can start recruiting children after judge rejects legal challenge
News.content:
A high-profile clinical trial of drugs that can delay puberty in children questioning their gender can go ahead after the High Court rejected a legal challenge by campaigners.

The Pathways trial, run by researchers at King's College London (KCL), will start recruiting more than 220 children aged between 11 and 16 years old from 1 August.

The study was commissioned to assess the benefits or risks of puberty blockers, after a landmark review into gender services found the evidence for treating young people with the drugs was "remarkably weak".

Campaigners who brought the legal action had argued the safeguards in place were inadequate and raised concerns about the long-term physical and psychological effects on young people.

The judge, Mr Justice Chamberlain, refused the application for a judicial review saying that none of the claims made by the campaigners had a realistic chance of success.

He said that each patient involved in the trial will have been assessed over "many months" by specialist doctors who will have "formed the opinion that a child has a reasonable prospect of receiving a clinical benefit from the treatment".

A spokeswoman for KCL welcomed the court's decision, saying the "safety and welfare of young people will remain our highest priority in carrying out this research".

Campaigners, including parents of gender-questioning children, said they were disappointed by the decision saying the "world is watching" a case which has "global implications and high stakes".

News.title: Andy Burnham to give regional mayors share of income tax
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will give all mayors of city regions in England a share of income tax revenue for the first time, as part of his drive to transfer power from Westminster to local leaders.

Burnham will also allow English strategic authorities to keep some cash from business rates collected in their areas, and gain greater control over services such as housing, transport, skills.

The government has not yet decided the exact portion of taxes mayors will get, with more details to be announced when Chancellor John Healey delivers his first budget in the autumn.

Opposition parties said the plans lacked detail and could lead to areas with weaker economies losing out on funding.

But Burnham said the move would "make good" on his pledge to "bring power home" to "every postcode in the country".

"Under our plans, more of the taxes raised in a community will stay in that community," the prime minister added.

First Secretary of State Louise Haigh told BBC Radio 4's Today programme areas without mayors would also benefit from investment because devolution powers would be held by new strategic authorities across England.

Strategic authorities bring together local councils to control regional issues such as transport and economic development, with decisions taken collectively by council leaders rather than a single elected mayor.

But Labour backbencher Perran Moon said the government's plans were "discriminatory" and could create a "two-tier system".

The MP for Camborne and Redruth in Cornwall said the area would never have a mayor or become a combined authority and so risked not having access to devolved powers that other areas would have.

"What we're asking government to do is to provide us with the same powers, the same funding that mayoral combined authorities have without the requirement of becoming a combined authority or having a mayor."

The government has also announced that mayors will be given a fast-track route to building new tramways, roads and light rail in their areas.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said the threshold at which local leaders need to seek approval for projects will rise to Â£500m, up from Â£200m.

News.title: England and Wales on course for driest July on record
News.content:
England and Wales are on course for their driest July since records began 190 years ago.

The Met Office reports that England has seen just 5.6mm of rainfall up to 30 July â just 8% of its long-term meteorological average for the month and less than half of the previous record of 13.4mm set in 1911.

For Wales it is 7.9mm of rainfall, also 8% of its long-term average for the month and almost a third of the previous record of 22.6mm, again set in 1911.

The UK as a whole is currently on track for its third driest July, and driest nationally since 1868.

News.title: Budget to be held in October, Healey announces
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey has announced the date of his first Budget will be Wednesday, 28 October.

In aâ¯video message,â¯ he said: "This will be a Budget that moves money and power out of Westminster, and into every postcode around Britain.

"It will be built on fiscal discipline. It will meet our fiscal rules. It'll give businesses and families some of the stability they need to plan for the future. Now, let's get on with the job."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said his government will stick to Labour's fiscal rules on spending and borrowing as well as the party's 2024 manifesto pledges not to increase income tax, VAT or national insurance contributions.

Burnham also said he will honour the fiscal rules imposed by Healey's predecessor Rachel Reeves, which include a pledge to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues by the end of the decade.

An influential think tank said earlier this week that the prime minister only has a small margin of error to do this, and that Healey may have to cut spending or raise taxes to meet Burnham's policy priorities such as such as extra defence spending and better social care.

Healey was Defence Secretary under Keir Starmer, but resigned after a row over defence spending commitments - saying he was "certain" that Britain shouldl lift its spending to 3% by 2030.

But questioned about funding on Thursday, Burnham's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting repeatedly refused to commit to that target.

"Before we set out specific spending commitments, we will also set out how we pay for them at the same time," he said.

News.title: Sainsbury's agrees to sell Argos for £120m
News.content:
Sainsbury's has agreed to sell Argos for Â£120m after a long process of trying to offload it as the supermarket chain aims to focus on its main food business.

Sainsbury's said it would be "business as usual" for Argos customers, staff, and suppliers. Shoppers will see no change as Argos will still operate in Sainsbury's shops, sell Habitat products, and offer Nectar points.

The buyer, Swift Partners, is a company that has been created to buy the brand and includes former Co-operative Group boss Richard Pennycook.

There are 667 Argos shops across the UK, with 201 operating as standalone stores and 466 operating within Sainsbury's. It also has more than 450 collection points.

Founded in 1973, Argos opened shops where customers browsed its catalogues and placed their orders, with products being delivered to tills from warehouses connected to the stores.

The Argos catalogue, once described by comedian Bill Bailey as the "laminated book of dreams", used to be a physical book.

Argos no longer prints this hefty tome, with its full range now available online instead. In store, customers can browse the product collection on tablet computers.

Sainsbury's has been trying to sell Argos - which has been seen as an underperforming brand - for some time.

Sainsbury's bought Argos â together with Habitat and all the other retail brands owned by Home Retail Group â in 2016 for Â£1.4bn. It then sold Argos financial services, which runs the Argos card, for around Â£720m in 2024.

In September last year, its talks to sell the rest of Argos to Chinese online retailer JD.com fell through.

Sainsbury's chief executive Simon Roberts said that all of Argos's nearly 14,000 staff would be transferred over to Swift Partners as part of the deal.

He also confirmed that Argos would continue to operate in Sainsbury's shops; Nectar will continue to be used across both Argos and Sainsbury's; and Sainsbury's will continue to sell Habitat products

Swift Partners' Pennycook said he believed "strongly in Argos's future and see real opportunities to invest and build on its progress".

The deal is expected to be completed in February next year.

Pennycook said there was the potential to open new standalone Argos shops â and did not rule out the possibility of the return of its print catalogue.

News.title: Passenger on British Airways mayday flight describes fear and shout of 'I don't want to die'
News.content:
A passenger on a British Airways flight that issued a distress call on approach to Heathrow Airport earlier this month has described the rising fear in the cabin and a lack of information from the crew.

Edward Killiwick had been travelling back from a friend's birthday party with his partner Julie, on the flight from Dusseldorf in Germany on 6 July.

He said passengers were told that the landing had been aborted, and then he felt a "very violent manoeuvre" and "did think we could crash". He and his partner had to comfort a woman who "completely lost it and started screaming, 'I don't want to die'".

The flight landed safely, but the incident is being investigated with assistance from BA.

The UK's Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) said it was "investigating a serious incident", and France's accident investigation authority, the BEA, said on Wednesday that the plane, an Airbus A320, had issued a distress call.

Edward said: "The violent manoeuvre almost felt like it was avoiding another aircraft. You could feel the engines going at full power.

"It was a bit odd going around in a holding pattern with no information. I thought if they're not talking, then they're not in a good place."

He said they were in a holding pattern for about 15 minutes.

The BEA said that as the plane approached Heathrow, there was a data system failure which triggered a stall warning.

The crew then flew the aircraft in a different mode called "alternate law", which removes some automated flight protection systems. Another stall warning then occurred at 3,000 feet â which experts say was likely to have been just miles away from the airport.

The urgency call the crew had already made was upgraded to mayday, indicating imminent danger.

A British Airways spokesperson said the airline was assisting the AAIB with its investigation and was not legally able to comment further at this stage.

Edward said: "I was definitely scared. After the violent manoeuvre I thought, there is definitely something very badly wrong here. I did think we could crash.

"I did think it was a possibility, and I think everyone else did."

News.title: Read the ransom notes from Nancy Guthrie’s ‘kidnappers’ who apologized for her death
News.content:
The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

Arizona authorities have finally released the ransom notes that appear to be from Nancy Guthrie’s kidnappers, who claimed they didn’t fully understand her failing health and apologized for her death.

Nancy, the 84-year-old mother of Today show star Savannah Guthrie, vanished from her home in the Catalina Foothills outside of Tucson six months ago. As local and federal authorities continued to search for Nancy, it slowly became apparent that police may be trying to recover a dead body, rather than trying to rescue the elderly mother from her captors.

Public speculation appeared to be confirmed Friday after the Pima County Sheriff’s Department released ransom notes sent to the Guthries days after Nancy was taken from her home as she slept in the early morning hours of February 1.

While the existence of the ransom notes was made public after they were sent to news outlets early in the investigation, this is the first time they’ve been released in what appears to be a desperate attempt from investigators to find new leads and close the case once and for all.

open image in gallery Arizona authorities have finally released the ransom notes that appear to be from Nancy Guthrie’s kidnappers, who were unaware of her failing health and apologized for her death ( NBC/Today )

The first ransom note that local CBS affiliate KOLD-TV 13 News received on February 2 was addressed to Savannah.

“We have your mother Nancy. She is safe but scared. She will be held for ransom and once payment is received she will be released unharmed. We will be holding her for a maximum of 7 days,” the note read.

The author of the note then gave specific instructions for an exchange of the cryptocurrency Bitcoin for Nancy’s safe return.

“You will need to send bitcoin in the amount of $4 million USD before 5PM on Thursday the 5th. If payment is not received, the ransom will be increased to 6 million USD which will need to be paid by 5PM on Monday the 9th.

“Once payment is received to the bitcoin address below she will be released within 12 hours of deposit to a safe drop off location back in Tucson. If payment is not recieved by the last deadline on Monday the 9th at 5PM, she will be killed,” the note read.

open image in gallery It’s been six months since Savannah Guthrie’s elderly mother was taken from her Arizona home in the middle of the night ( Getty Images )

The author warned Savannah not to “play games” with Nancy’s life.

“Your mother is aware of this and her life is in your hands. It is in the best interest of everyone to have this completed as soon as possible. You will not be able to contact me from here on out, there will be no negotiation. Do not play games, law enforcement will not be able to help you,” the note read.

Another note was sent to KOLD-TV 13 News on February 6, giving the grim news that Nancy had died while being held captive.

“We did not fully grasp the seriousness of her physical condition. We never intended to hurt her, that was not our intention. She perished shortly after she was taken. We believe it was heart related,” the note read.

“She is buried in nature now. Nothing you could have done could have changed the outcome. We want your family to know this and hope you all can find peace. We are truly sorry.”

open image in gallery One of the ransom notes demands $4 million in Bitcoin for Nancy’s safe return ( Getty Images )

Authorities had said early on in the case that Nancy had a pacemaker, a device that regulates the heart’s rhythm, that was disconnected from an app on her phone when she went missing.

Nancy’s children had voiced concern for their mother’s health in a social media video in early February.

“Her health, her heart is fragile. She lives in constant pain. She is without any medicine. She needs it to survive. She needs it not to suffer,” Savannah said at the time.

Savannah admitted in a later video that her mother may have died.

“We still believe in a miracle. We still believe that she can come home,” the visibly distraught TV journalist said. “We also know that she may be lost. She may already be gone. She may have already gone home to the Lord that she loves.”

open image in gallery ‘Tell us where to look for her,’ Savannah pleaded in a new social media video ( Instagram/@savannahguthrie via Reuters )

With the release of the ransom notes, the Pima County Sheriff’s Department is hopeful it will get more tips from people who may know the author.

“These communications reveal distinctive patterns of word choice, syntax, and phraseology that reflect the writer’s unique linguistic style,” the sheriff’s department said in a statement. “They also provide valuable insight into the person’s mindset, motives, and the evolution of their tone over time.”

While Savannah returned to the Today show in April, she and her family are still “in agony,” as the TV host put it in a new Instagram video, calling the situation “a nightmare that will not end.”

“We have done our part,” Savannah said. “We will never stop looking for her.”

Seemingly talking directly to Nancy’s kidnappers, Savannah then said, “I know that you’ve tried to do things the right way, so I’m asking you, begging you to do the right thing now.”

“Tell us where to look for her,” Savannah said. “Help us bring this situation to an end.”

News.title: Revolving door at 10 Downing St. is harming ‘special relationship’ between UK and US
News.content:
