World.title: Spain's legal dilemma behind Ceuta's record migrant arrivals
World.content:
Ceuta has seen its highest number of migrant arrivals in five years. According to Spain's Interior Ministry, around 50,000 people from Morocco, Algeria and sub-Saharan Africa have entered the Spanish enclave since Thursday, most by swimming around the southern breakwater at Tarajal beach. By Friday afternoon, around 48,000 had already returned to Morocco voluntarily.

 

Behind the bottleneck are two legal issues that have collided at the worst possible moment. The first stems from a case dating back several years, in which an Algerian migrant challenged his summary return to Morocco, arguing that he had entered Ceuta by swimming rather than by breaching the border fence or climbing over razor wire.

Ceuta's court, followed by the High Court of Andalusia and ultimately the Supreme Court, all ruled in his favour, establishing a key legal precedent: migrants who arrive by swimming do not "cross a border containment element", a legal requirement for carrying out summary returns without first opening an individual case file under Spain's Aliens Act. In practice, this means a large proportion of those now crossing at Tarajal cannot be immediately returned under that mechanism.

The second legal development is more recent. On 8 July, the Supreme Court (STS 868/2026) struck down several provisions of the 2024 Aliens Regulation, including one that had weakened the authorities' obligation to provide immediate care to unaccompanied foreign minors found on Spanish territory.

The ruling strengthens, rather than weakens, protections for migrant children. However, Vivas has described it as an additional obstacle to managing the arrival of unaccompanied minors and has openly called to "legalise" summary returns in their case.

On that basis, Ceuta's government has backed a bill tabled by the People's Party (PP) in Congress to amend the tenth additional provision of the Aliens Act. The proposed reform would explicitly extend the special border rejection regime to anyone attempting to enter Ceuta or Melilla irregularly through any unauthorised point, whether by land or by sea.

The stated aim is to provide legal certainty for the Civil Guard, whose unions, including the AUGC, have for weeks been calling for a clearer legal framework so officers can act without being caught between judicial rulings and mounting pressure at the border.

The 2011 migration crisis left images like this AP Photo

A divided political debate

The proposal is also opposed by organisations including Coordinadora de Barrios, No Name Kitchen and the Jesuit Migrant Service, which represent some of the migrants affected by returns without due process. They argue that the reform would undermine individual safeguards, particularly for unaccompanied minors.

The PP's bill is still at an early stage, and its passage through Congress could take months while pressure at Tarajal shows no sign of easing.

Any reform directly affecting the status of unaccompanied minors will also have to contend with the line of case law reaffirmed by the Supreme Court on 8 July, raising the prospect of further legal challenges if the bill is approved in its current form. Underlying the debate is the need to ensure any changes comply with the European Pact on Migration and Asylum, a balance that neither Ceuta nor Madrid has yet managed to strike.

The stories behind the border: who is crossing and how

The entrance to the CETI offers a different, more intimate view of the crisis. As reported by El Mundo, the road leading to the centre's entrance has become a makeshift camp, with families lying along the roadside under Red Cross blankets and improvised shelters made of sheets, cardboard and branches. At the gates of the facility, dozens of men queue to wash, kneeling beneath a street tap.

Among them is Mohamed, a 23-year-old Moroccan from Nador, whose testimony was reported by El Mundo. Mohamed said he spent 12 hours travelling by bus to Castillejos before swimming across to Tarajal in the early hours, without flippers, a wetsuit or a flotation device, enduring extreme cold during the crossing.

Mohamed spent three years living in Barcelona and speaks fluent Spanish. He said he had returned to Morocco two weeks earlier to visit his family and, lacking the necessary documents, chose to make the journey back via the irregular route. He cited the lack of opportunities and hunger in his country as the reasons for making the crossing.

Across the border, in Castillejos, El Faro de Ceuta reports that the Moroccan authorities have closed off part of the seafront promenade in an attempt to stop people, particularly minors, from entering the water. The metal fences erected there are easily bypassed, while buses carrying those intercepted take them further south, mainly towards the Sahara. According to the same outlet, a mother and her three children nearly drowned on Tuesday while attempting the crossing.

World.title: Inside Ceuta: Residents face fear and uncertainty as migrant numbers soar; bread is scarce, shops are closed
World.content:
The autonomous city of Ceuta has ground to a halt following the mass arrival of migrants from Morocco. Most shops remained closed on Friday, fresh bread was becoming difficult to find and the Ceuta government suspended this weekend's patron saint festivities as authorities struggled to regain control of the situation.

 

As AFP observed on the ground, the usual bustle of the central Calle Real has given way to groups of migrants gathered in the streets, while the shutters of many businesses remain down. In the city centre, home to around 84,000 people, only a handful of pharmacies and a restaurant belonging to a well-known chain were open.

The Ceuta Business Confederation has advised shops and other businesses not to reopen "until security can be guaranteed", amid continuing uncertainty and the deployment of additional security forces.

Health sector sources contacted by Euronews said medical services were under severe pressure despite reinforcements being called in. The most common cases being treated include hypothermia, anxiety attacks and fractures.

"We are running out of bread. There was no fresh bread today because the bakeries are closed," municipal street sweeper Miguel Ángel Campana told AFP. He said some residents feared migrants could try to enter homes "asking for water and other things" and urged neighbours to "keep an eye on their balconies". Across the city, migrants could be seen stopping passing vehicles to ask for food, money or to borrow mobile phones to contact their families.

Migrants rest outside the Temporary Immigrant Centre (CETI) after crossing from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on 31 July 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Local authorities estimate that around 60,000 people have crossed irregularly from Morocco into Ceuta since the early hours of Thursday, many swimming around the border breakwater. The Spanish government says more than 37,500 have already returned to Morocco.

Police have been directing large groups of migrants, many of them young people, towards the border crossing to facilitate their return. The crisis has also triggered an intense political and diplomatic response, with the army deployed in Ceuta and several European countries criticising the way the situation has been handled.

"It remains a heartbreaking situation from a humanitarian point of view, seeing so many people with nowhere to go, without food or water, because the few services available for them are completely overwhelmed," a Ceuta resident interviewed by Euronews said.

At the same time, concern among residents is growing.Mohammed, a taxi driver from Ceuta, believes many migrants have decided to return to Morocco after seeing the conditions awaiting them in the city."They thought they knew what they were going to find here and they have been confronted with reality," he told AFP. Some had told him they were returning "because they had no food".

"There is nothing here. Those of us who are from here are struggling to get by. We are having a hard time," he added.

Mohammed said he and other neighbours stayed awake until the early hours of the morning for fear of possible robberies. "I have nieces who are afraid," he said.

That sense of unease is shared by 56-year-old Yolanda Moreno, who said she had felt "afraid from the start" of the migration crisis. "It was like during the pandemic: the feeling that it was better to stay at home than to go out onto the streets," she told AFP.

Another resident interviewed by Euronews also expressed concern that tensions could escalate, saying people increasingly feared violence. "This morning I was shocked to see people from here, from the neighbourhood, with lots of knives, trying to take justice into their own hands," she said. "I just saw one boy with a katana running after a Moroccan boy, without really knowing what was going on."

The scale of the crisis has forced the Ceuta government to cancel the patron saint festivities that were due to begin on Saturday. At the fairground, rides remain covered with tarpaulins and motionless — a striking symbol of a city whose normal rhythm has been brought to a halt as it struggles to cope with one of the largest migrant arrivals in its history.

World.title: Wildfire breaks out near Athens, prompting evacuation alerts
World.content:
A wildfire has broken out in a forested area in Aspropyrgos, west of Athens, prompting evacuation alerts and a major firefighting response.

 

According to the fire service, the blaze broke out at around 15:29 in forest land on the slopes of Mount Poikilo, in the Aspropyrgos area, and is moving south.

Firefighting forces have been reinforced. A total of 108 firefighters are operating at the scene with six ground teams from the 1st EMODE special wildfire unit and 27 vehicles. Five aircraft and six helicopters have also been deployed for aerial firefighting, one of them for coordination.

Related Crete wildfire kills two firefighters as fierce flames spread in Greece

Water tankers from the municipalities of Aspropyrgos, Fyli, Petroupoli and Peristeri are also assisting. In total, two messages have been issued via the 112 emergency alert system: the first at 16:03 informing people in the wider area about the fire, and the second at 16:22 calling on those in Afaia Haidariou and Ano Dasos Haidariou to move towards Peristeri via Athinon Avenue.

An earlier alert issued via the 112 emergency alert system had called on people in the wider area to remain on standby.

The fire service said the area is classified as Category 4 today, indicating a very high risk of wildfires, while the Western Attica Arson Crimes Investigation Unit has been activated to investigate the cause of the blaze.

Throughout the operation, the Fire Service's Operations Coordination Centre (ESKEDIK) has been receiving continuous imagery from a drone equipped with thermal and optical cameras.

World.title: Migrants in Ceuta cannot move to other countries, EU says
World.content:
The European Commission said on Friday that no irregular migrants have moved from Ceuta to the European mainland.

 

While the sudden migration crisis in the Spanish enclave has sent shockwaves across Europe and prompted calls to suspend Spain from the Schengen free-movement area, EU officials insist that migrants who crossed the border irregularly will not headto other member states.

"There are no onward movements today towards the European continent," an EU official said, claiming that migrants will not be able to freely move through Europe, as someleading right-of-centre figures across Europe are suggesting.

Around 60,000 migrants, mostly Moroccans, stormed the Spanish enclave in Africa on Thursday in the largest surge of irregular arrivals ever recorded on EU territory. Rather than expressing solidarity, several EU countries—including Italy, Finland and Denmark—accused the government of Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez of failing to adequately protect Europe's external borders.

Although Ceuta is Spanish territory, it is subject to special rules governing free movement. "Checks on people leaving Ceuta and Melilla remain in place under the Schengen system. For this purpose, they are treated as the EU's external border," a European Commission official said.

Schengen’s free-movement rules also apply only to EU citizens, people with valid residence permits, and travellers who meet the conditions for legal entry.

By contrast, people who enter Ceuta without authorisation cannot board ferries or flights to mainland Spain without first undergoing identity checks, making it difficult for them to leave the enclave.

If an irregular migrant applies for asylum, detention measures may be applied through an accelerated asylum procedure that entered into force last June.

Pending a decision on their asylum claims, applicants are not permitted to leave Spain and are liable to be returned if they are found elsewhere in the European Union.

Only beneficiaries of international protection enjoy the right to move across the Schengen area, but Morocco is considered a “safe country of origin” under EU rules and its citizens are in principle not eligible for protection.

According to the EU Agency for Asylum, Moroccan citizens have a very low recognition rate (6%), meaning that the vast majority of those who crossed into Ceuta are expected to receive return orders to their country of origin.

According to the Spanish authorities, nearly half of the people who entered Ceuta on Thursday have already voluntarily returned to Morocco.

World.title: Liberia sacks officials after record cocaine seizures worth $336 million
World.content:
Liberian President Joseph Boakai has sacked a dozen government officials and referred several others for investigation after a series of major drug seizures prompted public calls for tougher action.

 

A statement released late on Thursday said the dismissals included airport operations staff and senior law enforcement supervisors.

Earlier this month, Liberian authorities seized nearly four tonnes of cocaine worth an estimated $317 million (€277 million) near Roberts International Airport.

It followed another major seizure in June, when about 238 kilograms of cocaine worth an estimated $19 million (€16.5 million) was found hidden among ordinary commercial cargo, including Maggi seasoning cubes, at the airport.

The President ordered "the immediate dismissal, suspension and investigation of several officials of government and law enforcement personnel following his review of the latest status report on ongoing investigations into major narcotics trafficking cases".

Those dismissed included the airport's deputy director for operations, the police commissioner for criminal investigation, intelligence and Interpol, and the deputy director for administration at the National Security Agency (NSA).

The statement added that Boakai had also dismissed "all government employees and law enforcement officers indicted" in connection with the two major drug seizures. Those individuals were the airport's director of security and the deputy commander of the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency at the airport, it said.

He also dismissed four employees from the National Security Agency (NSA) and the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, referring their cases to the Ministry of Justice for prosecution.

Following the initial airport drug seizure in June, Boakai launched a coordinated investigation to ensure that "every individual found responsible is fully accountable under the law".

According to the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, West Africa is a key transit hub for cocaine bound for Europe.

Several hundred protesters additionally took to the streets of Monrovia two weeks ago demanding quick action and rapid charges, in a protest organised by the civic group stand.

World.title: Italy suspends Schengen with Spain over Ceuta migrant crisis, closes air and sea borders
World.content:
Italy's Interior Ministry has ordered the closure of the country's sea and air borders with Spain, temporarily suspending the Schengen free movement regime between the two countries.

 

The move was announced on Thursday evening by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Deputy Prime Ministers Antonio Tajani and Matteo Salvini following the arrival of thousands of migrants in the Spanish North African enclave of Ceuta.

"The temporary suspension of Schengen with Spain is a necessary choice to safeguard the security of our citizens and defend the European borders. A measure provided for by the treaties and made unavoidable today," Tajani wrote on X.

"The migrant crisis in Ceuta reminds us that the management of the Union’s borders is a shared responsibility among our countries, one toward the other. We must work together to prevent uncontrolled migrant flows from entering EU territory, with all the consequent risks and the threat of terrorism, which must be countered without hesitation."

The decision was formally approved on Friday morning during a meeting at the Interior Ministry chaired by Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi, based on assessments by Italy's Committee for Migration Analysis and Border Security.

France has also decided to strengthen controls along its land border with Spain, President Emmanuel Macron announced, while offering support to the Spanish authorities to help manage the emergency in the North African enclave.

Spain and the EU react

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez hit back at Italy on X, arguing that "solidarity and empathy are optional. Respect for European treaties and the facts is not." He cited Frontex figures showing that Italy recorded more irregular entries than Spain between 2021 and 2026 and called for "a strong and united European Union."

On Thursday evening, Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares condemned his Italian counterpart Antonio Tajani's call to suspend the Schengen agreement and summoned Italy's ambassador to Madrid for explanations.

According to Italy's ANSA news agency, Spain's Foreign Ministry stressed that the migration crisis in Ceuta "has nothing to do with the regularisation of migrants approved by the Spanish government", but was instead triggered by an interpretation of the recent Supreme Court ruling on migrants who entered by swimming, which was "exploited by mafias and criminal organisations".

By Friday, however, several EU countries had moved closer to Italy's position, including Finland, the Netherlands, Denmark, the Czech Republic and Sweden.

"Spain has completely failed to protect the external border of the Schengen area from incursions. This cannot continue," Finnish Interior Minister Mari Rantanen wrote on X.

"The situation in Ceuta is unacceptable and I am in close contact with the Spanish authorities. I reiterate that there are no movements towards mainland Europe or other member states," European Commissioner for Home Affairs Magnus Brunner wrote on X.

"The Schengen Borders Code," Brunner added, "contains special provisions that apply to Ceuta and Melilla, and checks on people departing from Ceuta remain in force."

Against the backdrop of an election campaign ahead of next year's general election, the proposal to suspend Schengen has sparked intense political debate in Italy and drawn praise from several European far-right parties, including France's National Rally, Germany's Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the UK's Reform UK.

World.title: Trump calls Ceuta migrant surge 'terrible' as White House blames far left
World.content:
US President Donald Trump on Friday used the mass migrant crossings into Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta to warn Americans that the United States could face a similar situation if Democrats return to power, as the crisis also fuelled fresh political tensions in Europe.

 

"It's terrible. Remember that picture. That's going to be us in three years if the wrong side gets in," Trump told Fox News. "If the Democrats get in, you will not live a very good life."

Trump, who has made immigration a central pillar of his presidency, used the events in Ceuta to reinforce his long-standing argument for stricter border controls.

The White House blamed "far-left globalist policies" for the situation in Ceuta, where at least 43 people have died, many while attempting to swim from Morocco to the Spanish enclave.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez travelled to Ceuta on Friday, blaming people-smuggling networks for the mass crossings and saying their actions "deserve our reproach and our condemnation in the strongest possible terms".

According to Spain's Interior Ministry, around 37,500 people who entered Ceuta irregularly since Thursday have already been returned to Morocco.

The European Union has stressed that no migrant crossings from Ceuta to the Iberian Peninsula have been recorded. "There are no migratory movements towards the European continent," a senior EU official said on Friday.

Fresh tensions with Washington

The latest developments risk opening another front in the often strained relationship between Washington and Madrid, only weeks after Trump and Sánchez appeared to ease tensions during the FIFA World Cup final in New Jersey on 19 July.

Their main disagreement remains defence spending. Spain continues to reject NATO's target of spending 5% of GDP on defence, which Sánchez has described as "unreasonable and counterproductive". Trump has repeatedly demanded that European allies increase military spending and has warned the United States could reconsider its commitment to NATO if they fail to do so.

Musk joins criticism

Elon Musk also weighed in on the events in Ceuta with a series of posts on X.

In one post, he compared footage of migrants climbing into the enclave to a scene from the zombie film World War Z, writing: "Wow, the situation in Spain looks crazy!"

Hours later, Musk described the post as "a joke" before sharing another video of migrants arriving in Ceuta alongside footage from the US-Mexico border during Joe Biden's presidency, writing: "This was the United States under Biden."

World.title: DR Congo Ebola outbreak becomes world's second-largest ever
World.content:
DR Congo’s fast-spreading Ebola outbreak has exceeded 3,500 cases, overtaking the country’s deadliest epidemic and becoming the world’s second-largest ever. The Bundibugyo strain has no approved vaccine or treatment.

The Democratic Republic of Congo's (DRC) latest Ebola outbreak has surpassed the total number of cases recorded during the country's deadliest epidemic between 2018 and 2020.

That epidemic killed nearly 2,300 people among about 3,500 infections.

Congolese officials said on Friday that in this year's outbreak 3,532 Ebola cases, including 1,556 deaths, have now been confirmed across five provinces.

Second-Largest Ebola Outbreak on Record

The outbreak has grown into the world's second-largest Ebola epidemic.

"It's the fastest-spreading Ebola epidemic that we have ever seen," said Carl Skau, acting executive director of the UN World Food Programme told ​Reuters.

"The world needs to pay much more attention," he added.

The outbreak has proven unusually deadly, killing five times more people in its first three months than previous Ebola outbreaks had by the same stage, according to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention.

Only the 2014-16 West Africa outbreak was bigger, with 28,616 cases reported across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), Ebola is a severe and often fatal disease that spreads from infected animals and through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people.

Experimental vaccines raise hope

The outbreak is being caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which no approved vaccine or treatment currently exists.

However, vaccine research is gaining momentum — the WHO has described a vaccine being developed by Singapore-based Hilleman Laboratories as the most promising candidate against the outbreak.

A separate Bundibugyo vaccine is also under development by the University of Oxford. Last week, the first volunteer received a dose as part of an ongoing clinical trial.

In DRC, fighting Ebola means fighting misinformation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ebola Spreads Amid Conflict and Instability

The outbreak is centred in Ituri province in northeastern DR Congo, near the borders with South Sudan and Uganda.

Health officials say the true scale of the epidemic remains unclear.

Since the outbreak was declared, cases have risen rapidly. Confirmed infections increased from 2,000 on July 15 to more than 3,500 within weeks.

The virus has also spread to four other provinces. These include North Kivu and South Kivu, where large areas are controlled by the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group.

DR Congo is grappling with ongoing instability in its eastern regions, where conflict involving the M23 rebel group continues despite peace efforts.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

World.title: UK court allows plans for Chinese 'super' embassy to advance
World.content:
A court dismissed a legal challenge against Beijing's new embassy in London, which could become the largest in the UK. The case, brought by a neighborhood association, argued the embassy poses a security threat.

A UK High Court on Friday threw out a challenge against UK authorities' decision to permit a new Chinese super embassy in central London.

The challenge was brought by a neighborhood group called the Royal Mint Court Residents' Association (RMCRA), which represents families and businesses in roughly 100 properties around the planned embassy site.

What was the court case about?

The RMCRA argued the presence of the embassy could increase the risk of terrorist attacks, lead to the targeting of dissidents and be used to enforce "draconian" Chinese laws in the UK.

The association also claimed that the embassy could pose a fire risk, arguing that Chinese authorities might ignore safety obligations that would be difficult to enforce because of diplomatic immunity on the embassy site.

On that basis, the group argued the development should not have been approved by the UK government as well as the London Borough of Tower Hamlets.

Yet in its ruling on Friday, the High Court said the "RMCRA ​did not produce reasonable ⁠and convincing evidence of the likelihood that a violation of human rights ⁠affecting them ​personally would occur."

In a move that was widely seen as a goodwill gesture toward Beijing, the embassy received approval from the UK government shortly before then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer visited China in January this year.

Plans for Beijing's super embassy have drawn opposition and protests from nearby residents and diaspora groups (file photo) Image: David Cliff/NurPhoto/picture alliance

What makes a 'super embassy'?

If completed, the new Chinese embassy would be the largest embassy in the UK.

Beijing plans to build the embassy on the site of the former Royal Mint, next to the Tower of London. The site covers around 20,000 square meters (235,000 square feet).

Beijing purchased the property in 2018 for a reported $327 million (€283.9 million), with the intent of relocating its embassy there from its current premises in Portland Place.

London's new China super embassy — a threat to HK activists? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

RMCRA vows to continue fight

In response to the verdict, the RMCRA said it would seek permission to appeal, hoping to take the case to the UK Supreme Court.

"Beijing thinks this judgment is the final word. It isn't. The appeal is already in the works," Luke Pollard, head of the RMCRA, said in a statement.

Opposition to the project extends far beyond local residents.

Activists from Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement living in exile have also been skeptical of the project, telling DW they fear the embassy could help Beijing suppress dissidents abroad.

The UK is home to the world's largest Hong Kong diaspora, with an estimated 285,000 people of Hong Kong origin living in the country.

World.title: Why Europe's wildfires are getting harder to stop
World.content:
Wildfires may start with a single spark, but experts say climate change, drought and decades of forest management decisions have created the conditions for Europe's biggest blazes.

Wildfires almost always need a spark to ignite, whether it's lightning, arson, or a car's hot exhaust pipe touching dry vegetation.

In France's historic summer wildfires, authorities blamed a brush-clearing machine being operated around a high-voltage power line. Spanish investigators concluded that sparks from heavy machinery were behind major blazes there.

But scientists say those findings only explain how Europe's historic wildfires began, not why they grew into the megafires that have devastated the continent this summer.

Across Europe, a combination of human-caused climate change, insufficient planning and forests planted in ways that allow flames to spread quickly are fueling fires, say experts.

"It's not that wildfires are magic and just start. You have to have the right climatic conditions," said Silvia Abruscato, coordinator of FoRISK, a pan-European forest risk management hub.

Has Europe lost control of its wildfires? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Climate change is loading forests with fuel

Scientists point to three ingredients that determine whether a wildfire will spread rapidly: the amount of vegetation available to burn, how dry that vegetation is, and the weather conditions around a fire.

"When all three of these conditions are very much fire-prone and they align, then you have this kind of fire event," said Francesca Di Giuseppe, a fire forecast project coordinator at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.

Climate change is making these conditions more common and intense. A rapid analysis from World Weather Attribution found global warming made the extreme weather behind Spain and France's summer wildfires much more likely.

Residents watch smoke rise near Lege-Cap-Ferret, one of many towns caught in a summer of 'hydroclimatic whiplash' Image: Julien De Rosa/AFP

One reason is a phenomenon called hydroclimatic whiplash, where ecosystems suddenly swing between wet and dry conditions.

Essentially, as the planet warms, the atmosphere holds more moisture, intensifying rainfall that fuels plant growth.

"This has created an abundance of biomass that then has rapidly dried during a sequence of heat waves," Di Giuseppe said.

In spring, a warmer atmosphere draws water from soil and plants. Drought worsens, vegetation dries out, and landscapes become far easier to ignite. In simple terms, wet winters grow fuel, and dry springs turn that fuel into perfect kindling.

This summer, that's meant fires breaking out almost simultaneously in France, Spain, Greece, and Turkey — all driven by the same broad pattern of heat and drought.

Making matters worse, the fires themselves add to the problem. This year's blazes have already emitted nearly 18 million tons of planet-warming CO2, according to EU figures.

Spain turns to grazing to curb wildfires To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Some forests are built to burn

Once a fire begins, it can take thousands of firefighters days or weeks of effort to contain the flames. That's partly due to the way forests have been managed over decades. Across parts of Europe, large areas have been planted as monocultures, dominated by a single species grown for quick timber.

"Some of the fires we've been seeing in France and Spain are in places where you have these very flammable trees which are quite fine and they often are growing close together so fire spreads really easily," Doug Kelley, a land surface modeler at the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology, told DW.

More than three-quarters of the Landes de Gascogne forest in southwestern France, which is currently ablaze, contains maritime pine. Created after Napoleon III ordered the region's marshes to be drained and planted with pine in 1857, it became Europe's largest man-made forest.

But the pine species sheds coarse needles that blanket the forest floor, providing bountiful fuel for fires. Because the trees are of similar age and height across vast areas, they are particularly vulnerable to fast-moving fire.

Another fast-growing timber tree is the eucalyptus. In Portugal the oily species — which represents more than a quarter of the country's forestland — burned far and wide in 2017's deadly wildfire season.

"In some regions of Europe, farmland and lower-biomass shrubland were replaced by fire-prone conifer or eucalyptus species of higher economic profitability, increasing the risk of fire," the European Commission wrote in a case study report on the 2017 Portuguese wildfires.

That includes Spain, where some 3 million hectares (7.4 million acres) of former farmland and pasture were planted with pine and eucalyptus during and after the Franco dictatorship, which lasted from 1939 to 1975.

Helicopters drop water over Spain's Avila province, where scientists say this year's extreme fire weather was made much more likely by climate change Image: Miguel Riopa/AFP

Preventing the next disaster

Firefighters will always play a crucial role in suppressing wildfires. But experts say reducing risk before fires start is just as important. That starts with tackling the greenhouse gas emissions driving climate change and intensifying weather extremes.

"Trying to prevent in the first place the landscape becoming so flammable is one of the most effective ways to try to avoid this kind of extreme fire behavior," said Di Giuseppe.

Replacing monocultures with mixed forests would also go a long way. Forests with a wider variety of species are generally better able to withstand drought, windstorms, insect outbreaks, and fires, because different trees respond differently to environmental stresses.

Germany offers an instructive case for forest management. Demand for timber after World War II led to spruce being planted across mountain ranges like the Harz in former East Germany. But these monocultures proved vulnerable to drought and bark beetle infestation. Foresters are now working to convert them into mixed forests to improve resilience.

Planting broadleaf, deciduous trees — such as oak, beech, or maple — can help, as they typically store more moisture than conifers. Trees with thick bark, fewer low-hanging branches, and a higher moisture content tend to be more fire-resistant.

A post-event simulation study of Portugal's 2017 blazes found fires that overwhelmed firefighters in pine and eucalyptus stands, with flames over four meters tall, could be contained in broadleaf forest, where flame heights dropped to under a meter and a half.

Forestry experts also recommend creating breaks between rows of trees to slow fire spread as well as pruning lower branches so flames can't jump quickly to the canopy. Clearing the forest floor of incendiary leaf litter and dead wood, and using controlled burns to reduce underbrush prior to wildfire season helps too.

"We need to manage our forest well in order to avoid such big disasters from happening. So prevention, prevention, prevention," Abruscato said.

World.title: Sudan civil war: When drones strike the classroom
World.content:
Children in Sudan's besieged city of el-Obeid are afraid to go to school as drone attacks hit civilian infrastructure. Aid groups warn of a worsening humanitarian crisis.

Flattened houses and rubble where a school once stood: These are the scenes that have appeared in footage of the Sudanese city of el-Obeid published by Ayin Network, a nonpartisan Sudanese media outlet.

Drone attacks by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have caused enormous damage to civilian infrastructure, including power grids, transformers, water treatment plants, schools, universities and hospitals in the capital of North Kordofan.

The local population is struggling to survive, according to Ahmed Awad, a native of el-Obeid and a project manager for children's rights organization Plan International there. The city — whose population previously numbered half a million but has now become home to several hundred thousand people who are displaced — is under siege, he added.

There is a shortage of medical supplies as well as food and safe, clean water, and Awad said he saw long lines of people at just one water pump: "Sometimes you can spend all day to get one liter of water for two or three days." Most of the time, children and teenagers are the ones sent to fetch water.

Millions across Sudan are going hungry, including over 825,000 children under 5 suffering from severe acute malnutrition Image: AFP

He added that a drone had hit a primary school and killed three children, which had caused trauma among other children, many of whom no longer dared go to school.

"One of the mothers said three of her children cannot sleep because they are always in fear of something happening again," he said.

Even when they're sitting in their classrooms, they live with the constant fear that a drone could strike at any moment. Awad and his colleagues at Plan International are working to provide psychological support to the affected children.

Sudan's strategic crossroads

El-Obeid is a strategically important location. The city is a trading hub in the middle of the desert on the only major route between Sudan's capital, Khartoum — which is controlled by the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) — and the western Darfur region, large parts of which are under the control of the RSF.

El-Obeid is currently controlled by the army, which has some 13,000 soldiers stationed there, and has been on the front line since fighting shifted from Darfur to Kordofan at the beginning of the year. The RSF has deployed troops to about 30 kilometers (18.6 miles) beyond the city limits, and has been using drones to bomb civilian infrastructure.

Warnings of mass atrocities

Analysts, aid organizations and the United Nations have warned that the RSF could soon capture el-Obeid. They fear a similar scenario to that which unfolded in the city of el-Fasher in the neighboring state of North Darfur in October 2025, when the RSF began by bombing infrastructure before storming the city after an 18-month siege.

Earlier this year, a UN Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan presented to the United Nations Human Rights Council in Geneva detailed atrocities in the capture of el-Fasher and identified "hallmarks of genocide."

“We warn that an escalation of the situation could lead to a repeat of the horrific human rights violations and abuses against civilians that we documented in Al-Fashir,” numerous human rights organizations said in a joint appeal.

"We are alarmed by the ongoing hostilities around the city, including frequent drone strikes," said Pekka Haavisto, the UN chief's personal envoy for Sudan, in June. "These are already affecting the civilians and disrupting humanitarian aid to the city. Any further escalation of the situation would place thousands of people at risk."

Growing up under drones

The situation is particularly dire for the children trapped in el-Obeid, says Francesco Lanino, deputy country director of the children's charity Save the Children in Sudan. Drone attacks on schools and displacement camps have caused severe trauma.

Lanino recently visited the Tawila displacement camp near el-Fashir in Darfur, which was taken over by the RSF in October. There, he encountered children struggling to process what had happened to them.

"We met several children who refused to speak afterwards," Lanino said. Many found it difficult to understand why they had experienced such violence.

Lanino is concerned about the long-term impact of the conflict. "If these traumas are not addressed, they could seek revenge, because all this stress, all this trauma, could erupt in a new wave of violence."

Sudan's army has launched a new offensive in Kordofan from the capital, Khartoum, and says it has taken control of the 360-kilometer-long highway linking Omdurman, Khartoum's twin city, with el-Obeid.

SAF Chief of Staff Abdel-Fattah al-Burhan recently inspected the newly captured areas in North Kordofan by helicopter and congratulated his troops. The advance has reopened supply routes to SAF units in El Obeid.

Residents of the previously besieged city celebrated the arrival of army forces, as the immediate threat appears to have receded for now.

As they retreated, RSF fighters looted markets and villages in North Kordofan and committed human rights violations against local residents, according to the Sudan Tribune media platform.

Last Monday, RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as "Hemeti," told commanders in the affected areas they no longer needed to wait for orders from the high command and could instead launch counteroffensives at their own discretion.

The move could lead to further attacks on civilians and additional looting.

World.title: From petitions to memes: How students made dissent visible
World.content:
From imperial China to present-day India, student movements have repeatedly adapted the tools and symbols of their age to challenge authority.

It was a clip destined to go viral.

On July 22, 2026, in rainy Mumbai, India, a casually dressed young woman stepped in front of a slow-moving police van carrying detained students. She placed her palm on the hood, forcing the vehicle to stop.

Mobile phones captured the moment from every angle. She too, raised her own phone and recorded the encounter. Within hours, the clip spread across India and beyond.

It became one of the defining visuals of the Cockroach Janta Party protests, a movement in which students demanded transparency and accountability, following leaks in India's medical entrance exams.

But the power of the moment lay not only in what she did, but in how quickly it was seen. A single gesture, a young woman confronting authority, became a symbol shared across millions of screens.

While the clip belongs to a generation raised on social media, the impulse behind it is much older.

From court petitions and revolutionary posters to photographs, umbrellas and memes, student movements have repeatedly adapted the tools and symbols available to them, turning them into vehicles for dissent.

India's Cockroach movement — and why it matters To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Communicating dissent at court

Long before television or social media carried dissent across borders, students still found ways to make their grievances heard.

In Eastern Han China, for instance, scholars at the Imperial Academy (Taixue) aligned with reform-minded officials in opposing powerful eunuchs at court, whom many viewed as corrupt and politically overbearing.

They voiced their objections through public criticism, political networks and petitions.

In an era when political communication moved through official channels, petitions were among the established ways of bringing grievances before the throne. Written in formal language and delivered through the bureaucracy, they carried student concerns directly into the state's communication system.

Multiplying dissent through posters

Centuries later, communication and protest mechanisms evolved.

In Paris in 1968, students challenged university authorities and a conservative postwar social order. As demonstrations spread across the French capital and drew in workers, one of the movement's most enduring contributions emerged from a basement workshop at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts.

The posters of the Paris 1968 protests were collectively created without credit to any one person Image: Philippe Gras/IMAGO

The Atelier Populaire ("People's Workshop") printed thousands of posters during the protests, many of them overnight. Their bold graphics, silhouettes and slogans became the visual language of the movement. Produced collectively, many carried no individual author's name, helping transform protest into a shared public voice.

The posters and their messages could appear in dozens of places overnight, giving the protest a wide local visual presence.

When a photograph became global witness

Protests also became more impactful when images could be transmitted across borders.

In Soweto in June 1976, Black South African students marched against the apartheid system's education policies, rejecting Afrikaans as a compulsory medium of instruction in Black schools. Many saw it as the language of an oppressive state and a barrier to equal education.

As thousands of students took to the streets, police opened fire. Amid the chaos, South African photographer Sam Nzima captured the image that would travel the world: 13-year-old Hector Pieterson being carried away from the scene after he was fatally shot.

The iconic photograph of the fatally wounded Hector Pieterson being carried by a classmate highlighted apartheid's atrocities Image: ZUMA/IMAGO

The photograph became one of the defining images of apartheid. For many outside South Africa, it served as the lens through which the students' protest was seen and understood, helping build international awareness of and opposition to apartheid.

When images become iconic

In the spring of 1989, students gathered in Beijing's Tiananmen Square demanding democratic reforms, freedom of expression and an end to corruption. As the protests grew, so did the need for symbols that could communicate their message beyond the square.

In the final weeks of the occupation of Tiananmen Square, students built the Goddess of Democracy. Facing Mao Zedong's portrait, the 10-meter statue became a powerful symbol of the movement.

Students had positioned the Goddess of Democracy opposite the poster of Mao Zedong in Tiananmen Square Image: 64memo

But while the students created one icon, history would produce another. After the brutal military crackdown on the protesters, a photograph of a lone man, later known as "Tank Man," standing facing a column of tanks traveled around the world.

Global media did not create these symbols, but amplified them. Cameras, newspapers and broadcasters transformed these local acts of defiance into enduring images of resistance.

From organizers to participants

Over time, protest communication no longer flowed only from organizers outward. Crowds and bystanders increasingly helped shape it.

In Chile in 2011, students demanding education reform used flash mobs, performances and public spectacle to draw attention to their cause. Protest was no longer just something people watched. It became something they could join.

In Hong Kong in 2014, students protesting Beijing's plans for electoral reform transformed everyday objects into political symbols. And what began as a practical response to pepper spray and tear gas soon became the defining image of the Umbrella Movement.

Umbrellas were both practical and symbolic during the 2014 Hong Kong student protests Image: Philip Fong/AFP

Modeled on Prague's original John Lennon Wall that was created after his murder in 1988 and went on to provide a space for people to express irritation with the communist regime, Lennon Walls in Hong Kong also became hubs of public expression, attracting thousands of people who left messages of support and protest on sticky notes attached to walls around the city.

From slur to symbol

And then there are the political platforms that shape which symbols become widely seen, as is the case in India recently.

Students protesting exam irregularities took an insult aimed at them and made it their own: "Cockroach" quickly became one of the movement's most recognizable symbols online.

A protester in New Delhi holds up a sign that reads ' I am a cockroach' Image: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

Memes and reels often spread faster than official statements, with students using them to respond to criticism, mock their opponents and rally support.

Like posters in Paris or umbrellas in Hong Kong, this particular instance shows how memes can transform a disparaging label into a powerful protest symbol.

Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier

World.title: Humanoid robots: Trump's latest China trade battle?
World.content:
The US has banned foreign-made humanoid robots, a market Chinese tech firms dominates. Although Washington cited national security risks, analysts think Donald Trump is buying time for US robot makers to catch up.

In the latest sign of China's threat to the United States's tech dominance, the Trump administration on Tuesday banned new foreign-made humanoid and four-legged robotsfrom entering the country.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) cited "unacceptable risks" to national security for the decision.

The FCC noted how the robots "collect data that could be leveraged by malign actors to surveil Americans, enhance the capabilities of foreign intelligence services, or to remotely commandeer the robots."

The move is widely seen as aimed squarely at China, which accounted for 85% of humanoid robot deployments last year, according to British bank Barclays.

Humanoid robots steal the show at German trade fair To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How serious is the security threat from Chinese robots?

US officials warn that Chinese humanoid and quadruped (four-legged) robots can collect detailed location and personal data, be controlled remotely and pose risks for critical US infrastructure. Specific concerns center on the robots' potential dual-use — civilian and military purposes.

Unitree Robotics, a leading Chinese robot maker, appears on the Pentagon's list of firms with links to the Chinese military. Its robots have been used in army exercises.

Researchers have also shown that Unitree robots have security flaws that let attackers take control with a voice command and then use one robot to control others.

Washington is also concerned that a large cohort of low-cost Chinese robots could feed real-world data back to Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) systems, which are fast catching up with their US rivals.

The threat, however, is largely theoretical as most commercial humanoid robots are in early stages of development.

China has the edge over the US in humanoid robot deployment Image: Imaginechina/Sipa USA/picture alliance

China has rejected the accusations, insisting the US is using national security as a pretext for protectionism to suppress Chinese technology. Beijing is expected to impose countermeasures, which could include curbs on the raw materials US robotics firms urgently need to scale up production.

The Trump administration has made no secret of its desire to help the domestic US robotics industry, which in turn supports the country's nearly trillion-dollar AI buildout. According to industry watchers, US President Donald Trump wants to ensure the likes of Figure AI, Tesla Optimus and Agility Robotics are protected from high-volume Chinese producers, whose robots often cost half the price or less of their US rivals.

Washington has put similar curbs on Chinese drones and solar panels and now levies a 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles.

Will the ban help US robot makers catch up?

The ban is widely seen as Trump's attempt to buy time, having been caught off guard by how quickly China scaled robotics production.

According to Omdia, a tech research house, China has six firms in the Top 10 robotics rankings. Those firms shipped nearly 11,600 humanoids last year, versus a few hundred by US firms.

In March, Bank of America forecast around 90,000 shipments by the end of this year.

Elon Musk has big plans for Tesla's Optimus humanoid robot Image: CFOTO/picture alliance

The US is widely seen as stronger at making a robot's brain smart through advanced AI, while China leads at mass-producing cheaper robots with bodies that move better thanks to high-performance actuators or robotic muscles.

Rush Doshi, director of the Initiative on China Strategy at the Council on Foreign Relations, described the ban as "one of the most significant actions taken so far in support of the US robotics ecosystem."

Evan Beard, CEO of Standard Bots, a maker of robot arms, thinks the Trump administration is sending an "unambiguous" message to China.

"Robotics is a technology America must lead and own — and foreign-subsidized robots will not be allowed to unfairly dominate US robotics..." Beard wrote on X.

Critics, however, think the ban could slow US AI innovation as researchers currently benefit from being able to run tests on budget-friendly Chinese robots.

"Restrictions can reduce security exposure, but they do not by themselves create a competitive domestic ecosystem," Georg Stieler, an advisor to the robotics industry, wrote on X.

CNBC, a US business television channel, cited Marc Einstein, a research director at Counterpoint Research, as saying the ban was "bad news for Chinese humanoid producers planning their IPOs in the coming months."

Einstein warned that Beijing could now "further restrict rare earth sales to American companies and … Chinese market access for American companies like Tesla and Nvidia."

Drones, robots and the race to save lives To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How big could humanoid robots become?

Barclays estimates the market, currently worth just $2 to 3 billion (€1.7 to 2.6 billion), could reach $200 billion by 2035 in the most optimistic scenario, if the robot's brains, brawn and batteries can be improved.

Elon Musk is even more bullish, saying Tesla's Optimus could become "the biggest product ever" with long-term sales potentially reaching $10 trillion.

At scale, he believes the robots, which currently sell for about $100,000, could eventually cost $20,000 to $30,000 each — cheap enough for factories, warehouses and later homes.

Combining Barclays' forecast with Musk's target price points to roughly 7 to 10 million humanoid robots being sold each year by 2035.

In the near term, humanoids are expected to take on repetitive and physically demanding jobs in warehouses and factories. Later, they could expand into health, elderly care and household chores.

Edited by: Rob Mudge

World.title: Germany news: Unemployment tops 3 million as industry slumps
World.content:
07/31/2026 July 31, 2026 Merz calls for action from Spain, Morocco

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday urged Spain to quickly regain control of the situation in Ceuta after some 50,000 migrants stormed the Spanish North African territory from Morocco over the past several days, overwhelming authorities.



The situation has sparked a raging political debate in the EU over border security.

"The protection of the European Union's external borders," said Merz, "is crucial for combating illegal migration."

"Spain wants to, and must, bring the situation in Ceuta under control as quickly as possible," he said.

Merz welcomed Madrid's pledge to prevent the migrants from traveling onward to mainland Europe, where France has already announced new security measures along its border with Spain.

Speaking with Germany's DPA news agency, Franziska Hoppermann, whom Merz recently appointed secretary general of his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party, also warned that, "Illegal migration threatens our country and our society. There must be no loss of control at the borders."

Beyond admonishing Spain, Merz also called on Morocco to "take back the illegal migrants immediately."

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt reiterated that Germany would maintain, "Flexible and targeted border controls with other EU states," adding, "We will extend the option for internal border controls beyond September" when they are set to lapse if not renewed for another six months.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said he had been in touch with his Spanish and Moroccan counterparts and welcomed "Morocco's willingness to continue working closely with Spain to ensure the security of the shared border and to readmit the migrants from Ceuta as quickly as possible."

World.title: Eco wins: From death strip to nature haven and other green surprises
World.content:
A Cold War relic becomes a biodiversity haven, a Pokemon Go for trees and seagrass gets a second life. This week's eco wins come from some unexpected places.

After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the border zone that divided West and East Germany was left largely untouched. Today, the nearly 1,400-kilometer (870 miles) stretch, once known as the death strip, is a "green belt." It's home to around 7,500 species of insects and spiders, hundreds of them endangered, as well as otters, wildcats and birds on the brink of extinction.

Because the military zone was sealed off for decades, species that have vanished elsewhere in Germany were able to take hold here. Now 88% of the area is under protection, and cycle paths and information panels allow visitors to explore what was once completely off-limits.

Read the full story here: East-West border death zone now Germany's biodiversity oasis

An urban tree database

Not all heroes wear capes, but some do form a canopy. Urban trees quietly cool neighborhoods, reduce flooding and improve our wellbeing. But in many cities, trees are under pressure from heat, drought, traffic and too much concrete.

Now, a citizen-science project in Germany is helping people map and monitor the trees around them. Think Pokemon Go, but for urban nature and with real-world benefits for the climate.

Seagrass goes from beach nuisance to building material

On Poel, a German island in the Baltic Sea, washed-up seagrass is being turned into sustainable insulation for homes, while helping clean local beaches in the process.

As demand for eco-friendly construction materials grows, the project is attracting interest from across Europe and could give new value to a resource that was previously viewed as waste.

World.title: Marruecos manda parar el éxodo de 50.000 migrantes sobre Ceuta
World.content:
Rabat ha mandado parar este viernes el éxodo de más de 50.000 migrantes irregulares, en su mayoría hombres jóvenes marroquíes, desencadenado la víspera en la ciudad autónoma española de Ceuta, en un reflujo de retorno casi completo al término de la jornada en el paso de Fnideq (la antigua Castillejos), la parte de la frontera terrestre correspondiente al país magrebí. La creciente llegada de centenares de indocumentados a nado hasta la costa ceutí acumulada hasta el pasado lunes se multiplicó exponencialmente el jueves, en la mayor crisis diplomática con Marruecos y cinco veces más amplia que la registrada también en Ceuta en mayo de 2021 por la hospitalización en secreto en España del líder del Frente Polisario, Brahim Gali. Esta Marcha Verde de baja intensidad se ha producido sin una orden de mando conocida ni una causa explícita, al menos por ahora. Pero resulta claro que la patente inhibición inicial de las fuerzas de seguridad marroquíes ha amplificado hasta cotas inquietantes, cuyos embates se han sentido en toda Europa, la magnitud de una crisis aparentemente organizada desde el eco de las redes sociales. Este viernes habían regresado 48.500 de las 50.000 que habían llegado a entrar.

Las fuerzas de seguridad marroquíes sellaron con eficiencia desde la tarde del jueves los accesos principales a la frontera ceutí del Tarajal para evitar un aluvión humano sobre las instalaciones fronterizas. Sin embargo, toleraron el paso de decenas de miles de personas por el espigón que separa Ceuta de Castillejos, primero a nado y luego mayoritariamente por la playa y las rocas costeras.

Las fuerzas auxiliares marroquíes, un cuerpo parapolicial de apoyo, se dedicaron en la frontera y en los accesos a Castillejos a dirigir los pasos de la multitud de migrantes irregulares, como en cualquier otra aglomeración que se produce en el país magrebí. Policías y gendarmes montaban guardia mientras tanto.

La inhibición de las fuerzas de seguridad en la crisis migratoria ha sido patente, en particular desde el mediodía del jueves y hasta bien entrada la mañana del viernes, cuando comenzaron a despejar con gases lacrimógenos y cañones de agua a presión la aglomeración de jóvenes en la frontera hacia el centro urbano de Castillejos.

El Gobierno de Rabat ha guardado silencio. La embajadora de Marruecos en España, Karima Benyaich, ha sido la única fuente oficial en pronunciarse, al desvincular a su país de la irrupción masiva de migrantes en Ceuta y achacar a las “mafias criminales” que tratan con seres humanos la responsabilidad exclusiva del nuevo desbordamiento de la frontera de Ceuta.

Benyaich, una diplomática próxima al rey Mohamed VI, ya ocupaba en la crisis migratoria de 2021 el mismo cargo en la legación de su país en Madrid, de la que se ausentó durante cerca de un año tras ser llamada a consultas a Rabat poco después de que se hiciera público el ingreso del líder del Polisario en un hospital de Logroño. Ahora ha ensalzado la “colaboración ejemplar” de Marruecos con España en la solución de la última crisis.

Coincide con las tesis mantenidas este viernes por el presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, en su visita a Ceuta. También ha responsabilizado de la crisis “a las mafias que trafican con seres humanos” y ha alabado la interlocución “constante, fluida y muy razonable [con Rabat], a diferencia de lo que sucedió en el año 2021”.

Madrid y Rabat comparten que la causa ha sido una interpretación “interesada” por parte de las mafias de la reciente sentencia del Tribunal Supremo, que determinó que no se puede devolver en caliente a quienes entren a nado en Ceuta y Melilla. Las organizaciones criminales controlan la travesía marítima de migrantes irregulares hacia España, que rinden miles de euros por pasajero, pero no parecen ser tan relevantes a la hora de llegar a pie hasta la frontera ceutí en un éxodo caótico.

En Marruecos se llegó a ofrecer desde las redes sociales y de forma anónima carta blanca y papeles en regla para quienes accedieran a las ciudades autónomas desde el mar, sin violentar las barreras terrestres. Si bien es cierto que el bulo de ‘visado para todos’ ha circulado profusamente en Marruecos, tanto en las redes sociales favoritas de los más jóvenes como en las favoritas de los adultos y en grupos privados de mensajería, está por ver el rendimiento monetario que la manipulación digital en cadena haya podido reportar a las mafias de la migración irregular. Y también el rédito político, geoestratégico o diplomático generado, así como sus posibles beneficiarios. Para España, la crisis solo parece arrojar números rojos.

La irrupción de decenas de miles de marroquíes en Ceuta ha puesto en jaque las relaciones entre España y Marruecos, que parecían encauzadas desde 2022, tras el abandono por parte del Gobierno español de su tradicional posición respecto al conflicto del Sáhara, pasando de la neutralidad al alineamiento con Marruecos. Sánchez se alineó entonces con el plan de autonomía como la solución política más viable para el contencioso de la excolonia española. Dos años más tarde, el presidente de Francia, Emmanuel Macron, dio otra vuelta de tuerca diplomática al considerar el plan de Rabat como “la única solución” posible para el Sáhara, cuyo futuro Francia solo contempla ya “bajo la soberanía de Marruecos”. El paso dado por París marca desde entonces una apreciable distancia respecto a Madrid a ojos de Rabat.

Fuentes gubernamentales han declarado a EL PAÍS que atribuyen la avalancha migratoria sobre Ceuta a la difusión, a través de las redes sociales, de la idea de que quien consiguiera llegar a nado a la ciudad española no podría ser repatriado, en aplicación de la reciente sentencia del Tribunal. También han reconocido que, sin la pasividad de las fuerzas de seguridad marroquíes, no habría sido posible una entrada tan masiva de personas. Pese a ello, el Gobierno español ha optado finalmente por obviar los reproches y centrarse en buscar una solución rápida a la crisis, sin que ni siquiera los servicios de inteligencia conozcan con certeza las causas últimas de la actitud marroquí en la frontera de Ceuta.

El reciente acercamiento de Madrid a Argel, archirrival regional de Marruecos. El avance en el Parlamento español de la legislación para conceder la nacionalidad española a los nacidos en el Sáhara Occidental y sus descendientes. El nuevo estatuto de la UE para Gibraltar, en su conexión con España. Hasta la disputa sobre el estadio que será sede de la final del Mundial de Fútbol de 2030, coorganizado por ambos países junto con Portugal.

Todas estas argumentaciones figuran entre las hipótesis manejadas por los analistas en el empeño de explicar la crisis migratoria en Ceuta. Pese a la necesidad urgente de pasar página, sobre lo que ha ocurrido estos días entre Castillejos y Ceuta planea, como ya ocurrió en 2021, un interrogante. Sí ha producido efectivamente presión política y diplomática mediante el uso de la inmigración irregular sobre una plaza de soberanía norteafricana que, junto con Melilla, es definida siempre por Marruecos como “presidio ocupado”.

World.title: Italia anuncia que suspende el acuerdo Schengen con España para los no europeos por la crisis migratoria en Ceuta
World.content:
Italia no tiene fronteras terrestres con España ni conexiones directas con Ceuta. A estas alturas, según ha anunciado el Ejecutivo español, casi todos los migrantes que cruzaron la frontera entre la ciudad autónoma y Marruecos han sido devueltos al país norteafricano: 48.300 de 50.000. Y, sin embargo, el Gobierno de Giorgia Meloni ha anunciado que suspende el acuerdo de libre circulación de personas en Europa, conocido como Acuerdo Schengen, por la crisis migratoria en la ciudad española del norte de África.

Tras el anuncio, a golpe de mensaje en las redes sociales de varios ministros y de la propia Meloni, ha llegado el matiz. Fuentes gubernamentales italianas, recogidas por la agencia Efe, apuntan que la restricción solo afectará a quienes no sean ciudadanos de la UE: “No supondrá ningún cambio para los viajeros españoles y europeos hacia Italia”.

La actuación ha tenido respuesta por parte de Exteriores. En un tuit, el ministro José Manuel Albares ha destacado que “la práctica totalidad de quienes entraron en Ceuta han vuelto ya a Marruecos” y ha recordado que no es posible desplazarse desde allí a la Península sin saltarse el control policial. “La integridad del espacio Schengen está absolutamente garantizada. Basta de confusión interesada”, ha zanjado.

Roma había planteado ya el jueves que se estudiara la suspensión de España de ese acuerdo, según ha anunciado el propio Gobierno transalpino. También lo han puesto sobre la mesa Finlandia y Dinamarca. Por el momento, solo el Ejecutivo que lidera la ultraconservadora Meloni ha dado este paso. Aunque en Helsinki su ministra de Interior, también ultra, ha afirmado estar lista para dar una orden similar. La ha corregido el primer ministro, Petteri Orpo: “Sánchez afirmó en 2025 que la frontera de Finlandia es la frontera de España. Lo mismo aplica a la inversa. España no está sola: Von der Leyen ha ofrecido la ayuda de la UE a España”.

No es lo mismo suspender a un país de Schengen que un país miembro del acuerdo decida suspender su participación total o parcialmente. Lo primero puede hacerse cuando se constata que hay deficiencias graves en el control de fronteras y se tiene que decidir en el Consejo de la UE. Lo segundo depende de la decisión del Ejecutivo que da el paso, tiene que estar justificado y debe notificarlo tanto a la Comisión como a los Estados miembros. Roma no ha dado el último paso todavía. La consecuencia será, si se confirma el paso, que habrá controles en puertos y aeropuertos.

En teoría, Italia da este paso por el temor −compartido con un amplio abanico de países de la UE− de que los migrantes que han cruzado ilegalmente la frontera en Ceuta lleguen al continente y viajen libremente por Estados miembros. “Se trata de una medida extraordinaria para salvaguardar la seguridad nacional y prevenir posibles repercusiones para nuestra nación”, ha apuntado la primera ministra Meloni en la red social X, explicando que se reintroducen “controles fronterizos en los enlaces marítimos y aéreos con España”.

La decisión de Italia ha sido respondida por el propio presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, que ha recordado con los datos de Frontex, la agencia europea de fronteras, que a través de Italia han entrado de forma irregular 478.000 personas entre 2021 y 2026 mientras que por España lo han hecho menos de la mitad, 234.760.

El capítulo del roce italoespañol ha llegado mediada una tarde en la que desde diversas capitales crecía la presión sobre España para que controlara la situación en la frontera con Marruecos y devolviera cuanto antes los que cruzaron la frontera el jueves. Y en eso, ha estado la propia Bruselas. “Las imágenes que llegan de Ceuta son inaceptables”, han sido las primeras palabras de Von der Leyen en su primera reacción a lo sucedido el jueves en la ciudad española del norte de África. “No podemos permitir que nadie entre en nuestra Unión sin cumplir con nuestras normas”, ha advertido. “Las redes de tráfico deben desmantelarse. Y las devoluciones deben ser rápidas, tal como permiten nuestras normas”, ha incidido, para después anunciar que la Comisión “trabajará en un apoyo operativo adicional a España, incluida la colaboración con Frontex”.

El mensaje de Von der Leyen no ha expresado solidaridad con España, algo que sí ha hecho el presidente del Consejo Europeo, António Costa: “Expreso mi solidaridad con España en la actual situación de migración ilegal en Ceuta”. “Aunque los nacionales de terceros países en Ceuta no disfrutan de libre circulación al territorio continental de España o al resto del área Schengen, la respuesta firme de España, que incluye retornos acelerados continuos, demuestra nuestra determinación para proteger nuestras fronteras exteriores, combatir la migración ilegal y desmantelar las redes criminales de tráfico de personas”, ha añadido el también ex primer ministro portugués.

Esta última frase es una respuesta clara a los Gobiernos de Estados miembros que han pedido estudiar la suspensión de España en el espacio Schengen. Sí que ha mostrado solidaridad, en cambio, el presidente de Francia, Emmanuel Macron, en una conversación con Sánchez. El líder galo, sin embargo, sí que ha señalado que ha pedido al ministro del Interior, Laurent Núñez, que adopte “todas las medidas necesarias” para reforzar los controles en la frontera con España, según han confirmado fuentes cercanas al Elíseo. El titular de Interior, que conversó este jueves con Albares y volverá a hablar hoy, anunció esta mañana que se ha activado la fuerza fronteriza de intervención rápida para “hacer controles más profundos”.

Estas fuentes señalan que “se están manteniendo contactos con las autoridades españolas y también con las marroquíes” para seguir de cerca la evolución de la situación y “mejorar la coordinación entre los organismos implicados”. Macron también ha señalado que Francia está dispuesta a prestar a las autoridades españolas “todo el apoyo necesario, incluso a través de la agencia Frontex, si así lo solicitan”, informa Raquel Villaécija.

El canciller alemán, Friedrich Merz, se cuenta entre los que han pedido que a España que resuelva rápido la situación. “España quiere y debe recuperar el control de la situación en Ceuta lo antes posible. Por ello, acojo con satisfacción la intención de España de no permitir que los migrantes ilegales entren en el continente europeo”, escribió en un comunicado en el que aseguró estar en contacto con el Gobierno español. Asimismo, afirmó que espera que “Marruecos readmita a los migrantes ilegales sin demora” y apeló a que el reglamento de retorno, aprobado en junio, se aplique “ahora de forma inmediata y exhaustiva”. Estas palabras llegaron antes de que Madrid anunciara que casi todos los migrantes que cruzaron de forma irregular han sido retornados al país africano.

Pero no todo han sido palabras de apoyo desde Alemania. Como era de esperar, desde el partido de ultraderecha Alternativa para Alemania (AfD), su líder, Alice Weidel, criticó que el canciller no se sume a Italia, Finlandia y Dinamarca a favor de suspender Schengen. “Merz quiere volver a dejar que esta crisis pase sin hacer nada al respecto”, criticó en la red social X, en la que previamente había alertado de que “es probable que el destino de la mayoría de esos migrantes sea Alemania” y había pedido suspender Schengen para que no se repita lo ocurrido en 2015. El tema de la migración es una de las principales bazas de AfD para recavar votos en Alemania, donde el próximo mes de septiembre hay tres elecciones regionales: Sajonia-Anhalt (donde AfD puede obtener más de un 40% según los sondeos y entrar así por primera vez en un Gobierno regional), Berlín y Mecklemburgo-Antepomerania.

La situación interior y lo sucedido en 2015, cuando la guerra civil de Siria provocó una avalancha de centenares de miles de refugiados en toda Europa, ha estado muy presente en la reacción de varios Gobiernos. También su composición política ha tenido su papel, como muestra el hecho de que en Finlandia, Italia o Suecia, los ultras participan o respaldan al Ejecutivo.

No es este el caso de Polonia. Pero su primer ministro, el primer ministro Donald Tusk, se ha mostrado exigente con España al pedirle que siga su ejemplo: “Hemos endurecido las leyes de asilo, los procedimientos fronterizos y ha construido barreras efectivas en su frontera con Bielorrusia, que es la frontera oriental de la UE. Hemos invertido miles de millones de euros y movilizado a miles de soldados, policías y guardias fronterizos”.

Otro asunto que ha estado presente es la regularización masiva que aprobó el Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez. Desde Austria, por ejemplo, se ha pedido que “ni un solo migrante ilegal llegue al continente europeo”. Su canciller, Christian Stocker, ha advertido que si la situación en España acaba por presionar en sus fronteras hará “todo lo posible para protegerlas”.

World.title: Recuperados 57 cadáveres en las aguas de Ceuta tras la entrada de 50.000 migrantes irregulares
World.content:
Al menos 57 personas han fallecido en el intento de llegar a España

El audio de esta noticia utiliza una voz sintética generada por Inteligencia Artificial y podría tener algunas inconsistencias.

Interior cifra en 48.300 las personas que, hasta las 18.00, habían retornado de manera voluntaria a Marruecos

Cerca de 50.000 inmigrantes, en su inmensa mayoría de nacionalidad marroquí, han entrado de manera irregular en Ceuta desde la madrugada del jueves, según las primeras estimaciones oficiales hechas públicas por el Ministerio del Interior poco antes de las 14.00. Esta cifra se ha traducido en la mayor crisis migratoria de la historia de la ciudad con una cara dramática: al menos 57 personas han fallecido en el intento de llegar a España, la mayoría ahogadas al intentar bordear a nado el espigón fronterizo de El Tarajal. No se descarta que el número de víctimas mortales aumente en las próximas horas. Los servicios mantienen desplegado un dispositivo de búsqueda en las aguas próximas a la frontera en el que participan dos grupos de buceadores (ocho agentes) del Grupo Especial de Actividades Subacuáticas (GEAS) de la Guardia Civil.

La cifra de entradas supera ampliamente la registrada en la anterior, la de mayo de 2021, cuando se calculó que burlaron los controles fronterizos más de 10.000 migrantes después de que Marruecos relajara los controles fronterizos. El número de entradas que se maneja supone prácticamente incrementar en un 60% la población del enclave, donde hay censadas 83.600 personas. Esta entrada masiva se ha reflejado desde el jueves en la presencia de una importante cantidad de personas en grupos que deambulan permanentemente por las calles de Ceuta y que han pasado la noche a la intemperie. Un residente describe de manera gráfica que lo que se está viendo en las últimas horas en la ciudad es como si hubiera “una manifestación constante”.

No obstante, en las últimas horas se está registrando el fenómeno inverso, el de miles de marroquíes que retornan de manera voluntaria a la cercana localidad de Fnideq (la antigua Castillejos) y que se cruzan con los que aún intentan entrar en España. Según Interior, hasta las 16.00 horas eran cerca de 48.300 los que habían hecho el camino de vuelta, el 96% de los que habían entrado. En algunos momentos, salían 150 personas por minuto. Este movimiento era esperado por las fuerzas de seguridad, que ya observaron retornos voluntarios similares durante la crisis de 2021.

Las cifras de entrada suponen un duro varapalo para las estadísticas del Ministerio del Interior sobre inmigración irregular. Según el último balance del departamento de Fernando Grande-Marlaska, entre el 1 de enero y el pasado 15 de julio, habían entrado en España de manera irregular 14.479 personas, que era un dato positivo, ya que suponía cerca de un 25% menos que en el mismo periodo del año anterior. En Ceuta, en concreto, habían sido 2.826, por lo que solo en la ciudad autónoma en un solo día se han multiplicado por más de 20 las estadísticas acumuladas en más de seis meses.

En el último informe de Seguridad Nacional, referido a 2025 y aprobado el pasado 21 de abril, el Departamento de Seguridad Nacional, dependiente de la Presidencia del Gobierno, ya se apuntaba que el año pasado la presión migratoria tanto en Ceuta como en Melilla se había visto “notablemente incrementada debido principalmente al fenómeno de nadadores que tratan de acceder sorteando el perímetro fronterizo a través del mar”, como ha ocurrido ahora. Sin embargo, esta tendencia no explica los sucesos de este jueves en la ciudad española, como tampoco la reciente sentencia del Tribunal Supremo que prohibía el rechazo en frontera ―las coloquialmente conocidas como devoluciones en caliente― cuando la entrada se produce precisamente a nado, según coinciden en señalar varias fuentes policiales.
