"One of the students said 'I don't want to miss a day of school because it's like being in my favourite soap opera, I just want to know what's going on'," Dr Willis said.

"There's a strong sense of connection to one another."

Physically and educationally different

Dr Willis said when the schools were proposed, principals "were having to do a lot of explaining" to parents about how the schools would work without broad open spaces.

She said students used green spaces and the schools were equipped with gymnasiums, but the curriculum was also designed with physical activity in mind.

Campuses use creative architecture to provide green spaces for students. (ABC News: Ned Hammond)

"[At a vertical school] in Adelaide, up to 30 per cent of the curriculum time is spent out in the community, and … [in Brisbane] the students are heading to Fortitude Valley, the local swimming pool, they're doing excursions to the art gallery," Dr Willis said.

"They're out and about in the city a whole lot more than students in our suburban schools might get to be out."

Ms Coogan said supervision, wellbeing and movement around the school all required "careful planning".

"Managing the movement of large numbers of students across multiple levels requires clear routines and expectations," she said.

" Ultimately, the challenges are very manageable, and the benefits, particularly the opportunities for collaboration, innovation and strong community connections far outweigh them. "

Dr Willis says the new design has enabled principals like Ms Coogan to think about being educationally different. (Supplied)

The schools being physically different allowed principals to consider how they might be educationally different, Dr Willis said.

She said FVSSC implemented a number of "trans-disciplinary" subjects, with students heading out into the community to base their learning in the real world.

"The type of activity might be different, but certainly movement is a big part of a vertical school."

'Stop thinking in silos'

With the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games fast approaching and amid a housing crisis, Dr Willis said cities would need to consider the lessons of vertical schools.

"We've got to stop thinking in silos and start thinking about the kinds of cities we want to live in," she said.

"And that includes schools."

As the city grows ahead of the 2032 Games, parents in South Brisbane are calling for a new school. (ABC RN: David Lewis)

Ms Coogan said while it was suitable and effective for FVSSC, "vertical schooling isn't the answer everywhere".

"The design needs to suit the local community, and the educational vision must drive the use of the building rather than the other way around."

In an open letter published in June, parents of students at West End State School (WESS) urged the government to consider a new school for the area at the former Visy site on the river.

The state government announced in June Lendlease will "take over" the Visy glass factory site in West End in April next year, with plans to build 4,000 apartments.

Parents are urging the government to consider a new school as part of the redevelopment of the old Visy site. (Supplied)

West End State School P&C president Vanessa Bertagnole said with the population around WESS growing, plans needed to be made now.

"Education infrastructure must be planned at the same time as housing, transport, parks and community facilities — not several years after new residents have moved into the area," Ms Bertagnole said.

" It takes six years to build a new school so the government is already behind. "

She said while the P&C would not "prescribe one particular building model", it would "be open to considering a well-designed vertical school if it helped secure a new school site in the inner city and the needs of primary school students were properly addressed".

"[Our priority] is to ensure the government secures land and delivers sufficient public education infrastructure, including classrooms, specialist learning areas and outdoor learning spaces, for the children who already live here and the thousands of families expected to move into the area," Ms Coogan said.

"A vertical school would still need safe and accessible outdoor play areas, adequate green spaces, sporting and recreation facilities, appropriate drop-off and active transport arrangements, and spaces designed specifically for younger children."

A spokesperson for the Department of Education said WESS had "sufficient capacity" and strategies were in place to manage future enrolments "in the short to medium term".

"The Department of Education will continue to monitor growth in the local school network to ensure all schools have capacity for in-catchment enrolments."

Minister for Education John-Paul Langbroek said the government was "delivering 22 new schools in the areas they are most needed".

"Under the former Labor government's decade of decline, several new schools were publicly announced and never built, with the funding secretly rediverted to other projects," Mr Langbroek said.

Want to have your say? Go to www.abc.net.au/yoursay

World.title: Outback teen trades riding boots for ballet shoes as she heads to Swiss dance school
World.content:
Growing up in outback Queensland, Maddy Murphy was just as likely to be in riding boots as ballet shoes.

If the North West teenager wasn't with her horse, she was practising pirouettes in her lounge room or at the Julia Creek dance studio.

The now-16-year-old will this month fly nearly 15,000 kilometres to the other side of the world to take a place at Switzerland's Tanz Akademie Zurich dance school.

"It's still a bit surreal, honestly. I always told myself this is what I want to do," she said.

Maddy began her dance journey at five, when her mother, Belinda Murphy, enrolled her at Julia Creek's newly opened Branches Performing Arts.

"She was always very theatrical," Ms Murphy said.

Loading...

Her teacher, Amy Tinning, said she noticed Maddy's "perseverance from a young age".

"Talent can only take you so far, but Maddy had this maturity and commitment that isn't very common in someone so young," Ms Tinning said.

From the bush to the big city

With a population of just 550 people, the rural township might have had a dance studio but it didn't have a high school.

When Maddy was 11, she packed her bags and leotards and moved more than 1,600km south-west to Brisbane for boarding school.

Maddy Murphy spent her high school days in the dance studio rather than a classroom. (Supplied: Chasing Moon photography)

But instead of after-school sport, she spent her evenings at the Prima Youth Ballet Academy.

A year later, the young performer persuaded her parents to let her take up dancing full-time and finish her traditional schooling through distance education.

"I saw other people were going full-time at my age, dancing all day and doing school at night online, and I felt that I really wanted to do that, too," Maddy said.

"I'd wake up, do some school, dance from nine till four, come home and do all my schoolwork and then do it all over again the next day.

" There were definitely hard times, don't get me wrong. The last thing you wanted to do when you came home from full days of dance was maths. "

When the Prima Youth Ballet Academy closed in early 2025, Maddy relocated to Dance North in Sydney, while continuing her schooling online.

Growing up, Maddy Murphy would travel to Mount Isa with her mother to compete at the local eisteddfod. (Supplied: Belinda Murphy)

"I just found this love for ballet because it's so hard. You have to make it look easy, but it's such a complex form of dance," she said.

She graduated from high school later that year at the end of year 10.

"The pressure of doing all those hours and then trying to do school at night by yourself at home. We just thought that she can always go back," Ms Murphy said.

Ticket to Europe

Prior to graduation, Maddy won first place at the Brisbane International Contemporary Dance Prix and was awarded a scholarship to travel to Switzerland in March and spend a week auditioning for Tanz Akademie Zurich.

"It was unlike anything I think I've ever experienced," she said.

"There was the pressure to do well, but you also have to have the mindset that, 'This is what I've worked for, I'm ready.'"

The 16-year-old was one of 21 other dancers from across the world to secure a place in the prestigious Swiss ballet school.

"It's still a bit surreal, honestly. I think it'll finally sink in once I start packing," Maddy said.

Her mother admits it'll be challenging having her eldest daughter living on the other side of the world.

"It's nerve-racking [because] it's not a flight from Mount Isa anymore," Ms Murphy said.

"But you can't bubble wrap them and you have to trust them."

Maddy Murphy hopes her journey inspires other outback children to dream big, regardless of their postcode. (Supplied: Jo Thieme Photography)

Prepared for anything

The teenager is spending her last few weeks on Australian soil back in North West Queensland, spending time with family and her horses.

"I will get homesick eventually because that's what happens. But I know I'll be OK with that because I've done it before," Maddy said.

Moving countries to train at Tanz Akademie Zurich will mean leaving behind her beloved campdrafting horses at home in Julia Creek. (Supplied: Belinda Murphy)

"I take bits and pieces of me from the outback to the city or wherever I go … that grit and hard work into my dancing.

" I wouldn't change a thing about my journey or where I've come from. "

Maddy will spend the next three to four years in training, with the hopes of becoming a company dancer upon graduation.

"There are no walls or boundaries in life unless you put them there," she said with a smile.

"You have just got to work hard and do what you love, and nothing can stop you."

World.title: 'Anxious to have his day in court', Alan Jones's trial is set to begin
World.content:
Alan Jones, once the biggest name in Sydney media, is "anxious to have his day in court".

He said as much at his first appearance at Sydney's Local Court in December 2024, telling a throng of media outside the court he would be defending "baseless" charges of indecent assault and sexual touching.

This week again, his lawyers told pre-trial hearings their client was "anxious" to get started.

Alan Jones surrounded by a media frenzy after his first appearance at Sydney Downing Centre Local Court in 2024. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

That day will come this week, as the veteran broadcaster prepares to face a lengthy trial, where he has pleaded not guilty to 22 charges, relating to six male complainants.

But the 85-year-old will not be defending himself to a jury, as was suggested at his first court appearance.

More than 70 witnesses will be giving evidence before one man — Judge Glenn Walsh.

"I am both the judge of law and the judge of fact," Judge Walsh succinctly put it during pre-trial hearings.

While the jury box will remain empty, the court room at the Downing Centre in Sydney's CBD is likely to be packed.

The former broadcaster's trial has garnered significant media interest, and there are already concerns the courtroom will not have enough seats for everyone.

High-profile arrest of a former radio king

The arrest of Sydney's most recognisable "shock jock" in 2024 was an extraordinary turn of events for someone who had held such power in political and social circles.

Alan Jones had an unmatched dream run of radio ratings, winning 226 consecutive surveys.

In that time, his influence meant he could air his political views, and politicians of all stripes would take note.

Mr Jones prided himself on speaking up for "the battler".

Mr Jones had a dream run of radio ratings, winning 226 consecutive surveys. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

He had been retired from radio for a few years, and was keeping occasional appearances on Sky News and online service ADH TV when in late 2023, a series of stories making allegations against him were published in the Sydney Morning Herald.

A year later, in November 2024, police arrived at Mr Jones's Circular Quay apartment, and escorted him away in an unmarked car.

NSW police commissioner at the time, Karen Webb, thanked her team for their work.

"There's no such thing as a matter that's too old to be investigated," she said.

Later that day, Mr Jones was mobbed by waiting media as he was let out of the Day Street police station on bail, with a notice to appear in court in a month's time.

"Allegations have been made, nothing has been tested, nothing has been proven," his then lawyer Chris Murphy said outside the police station.

Alan Jones leaves Day Street Police Station after he was granted bail following his arrest. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

The initial charges

Initially, Mr Jones was charged with 24 offences relating to eight complainants, including some charges of aggravated indecent assault.

Loading...

After his first court appearance, the broadcaster stopped to give a brief statement to waiting media.

"I will not be engaging in a running commentary in the media," he said. "But, I want you to understand this: these allegations are all either baseless or they distort the truth."

By September 2025, the charge sheet had increased to 44 counts relating to 11 complainants.

But during a court hearing that month, prosecutors said they would be replacing the most serious charges with lesser offences, while some charges were dropped altogether.

Stay up to date with The Case Of podcast The Case Of podcast will bring you all the key updates from the court hearings in Alan Jones's case.

Charges have since been dropped two more times, resulting in what will be taken to trial: 20 counts of assault with act of indecency and two counts of sexual touching relating to six complainants.

It meant the charges were a low enough level that they could be dealt with in the Local Court, a jurisdiction which can only issue a maximum sentence of five years for multiple offences.

Trials in the Local Court do not have juries, meaning Mr Jones's fate will be decided by Judge Walsh alone.

Allegations to be heard in court

Three weeks of pre-trial hearings have given some insight into the allegations Mr Jones is facing.

Prosecutors accuse Mr Jones of indecent assault against six men, including kissing them, touching their crotch or backside over their clothes, or in some cases, touching their genitals on their skin.

The incidents are alleged to have happened over a period between 2003 and 2020, at Mr Jones's apartment inside 'The Toaster' on Macquarie Street, at a public event or at his now-former property at Fitzroy Falls in the Southern Highlands.

Mr Jones's defence will argue he committed none of the alleged offences. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

Prosecutors will seek to paint Mr Jones as someone with a tendency to act on a sexual interest in younger men, while the defence will argue their client committed none of these alleged acts.

The trial itself is set to be lengthy and detailed, with 76 witnesses, including the six complainants, set to give evidence.

Judge Walsh told pre-trial hearings the registry file, which includes wads of paper evidence and legal documents, "now inhabits a whole room".

In a sign that coverage of this trial will be closely scrutinised by Judge Walsh, he required media to front up to court on Thursday represented by a lawyer, and apply to be able to watch and listen to the complainants' evidence from inside the court room.

And on Friday afternoon, on the eve of Monday's trial, defence lawyers for Mr Jones attempted to have media blocked from reporting the evidence of his alleged victims.

Barristers for Mr Jones argued the law allowed the judge to block or embargo the reporting of evidence given "in-camera", or privately, until some date in the future.

But Judge Walsh rejected that argument, ruling that the purpose of allowing media to watch and listen to in camera evidence was to prepare a fair report.

"I am unpersuaded that I have power to prohibit the publication of evidence," he said.

The first complainant to be heard, known only as "J", is due to take the witness stand and start telling their side of the story on Monday.

World.title: The Labor MPs chasing promotions after Vic leadership spill
World.content:
Labor MPs are jostling for promotions before new Premier Ben Carroll's cabinet is chosen at a caucus meeting on Monday.

Under Victoria's new leadership, fresh faces are expected to be elevated to cabinet to replace allies of former premier Jacinta Allan.

The new leaders

Premier Ben Carroll Read more Ben Carroll has represented the electorate of Niddrie, in Melbourne's north-west for more than a decade. He served as deputy to former premier Jacinta Allan for almost three years before stepping into the top job on Tuesday. Mr Carroll has been education minister since then, most recently dealing with protracted negotiations with Victoria's public school teachers. He was previously a lawyer and political advisor, including to former Victorian premier Steve Bracks. When he was younger, he worked at Kmart and the day after he was elected as premier held his press conference at a Kmart store. He is also the minister for WorkSafe, the TAC and medical research. Deputy Premier Gabrielle Williams Read more Gabrielle Williams has represented the Dandenong electorate for more than a decade. A lawyer and advisor before entering parliament, Ms Williams is the Minister for Transport Infrastructure, Public and Active Transport and Women and Girls. She moved to the role of deputy premier earlier this week.

Ms Allan's allies Harriet Shing and Lily D'Ambrosio on Thursday announced they were resigning from the ministry and would exit parliament at the November election.

Ms D'Ambrosio, who was long speculated to retire, was the last remaining minister from Daniel Andrews' first cabinet in 2014.

Along with Jacinta Allan, she was also the last remaining Labor MP from the Bracks-Brumby government.

While Ms Allan is yet to formally announce if she will re-contest her seat of Bendigo, her retirement from politics is widely expected.

Who's leaving

Jacinta Allan Read more For almost 27 years, Jacinta Allan has represented the Bendigo East electorate in Victorian Parliament. A career politician, she was elected in 1999 aged just 25 becoming Victoria's youngest ever female MP. She rose in the ranks under Daniel Andrews, gaining the transport infrastructure portfolio, and was elevated to deputy premier in 2022. Ms Allan took on the role of premier in Septemer 2023. Resigning from the top job earlier this week, she said she would spend more time with family and work to ensure Ben Carroll was re-elected as premier. Harriet Shing Read more Harriet Shing has represented the Eastern Victoria region in the Legislative Council since 2014. She has most recently served as health minister and previously as minister for housing and the Suburban Rail Loop. She announced on Thursday she would not re-contest her seat at the November 2026 state election. Lily D'Ambrosio Read more Lily D'Ambrosio has been the local member for Mill Park for more than two decades. She was most recently minister for climate action, energy and resources and the State Electricity Commission. But on Thursday, she said she had informed the premier she would not recontest her seat at the upcoming election. She told the ABC her proudest achievement was overseeing the renewable energy transition in Victoria. Along with Ms Allan, she is the last remaining of the Labor MPs who served in the Bracks-Brumby government.

It leaves Mr Carroll with three vacancies in his cabinet.

All three exits are from the dominant Socialist Left faction, which will meet on Monday morning to debate replacements before a full caucus vote is held later that day.

Under Labor Party rules, women must make up half the front bench. After this week's retirements, there are currently 11 women and eight men in cabinet.

Mr Carroll will then divvy up portfolios in a reshuffle. Jostling for a promotion got underway almost immediately.

Premier Ben Carroll will announce a new leadership team ahead of November's state election. (ABC News)

Mordialloc MP Tim Richardson has been guaranteed a ministry in Ms Allan's place.

Southern Metropolitan MP Ryan Batchelor was the favourite to take Ms Shing's cabinet position within the upper house, though Sheena Watt from Northern Metropolitan and North-Eastern Metropolitan MP Sonja Terpstra were also talking to colleagues.

Cranbourne MP Pauline Richards, Footscray MP Katie Hall, Albert Park's Nina Taylor and Sunbury MP Josh Bull were drumming up support for the remaining cabinet vacancy in the lower house.

These names could change, and MPs were expecting possible candidates to become clearer over the weekend.

Possible entrants

Tim Richardson Read more Mordialloc MP Tim Richardson was a government advisor before entering parliament more than a decade ago. He was recently promoted to cabinet secretary, and is now expected to be elevated to cabinet as part of a deal struck during Labor's chaotic leadership vote on Tuesday. Pauline Richards Read more Since 2018, former political advisor and local councillor Pauline Richards has represented the seat of Cranbourne, in Melbourne's outer-south east. She has previously served as government whip, a role that helps manage the day-to-day business of parliament. Ryan Batchelor Read more Ryan Batchelor, a first-term MP and former adviser to then-prime minister Julia Gillard, represents the Southern Metropolitan region in the upper house. Mr Batchelor is currently the parliamentary secretary for Emergency Services. Sheena Watt Read more Sheena Watt is Labor's first ever Aboriginal representative in Victorian Parliament and is currently the only Indigenous MP in the state. Since 2020, she has represented the Northern Metropolitan region after working in the community services sector. She is parliamentary secretary of Public and Active Transport and Community Sport Katie Hall Read more Since 2018, former communications and community sector worker Katie Hall has represented the electorate of Footscray. She is currently the parliamentary secretary for Housing and Building and Creative Industries. Sonja Terpstra Read more First elected to the upper house in 2018, the lawyer and former union worker represents the North-Eastern Metropolitan region. Nina Taylor Read more Nina Taylor has been in parliament almost eight years, first as an upper house MP and now as the member for Albert Park. The former councillor has held various ministerial support roles. Josh Bull Read more Labor MP Josh Bull has represented the electorate of Sunbury in Melbourne's outer north-west since 2014. Having previously worked as a teacher, he currently supports the treasurer as parliamentary secretary.

There was further speculation that Ms Allan allies Sonya Kilkenny, Jaclyn Symes and Maree Edwards could retire.

If Ms Symes remains, insiders said she is unlikely to remain Treasurer.

Industry Minister Colin Brooks was considered a possible contender for that position.

While her colleagues speculated Ms Kilkenny could follow Ms Allan out the door, she had her existing ministries guaranteed to her in a deal brokered at Tuesday's chaotic caucus meeting.

Mental Health Minister Ingrid Stitt was mooted for the more senior Health portfolio.

Ms Stitt and Mr Brooks were both among the delegation of ministers and MPs that informed Ms Allan on Monday she no longer enjoyed majority support of her caucus.

Attorney-general Sonya Kilkenny is expected to retain a ministerial portfolio after a short-lived leadership bid. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Tuesday's leadership change, after Mr Carroll declared his intention to contest and Ms Allan subsequently resigned, splintered the Left faction and has left the dominant grouping wounded.

Mr Carroll separately on Friday announced Treasury Secretary Chris Barrett would now lead the Department of Premier and Cabinet.

He replaces Jeremi Moule, who entered the role under Daniel Andrews in November 2020.

Mr Barrett's first job when he begins on Monday will be to work on standing up a royal commission into alleged corruption on the Big Build.

Minister Paul Edbrooke on Friday told reporters he did not expect any changes to his portfolios, Consumer Affairs, Cost of Living, Renters, and Men and Boys.

Shadow Attorney General James Newbury said the impending reshuffle would make no difference to the government's prospects.

"It doesn't matter who holds what portfolio. Frankly, none of them are fit to be in government, and I think Victorians know that. And I think come November, you will see Victorians cast their very swift judgment on this government."

World.title: In towns where thousands of homes are Airbnbs, renters want a tax
World.content:
Louise Dwyer and Mike Crouch remember a time when finding a rental in the NSW Northern Rivers was easy and affordable.

The couple lives in a temporary housing village in Mullumbimby established for those displaced by the 2022 floods.

The pod villages will close by the end of the year, and the couple is among the village residents struggling to find secure accommodation.

They have booked caravan parks and hotel rooms for the holiday period after their lease ends in December.

"Prior to the floods, we had really great affordable housing … for many, many years," Ms Dwyer said.

" If we were to get a two-bedroom house [now], we'd probably have to pay anywhere from $800 to $1,000 a week, which we don't have. "

Louise Dwyer and Mike Crouch say they are unable to afford a long-term rental big enough for themselves, their son and pets. (ABC News: Emma Rennie)

Ms Dwyer and Mr Crouch backed calls for a holiday rental levy, especially if the funds were directed towards housing support.

"Locals are being pushed out; they're being priced out of living in their communities, which is really sad," Ms Dwyer said.

Homelessness NSW is calling for a levy on short-term holiday rentals to bolster long-term rental stock, claiming it could raise around $50 million for housing support.

The proposed levy is based on a model introduced in Victoria last year, where a 7.5 per cent tax was placed on revenue collected by short-stay providers who rented their properties on platforms such as Airbnb and Stayz.

When announcing the policy, the Victorian government said the revenue would be spent on social and affordable housing.

Homelessness NSW chief executive Dom Rowe said it would help raise money for homelessness services and incentivise long-term rentals.

"In the last year, they were able to raise $85 million to go to those most in need, so that's a pretty impressive policy setting that we know works as it's worked in that other jurisdiction," Ms Rowe said.

"People are finding it really hard to find rental accommodation in the private rental market.

" And short stays basically take properties out of that long-term rental market and so makes it more difficult for people. "

Byron Bay is a popular destination for short-term accommodation rentals. (ABC North Coast: Emma Rennie)

Figures disputed

The advocacy group released an analysis of short-term and long-term rentals this week.

It has compared the number of long-term rentals advertised on realestate.com.au to the number of short-stay listings recorded by the state's tourism body, Destination NSW, across the March quarter.

Ms Rowe said there were 49,985 short-stay listings across the state compared to 22,347 long-term rentals.

The Mid North Coast had 4,676 Airbnb listings to 584 long-term rentals and the Northern Rivers, which includes Byron Bay, had 5,303 Airbnb listings and 393 ongoing rentals.

However, the Australia & New Zealand Short Term Rental Association board member Catherine Shields said the analysis was not "comparing apples with apples".

Catherine Shields owns a holiday rental business on the NSW south coast. (Supplied: Catherine Shields)

"Short-term rentals are available for most of the year because that's the nature of their availability," she said.

"Whereas permanent rentals are very tightly held, particularly in the Northern Rivers, and they probably only ever come up for rent once a year or longer."

The state government requires vacant homes and apartments used for short-term rental accommodation (STRA) in NSW to be registered.

There are currently 30,599 STRA registered statewide, including 2,987 in the Northern Rivers, 3,440 on the Mid North Coast and 9,972 in the Sydney area.

Ms Shields said some properties were listed across multiple websites such as Airbnb and Stayz, which could inflate listing figures and might explain the discrepancy in data used by Homelessness NSW.

Control measures hotly debated

The Byron Shire Council introduced a 60-days-per-year cap on holiday rentals in 2024, in an effort to encourage more properties back into the long-term market.

The measure yielded mixed results a year after its introduction.

Ms Rowe said a levy on rental income would be more effective.

"I think the cap is very difficult to police and short-term rentals can go from one platform to another, so it's difficult to track them online," she said.

The Short Term Rental Association has long made the case that many holiday rentals would not be affordable long-term rentals due to their market value.

"It's ironic that they think it's a good idea to get rid of the short-term rentals, but the number of people, particularly women, who are employed in that sector is really significant," Ms Shields said.

The short-term rental sector says many holiday homes in hotspots such as Byron Bay would still be unaffordable as long-term rentals. (ABC North Coast: Emma Rennie)

In a statement, NSW Planning Minister Paul Scully said the best way to increase long-term rental housing supply across the state was by increasing the overall housing pipeline.

"While we know there is always more to do, NSW has more homes under construction than any other state, with over 80,000 homes underway and more in the pipeline."

World.title: Stowaway school teacher who disguised herself as a boy on a tall ship
World.content:
Nearly a century has passed since a music teacher from Balaklava, South Australia, disguised herself as a young man and stole her way onto a Finnish tall ship at Port Lincoln bound for England, buoyed by a dream of a life at sea.

Her story is still an inspiration in an industry where women only account for 2 per cent of the 1.2 million seafarers worldwide and 5 per cent of the Australian seafarer workforce, according to the Australian Maritime Safety Authority.

Jeanne Day as she appeared in the Port Lincoln Times in June 1928 after reaching England. (Supplied: Trove/Port Lincoln Times)

A 2024 survey by the International Maritime Organisation found women made up 1 per cent of the total number of seafarers who worked at sea.

But women were not allowed to work on ships back in 1928 when 22-year-old Jeanne Day dreamed of a seafaring life.

So one night, when the German-built Herzogin Cecilie tall ship was docked in Port Lincoln, she cut her hair and dressed in trousers and climbed aboard to hide below deck.

She was initially discovered and removed from the ship but persevered, stowed away again, and eventually made it to Falmouth, England, where her adventurous tale was published in newspapers across the globe.

Research by staff at the National Library of South Australia found the barque was three days out to sea when hunger and thirst forced Ms Day out of hiding.

There was no time to return the stowaway to shore because the German-built Herzogin Cecilie was in a hurry.

The vessel was officially racing other ships carrying grain from Australia around Cape Horn to England.

The Herzogin Cecilie was wrecked on the Devon coast in 1936. (Supplied: Trove/State Library of Queensland)

The Perth Daily News, in May 1932, reported AJ Villiers published an account of the discovery of the stowaway, stating the crew "abandoned all hope of the race" with "hot resentment" and "superstition" about having a woman on board.

"I never saw such a dejected and thoroughly cast-down collection of seafarers in my life," Mr Villiers wrote.

" A woman in the ship! A young one at that! The race was lost. "

But much to the superstitious crew's surprise, the Finnish ship won the race for the fourth time, after sailing 22,531 kilometres in 96 days.

Despite Ms Day's presence on Herzogin Cecilie seemingly disproving the curse about women on ships, she was unable to convince the crew or any other ship to give her a job and she later worked as a maid at a hotel.

Do you know more? Email Jodie Hamilton at hamilton.jodie@abc.net.au.

A Russian fan

She may have had better luck in Russia.

In 1930, Brisbane's Daily Standard published a news story of a Russian woman who had spent eight years working on a Soviet steamer, the Sibler.

The article reported that Tatsiana Dienchenko had been "hoping to meet Jeanne Day, the Australian girl stowaway on the Herzogen Cecilie, who unsuccessfully sought seafaring work in London for six months".

But it was unclear if that ever came to pass.

Modern women sailors

Another woman inspired by Jeanne Day is Leading Seaman Rebecca Churches from the Royal Australian Navy (RAN), who has spent most of her eight-year defence career as a hydrographer mapping the sea floor.

Rebecca Churches says she is in awe of Ms Day. (Supplied: Royal Australian Navy)

Similar to Ms Day, Ms Churches was from a small rural town, Paynesville in east Gippsland, Victoria.

Her motivation for joining the navy was to be able to travel and experience the world.

She said women were considered equal to men on RAN boats.

"You definitely don't have to hide nowadays," Ms Churches said.

She enjoyed the camaraderie of being at sea and, like Ms Day, had travelled on a tall ship — circumnavigating Australia aboard the Young Endeavour.

"We have engines as opposed to just sails they had way back then," she said.

Rebecca Churches enjoyed working on the sailing ship HMAS Endeavour. (Supplied)

She was in awe of Ms Day.

"They went round Cape Horn and the seas … from what I've heard and what I've seen from the documentary Around Cape Horn, the weather just would have been intense and frightening, and especially if it was your first time at sea," she said.

"I think that's just incredible.

"I read they had really, really rough seas and … she was worried that the ship might capsize or have a knockdown or something like that.

"I can't even imagine how terrified she would have been.

"It's quite incredible that when she got to London, she wanted to get on another boat."

No taming rough seas

Ms Churches had experienced rough seas on modern navy ships.

"You're sleeping in your rack, and you're falling out of your rack, and it's just pretty intense when you're down below decks, and you can't really see," she said.

"Probably the worst weather I've been in is over the Bass Strait on Young Endeavour."

But the positives of being at sea far outweighed the negatives.

"I think it's the uniqueness of it," she said.

"There's not actually a lot of people that get to do this … it's really special.

Rebecca Churches says spending time on the tall ship HMAS Endeavour was a special part of her navy career. (Supplied: Royal Australian Navy)

"We do watches overnight …12am till 4am and it's pretty much dead silent.

"No-one's awake except for the people on watch on the bridge and just going out into the bridge wing and seeing the stars.

" Being in the middle of the ocean somewhere where there might be 10,000 metres of water below you is pretty special. "

Ms Churches said Ms Day's story was inspirational for women.

"I think she's an incredible woman and I think that people like her have in some way or another shaped and paved a way for women like myself who can now go to sea.

World.title: Bleached coral's 'incredible recovery' as cyclone cools water temperature
World.content:
As Queenslanders waited for Cyclone Alfred to make landfall, its meander along the coastline brought relief to heat-stricken corals.

After widespread coral bleaching in the Great Barrier Reef in the summer of 2024, the cyclone's formation in February 2025 brought cooler water to the World Heritage marine park.

The effect of that cool change can be seen most dramatically around Lady Elliot Island, the reef's southernmost coral cay.

Before: Bleached coral around Lady Elliot Island February 2024 . . After: Regenerated healthy coral in early 2026. . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Before and after images SLIDE Bleached coral around Lady Elliot Island February 2024 / Regenerated healthy coral in early 2026.

About 90 per cent of the island's bleached coral has returned to good health, and scientists are now eagerly awaiting a spawning event later this year.

"The water temperatures dropped about 2 degrees Celsius," Erin Watson, marine biologist and master reef guide, said.

Erin Watson says the reef around the island has recovered well from the 2024 bleaching event. ( )

" Now if you go out for a snorkel, the corals that did bleach, you wouldn't even notice had bleached in the first place. "

What is bleaching?

When coral is under stress, it expels the algae that lives in its tissues.

The algae, called zooxanthellae, provides food and gives the coral colour.

Without it, the coral cannot feed and its tissue turns transparent, exposing the white calcium carbonate skeleton.

Algae lives inside the coral's tissue, providing food and colour. ( )

One of the key reasons for coral bleaching is rising water temperatures due to climate change.

But coral bleaching is not always a death knell.

"If those environmental conditions like water temperature start to go back down again, the coral takes back its algae and it recovers," Ms Watson said.

"Because we didn't get a bleaching event [in 2025], we actually got a little coral spawning event."

2024 was the first time much of the southern part of the reef, including Lady Elliot Island, experienced coral bleaching. ( )

While there has been strong recovery in southern parts of the reef, other areas have not been as fortunate.

The Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS) said the 2024 bleaching event was the most severe and geographically extensive in its 40 years of monitoring the reef.

Mike Emslie says cyclones are a double-edged sword. ( )

Research team leader Mike Emslie said it caused "substantial mortality" with 40 per cent of reefs experiencing their largest annual decline in coral cover.

'Incredible recovery'

Dr Emslie described cyclones as a double-edged sword.

"They're known to have what's called this 'cooling wake' effect and can reduce the temperature of the water," he said.

"But the other side of the coin with cyclones is that they also produce a really large storm swell, and that storm swell can obviously impact the fragile coral skeletons and break them apart."

Christine Dudgeon is the project manager for Leaf to Reef, which is a research and rehabilitation program based on Lady Elliot Island.

Christine Dudgeon says frequent bleaching events do not give coral time to recover. ( )

"We're seeing incredible recovery," she said.

"The really big challenge of bleaching that we've seen in many parts of the Great Barrier Reef is when we have these back-to-back events or prolonged events … happening so readily.

"It doesn't give the environment time to recover in between."

Dr Dudgeon said because of Lady Elliot Island's proximity to the continental shelf, it had traditionally been more protected from environmental issues that affected the northern part of the reef.

Christine Dudgeon has been monitoring the reef's recovery. ( )

"We have lots of cold water upwelling," she said.

"It has a potential buffer against things like coral bleaching where the water can cool down and help the coral to survive and thrive a bit longer."

From bleaching to spawning

Researchers and staff on the island were hopeful this year's conditions would be favourable for reproduction.

Erin Watson is hoping for a significant spawning event this year. ( )

"After corals have bleached, it takes them a few years to build up their energy reserves to be able to spawn," Ms Watson said.

"Hopefully at the end of this year, we're going to get a really big spawning event."

Dr Emslie agreed it was likely to be a good year for spawning across the Great Barrier Reef.

"I'd say there'll definitely be spawning happening this year," he said.

"Most corals can recover quickly enough following that physiological stress imposed by bleaching to put the energy into reproduction."

World.title: Palestinians long for peace but doubt Trump's deal with Hamas will hold
World.content:
Palestinians in Gaza have expressed scepticism about Hamas's declaration it will lay down its weapons in a bid to kickstart the stalled peace process, concerned it will not actually change the situation in the war-ravaged strip.

On Friday, local time, US President Donald Trump heralded Hamas's agreement to "completely disarm", after months of backroom diplomacy to convince the militant group to make the concession.

But Hamas insisted its decision is conditional on Israel upholding its side of the deal, withdrawing its forces from large swathes of Gaza and ending its daily strikes on the strip.

Since the ceasefire was announced in October 2025, Palestinian health authorities in Gaza have reported more than 1,200 people killed in Israeli strikes, many of them civilians, including children.

"We welcome any agreement that is genuine and will actually be implemented," Rabih Al-Balawi, 57, told the ABC.

" Over the past three years, we've heard many agreements and proposed solutions, yet the situation on the ground has only continued to deteriorate. "

Rabih said he had been displaced 23 times during the war in Gaza, something even more difficult considering he cannot walk unaided.

"It seems Israel is refusing to reach any agreement until after the elections, waiting to see what happens," he said.

"From what I've seen, believing they will honour any agreement would be naive. These people keep neither promises nor agreements.

"We know Israel's history of expansion, and they never withdraw from occupied areas. It's impossible."

Sanaa Shreir hoped it would be the beginning of an improved humanitarian situation in Gaza. (ABC News)

Sanaa Shreir, 54, said she hoped it would mark the beginning of an improvement to the humanitarian situation in Gaza.

"Disarmament is not an easy issue for us, but given what our people are going through, it may be acceptable," she told the ABC.

"Israel's word doesn't mean much in reality. We can only hope that God makes this happen.

"Maybe that's how Trump sees it. As for us, we just hope they do something for these poor people, for our people who have suffered so much; our community has been devastated in every possible way."

'Weapons are only a pretext'

Hamas, which is considered a terrorist organisation under Australian law, had been involved in lengthy negotiations with mediators Egypt, Qatar and Türkiye.

It has said it will hand over its weapons, to be stored and supervised by the Palestinian technocratic body set up by Mr Trump's Board of Peace, known as the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG).

Israel has long insisted the weapons be removed from Gaza altogether, and to this point it has not even allowed NCAG to enter the strip.

Abu Ramzi Al-Salakhi does not believe Hamas will surrender its weapons. (ABC News)

Hamas has said it will disarm when Israeli forces withdraw from territory in Gaza, while Israel has repeatedly argued it will only pull troops from the strip once the militant group has completed that process, highlighting another sequencing issue.

"Hamas will never surrender its weapon; it would only hand them over to the authority that replaces it," Abu Ramzi Al-Salakhi, 70, told the ABC.

"There is a difference between not using weapons and giving them up.

"If it ever hands over its weapons, it would only be to Palestinians."

Hamas has also demanded an end to all strikes in the territory, while Israel has said over the months since the truce was declared that it would continue to attack threats posed by Hamas fighters and facilities.

Hours after Mr Trump's announcement, local authorities reported another attack.

"The enemy's warplanes kill innocent children, the elderly, everyone," Abu Ramzi said.

"Weapons are only a pretext. The attacks continue over and over again."

Israelis critical of deal

NCAG, which has been operating from Cairo, welcomed Hamas's announcement and the Trump declaration.

"This development represents an important milestone for our people in the Gaza Strip," it said in a statement.

"After years of conflict, destruction, and uncertainty, the priority today is to translate this progress into practical steps that have a tangible impact on citizens' daily lives."

Nickolay Mladenov, the high representative for Gaza under the Board of Peace, insisted that while the agreement was important, "what happens next matters even more".

"Implementation and verification have to be real. Withdrawal must move in lock step with decommissioning," he posted on X.

In the absence of a formal response from the Netanyahu government to the announcement, the void was filled by some of the most outspoken members of his coalition cabinet.

Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who quit the government in protest over the January 2025 ceasefire before rejoining when that truce collapsed weeks later, railed against the announcement and labelled it "not acceptable to Israel".

Itamar Ben-Gvir (centre) has spoken out against the deal. (AP: Ohad Zwigenberg )

"After the October 7 massacre, the blood of every Hamas man is forfeit — and therefore, a commitment to cease the eliminations of the terrorist organisation's murderers is tantamount to consenting for Hamas to regroup toward the next massacre," he posted on X.

"The targeted killings in Gaza must continue, encouraging emigration must happen, Israel must win."

One of Benjamin Netanyahu's political opponents, former Israel Defense Forces chief Gadi Eisenkot, also criticised the agreement.

"Once again, Israeli citizens are learning about a fateful agreement from foreign publications, and the outrageous gap between Netanyahu's promises and reality is exposed," he posted on X.

"He has capitulated in his political weakness without achieving the war's objectives, instead of ending it from a position of strength.

"The State of Israel must not accept a reality in which Hamas survives, rearms, and waits for the opportunity to carry out the next massacre!"

But Mr Trump said Israel was "very happy" with the plan. "Israel helped us," he told reporters at Camp David on Friday. "They've been very good."

Mr Eisenkot is surging in the polls ahead of the Israeli election, scheduled for October 27.

World.title: Dan Gorringe was a battling ruckman. He’s now a social media star and might even become an AFL rights holder
World.content:
Gorringe is edgy, but even the AFL wants him.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you’re a football fan under the age of 35, chances are Dan Gorringe is everywhere when you pick up your phone. Log on to Instagram, he’ll be there, over-celebrating a Carlton win or mourning a loss. You’ll find his mildly more serious football views on his Dan Does Footy YouTube channel. On TikTok, you’ll get his almost instant hot takes, delivered in his typically edgy style. Dan Does Footy podcast host and social media identity Daniel Gorringe has become a key player in the AFL’s targeting of the youth market. Chris Hopkins He’s labelled goalkicking great Matthew Lloyd a “dirty rat”, called prominent broadcaster Gerard Whateley a “muppet”, and told arguably the greatest player of all time Leigh Matthews to “f--- up”. He has had commercial partnerships with corporate bookies, sports drinks and alcohol brands. It will come as a surprise, then, that Gorringe the footballer was the polar opposite in personality. “He was as straight as six o’clock,” his first senior coach Guy McKenna said. Former Carlton captain and one of Gorringe’s closest friends Sam Docherty, who was unwittingly embroiled in his stoush with Whateley, said his former teammate was rarely the centre of attention in the Blues locker room.



“He was fairly quiet, [but] still very funny,” Docherty said. “If you listen to him speak, he’s probably socially anxious and awkward through footy because he didn’t know where he stood or what he was doing. He always had that funny side to him. “He joked around with a small group of mates as opposed to the whole locker room. Most people who played with him would have thought he was fairly reserved and didn’t speak very much.” Dan Gorringe takes on North Melbourne’s Todd Goldstein in a ruck contest in 2016. Getty Images In many ways, Gorringe is the most unlikely of football personalities: polarising, unfiltered and contemptuous of traditional media. But even the AFL wants him. Traditionally, it has taken a long and distinguished on-field career for a retired player to make it in the media. Though a No.10 pick in 2010, his 26 games for Gold Coast and Carlton fall well short of the mark. As a player, his most memorable moment came in retirement when he clattered into comedian Dave Hughes in a legends charity match. But the world of social media does not follow the same rules, and there are few in Australian sport better at playing this game than Gorringe, who has a team of more than 10 full-timers and additional casual and part-time staff behind the scenes managing content and his commercial partnerships. His success is no accident.



The former ruckman has a greater digital presence than some clubs. His 378,000 followers on Instagram is well over double that of Gold Coast, the club that drafted him. His 43,200 subscribers on YouTube is close to 50 per cent higher than another of his former teams, Carlton, and his TikTok following of 298,000 is more than the Blues and Suns combined. His average of more than 300,000 views and 20,000-plus engagements per content item across Instagram, TikTok and YouTube makes him “one of Australia’s highest-performing independent sports creator brands”, Nathan Powell, the chief product and strategy officer at AI-powered creator technology platform Fabulate, said. “Dan has managed to build something that’s much harder than simply accumulating followers,” Powell said. AFL CEO Andrew Dillon with influencer Dan Gorringe, announcing the league’s first official watchalong. AFL “He’s built a highly concentrated Australian sporting audience that consistently chooses to engage with his content. The audience is also predominantly male and heavily concentrated in the 18-to-34 demographic, which is one of the most valuable audiences for sporting organisations and advertisers. “That tells me people aren’t just following Dan because they know who he is – they’re following him because they genuinely value his perspective on sport and the content he creates.” No wonder the AFL has Gorringe on its books as part of what its customer and commercial boss Bec Haagsma says is a “rapid transformation and evolution of our fan engagement and fan experience strategy”. They see Gorringe as pivotal to targeting the younger market – those under the age of 34.



In collaboration with the league’s broadcast partners, Gorringe appeared on The Ultimate Footy Watchalong for the Fremantle v Sydney and North Melbourne v Melbourne games, streamed live on the AFL’s YouTube channel, Kayo and 7plus. “Watchalongs”, where fans stream themselves watching a game live and connect online in real time, are a new concept in Australia and, if experience overseas is any indication, here to stay. “It goes back to the idea that media is changing, and social media is a massive part of the media industry,” Michael Neill, the head of Fox Footy, said. “It won’t get any smaller. We’d be foolish if we didn’t look at these new ideas and different ways to broadcast. “The immediacy of his posts and how he gets his opinion out there really quick, it’s out there and it’s different. “It comes from an ex-player’s perspective as well, and from someone who’s very smart when it comes to communication and how to get his message out there.” For Seven, it gives the network another way to reach the younger market.



“Working with creators who love the game allows us to connect with audiences in authentic new ways,” Seven’s head of sport digital Kirsty Bradmore said. “We are continually exploring more ways to innovate our broadcast offering for viewers across Australia.” This collaboration drew 250,000 live viewers across the league’s YouTube channel, Kayo, Foxtel and 7plus to watch while Gorringe and co-hosts – Seven reporter Xander McGuire and Collingwood AFLW captain and Kayo personality Ruby Schleicher – casually discussed the game, as opposed to the serious analysis on the main coverage. Socceroos goalkeeper Patrick Beach, a GWS fan, featured at half-time. ‘People aren’t just following Dan because they know who he is – they’re following him because they genuinely value his perspective on sport and the content he creates.’ Nathan Powell of creator technology platform Fabulate “Dan has been with us for a year now doing some hardcore engagement stuff,” Haagsma said. “He’s part of that strategy. For us, looking at how we attract, retain and engage with our avid fans is a different proposition to our younger fans. “We knew we needed to engage a different strategy. We can’t put highlights on TikTok and go, ‘That will bring the kids in’. Dan has got a voice that we know speaks in a different way, and just resonates. He’s authentic in his point of view, and he loves the game.” Gorringe’s channel markets itself as “unfiltered and unqualified”. The wider football community saw this side in March after he aired a voice memo left by Docherty of a candid and expletive-laden analysis of his former club’s failings in their thumping by Sydney on the opening night of the season. Gorringe did not check with Docherty if the message was to be aired, as is the practice in mainstream media, drawing condemnation from Whateley – who slammed him for “reprehensible behaviour”.

World.title: Knock on wood, but I think I’ve wasted enough time on silly superstitions
World.content:
August 1, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

We were sitting outside in the sun, on the broad steps of Sydney’s new fish market, when a bird flew overhead and launched a massive poo on the young woman sitting in front of us. The “dropping” was enormously accurate and voluminous, covering all of her left hand, part of her left arm and much of her dress. Keen to make her feel better, I told her: “They say it brings good luck.” What’s so bad about a black cat? Getty Images Her boyfriend turned with a smile. “In that case,” he says, “she’s in for a lot of good luck. Heaps of it.” At which point he began helping with the laborious clean-up. What are the origins of these superstitions? Who was the first person to see someone cop a flying splodge of bird poo, and then say: “They say it brings good luck”?



I understand the principle: something unfortunate has happened, so you want to make the person feel better. But why bird poo? We don’t offer this consolation after other misfortunes. If someone smacks their head into a low-lying branch, we don’t say: “Lucky dog! You better buy a lottery ticket.” If you get mugged, the thief pushing you to the ground and stealing your phone, the next person along doesn’t help you to your feet with the cheery observation: “Well, there’s nothing like a violent mugging to bring a bit of good luck.” Most superstitions make no sense. Why does a rabbit foot bring great fortune? It certainly didn’t work for the rabbit from which it was removed. And what’s so bad about a black cat? You wouldn’t dream of judging a person according to the colour of their skin, but apparently cats are fair game. It’s true my generation didn’t have YouTube or Netflix, but frankly we were flat-out keeping the devil at bay. When I was growing up, we lived in a world of superstitions. We were told not to step on the cracks in the pavement, to avoid the number 13, and to never open an umbrella when indoors. Saying something positive about oneself or hopeful about the future was generally frowned upon. But if you insisted – “hopefully I’ll pass my exams”, “no way will I crash my bike” – you had to immediately say “knock on wood” and then find some wood on which to knock. Since most 1970s houses were constructed from a mix of fibro, brown linoleum and orange Laminex, this was often hard to achieve.



Also, every time someone sneezed you had to say “bless you”, which apparently stopped the devil from using that moment of inattention to enter their soul. If you spilt salt, you also had to throw some over your left shoulder (using your right arm) which had the excellent effect of blinding the devil as he hovered at your shoulder. It’s true my generation didn’t have YouTube or Netflix, but frankly we were flat-out keeping the devil at bay. Special occasions such as birthdays were marked by a dinner of roast chicken, the climax of which involved two people grasping the “wish bone” and tearing it in two, good fortune going to the person who ended up with the larger bit of bone. The chicken, already having been throttled, plucked and baked, might have wondered about the purpose of this final indignity, yet it was not possible to eat a chicken while leaving its furcula alone. At Christmas, meanwhile, a silver sixpence would be baked into the Christmas pudding, ready to bring good luck to whoever found it. Or bad luck if you were a seven-year-old and ended up with it stuck in your windpipe, a leading cause of Christmas hospitalisations. The same coin, should it be located in the pudding or returned later by the surgeon, could then be offered as payment for a kitchen knife should you wish to give a knife as a present. It was bad luck to give knives as gifts – it would “cut” the friendship – so the gift had to be turned into a purchase. We were also told we could get rid of warts by “washing our hands in moonlight”, or rubbing them with a piece of meat which you’d then bury in the backyard. If you’ve ever found an old chop bone in your backyard, it was buried there by some warty kid.



You may think this was a charmingly enchanted world, but it did add a lot of fuss to the simplest of tasks, as we were constantly forced to leap over cracks, throw salt over our shoulders, and search for wood to knock upon. In hay fever season, you’d bless more people than the local priest. Related Article Opinion

Health I’m just a creature of habit. Sometimes that creature is a gorilla Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist Did any of the superstitions make sense? Perhaps a couple. I still avoid walking beneath a ladder, based on the practical consideration that a bucket of paint might be up there somewhere, ready to fall on my head. I also believe that it’s bad luck to put shoes on a table – the bad luck being the transmission of some nasty bug, picked up off the floor of a Sydney bus. As for those low-flying birds at the Sydney Fish Market, I’m betting they did bring good luck. That young woman’s boyfriend was so solicitous, tenderly dabbing her with napkins. It was probably the confirmation for which she’d been hoping: this one was a keeper. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: An ‘informal’ will and the missing jewellery: What will happen to Virginia Giuffre’s $30 million estate?
World.content:
Virginia Giuffre was trying to reclaim control. In early January 2025, she was allegedly assaulted by her husband, Robbie Giuffre, during a family holiday in Dunsborough, Western Australia. Robbie then secured a family violence restraining order against Virginia, which banned the prominent Epstein accuser from contacting her two youngest children for six months. It also meant she was not allowed to go to the family’s beachfront home in Perth, which is where her belongings – including important documents, her memoir manuscript, jewellery and mementos – were kept. So Virginia decided to take back some control and spoil herself.



Virginia’s carer, Cheryl Myers, estimates the mother of three spent about $100,000 at luxury jeweller Linneys, and a local pearl retailer, on jewellery for her mother, and diamond rings and necklaces for herself. She had the money to splurge. As Good Weekend senior writer and Walkley Award-winner Melissa Fyfe and WAtoday journalist Carla Hildebrandt reveal in The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald’s four-part investigative podcast, Virginia, the payments Virginia received from various confidential settlements with prominent people – such as the man formerly known as Prince Andrew – came to the equivalent of $US25 million ($35.6 million).



What’s remarkable about this shopping spree is not the amount of money Virginia spent. Rather, as Fyfe and Hildebrandt reveal in episode four of Virginia – out today – it’s that, more than a year on from Virginia’s death, no one seems to know where the jewellery is. Related Article Visual story

Domestic violence ‘Mommy pls call’: The secret ‘scrapbook’ of Virginia Giuffre “Everybody wants to know about the jewellery,” says Myers. “A couple of days after Virginia had passed, one of Virginia’s friends called me, and asked me, ‘Where was the jewellery?’ And I was like, ‘I’ve got no idea’. “She said, ‘Well, we’ve been to the house, me and Rob, and we’ve looked everywhere for the jewellery, and we can’t find any’. And I said, ‘Well, I don’t know’.” But the jewellery is only one part of the puzzle. Virginia also had a chunk of money in cryptocurrency, and now no one knows what happened to that investment.



Virginia Giuffre is pictured here outside a Manhattan court after Jeffrey Epstein’s death in 2019. She received the equivalent of $US25 million in confidential payments after multiple legal battles over the years. AP Following Virginia’s suicide in April 2025, the rift between her family in the United States, including her two brothers, and Robbie worsened. They are now embroiled in a legal battle over Virginia’s estate, which is estimated to be worth up to $30 million, including the compensation payments, assets, investment properties and book royalties. Virginia, whose divorce from Robbie had not been finalised before her death, died without a valid will. She was supposed to sign it on April 26, 2025 – the day after she died – and had marked this date on the magnetic whiteboard on her fridge. Myers and Virginia’s Perth lawyer, Karrie Louden, say Virginia had an “informal will” expressed to Louden and also emailed to her accountant in February 2025.



“I don’t want Robbie blowing my children’s money on himself.” Virginia Giuffre’s diary notes, written before her death This is backed by Virginia’s brothers and their wives. The “informal will” stipulates a small amount of money going to Virginia’s family and friends, including Myers and her brothers, but the bulk to her children and a small amount to Robbie. They say she wanted the money held in trust until the kids turned 25. Related Article Investigation

Good Weekend Isolated, scared, forlorn: The heartbreaking final months of Virginia Giuffre’s life According to court filings, Virginia’s sons Christian and Noah – backed by their father – are arguing their mother lacked “testamentary capacity” when the informal will was created. If Christian and Noah win, Robbie stands to inherit just over a third of what’s left after the divorce settlement, with the remainder divided between the three children: Christian, Noah, and their daughter.



That would make Robbie the main beneficiary, and most likely the administrator of Virginia’s worldwide estate. “What a terrible, tragic story that everything that she fought for against monsters of sexual assault on the most powerful level, every single dollar is going to go back into the hands of her final abuser, and that’s the last chapter,” says Sky Roberts. “Can we imagine that that’s the way the story ends? Because I can’t, and I can’t live with that.” Listen to the fourth episode of Virginia – where hosts Fyfe and Hildebrandt reveal Virginia’s arrest weeks before her death, the real story behind the bus crash that prompted Virginia to tell the world she had days to live, the complicated truth behind her posthumous memoir, and how Virginia’s suicide is part of a wider, systemic problem that is impacting other Australian women – in the player above, wherever you get your podcasts, or click here.



A statement from Robbie Giuffre’s lawyers says the following: “What appears to be an orchestrated attempt by persons to gain financially from Virginia’s death by making unsubstantiated allegations, when they should have been aware of Virginia’s medical conditions, is simply disgraceful. “In the late Virginia Giuffre’s book published and titled Nobody’s Girl, Virginia praised and thanked Robert for his support of her throughout their marriage and in particular, her struggle to be heard.” If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), Lifeline 131 114, or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636.
