World.title: If you wanted to create the ultimate ski resort, this place would be the template
World.content:
InspirationSki holidays If you wanted to create the ultimate ski resort, this place would be the template Jim Darby August 1, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When it comes to rating snow resorts, so much of it is subjective. By and large, skiers and snowboarders relate in a tribal way to one or two destinations, sticking with them from their early days and gathering, over the seasons, an intimate understanding of the way they work. A big mountain with ski-in/ski-out village and 750cm average annual snowfall. Big White Ski Resort Suppose you’re a traveller though, looking to explore some new terrain, what do you look for? One thing that immediately springs to mind is how much snowmaking there is. If there is major snowmaking infrastructure, that isn’t necessarily a negative, it’ll guarantee coverage. But if you come across a popular destination with little or no snowmaking, then that’s telling you a lot about the quality and reliability of its snow cover. Somewhere like Canada’s Big White, for example. Indeed, if you were setting out to build your fantasy snow resort, you could do worse than use Big White as a template. The highest peak in British Columbia’s Okanagan Highlands, the resort has an average annual snow fall of 750 centimetres, making for an operating season nudging five months.



You’d want your fantasy resort to be close to an airport – for Big White, Kelowna is 55-minutes down the road. You’d want it to have a village with some scale but still some character and heart, where most of the accommodation was ski-in/ski-out. 



It was in a perilous state financially and the story goes that the patriarch, Desmond Schumann, bought it for one Canadian dollar. He also had to honour about $C4.5 million in debt that came with it, but what he got was the lease on the existing snowfield and vast areas beyond and the ability to develop the real estate in the village. So it was “see you later” Hotham and “how’s it going?” Canada. The resort chief executive is Schumann’s grandson, Peter Plimmer, a keen skier but also a keen mountain biker, with an aim to expand that side of the business, which is booming in some parts of Canada. But back to our fantasy snowfield – what matters as much as anything is the quality of the terrain, the runs you’ll be using. The groomed terrain here is seemingly endless, miles and miles of smooth runs, sometimes steep, sometimes with some big rolling bumps to better let you work the shape of your skis (or board). They’re like big, long, beautiful fairways. Fresh tracks at Big White. My guide, Gavin Crawford – another Mount Hotham veteran who now calls Big White home – shows me the mountain, and it takes most of the day to cover it. His tip on the groomed runs? “Ski Sun Run early, the groomer drivers use it to head home and make their final pass on skier’s left of the run.”



Much of the terrain (54 per cent to be exact) is of the cruisy intermediate kind, but there are also steeps up high for more of a challenge, a terrain park for the young and restless and some long beginner runs. And then there are the trees to ski through and the snow ghosts – trees in their frozen winter state – to ski around, all of this with views into the vast mountain ranges into the distance. And if you need a hand to find your way here, mountain hosts lead 90-minute complimentary mountain tours departing from the village centre daily at 10.15am. Apart from the village centre, there are base areas for day visitors who might be staying in Kelowna, for example. Big White also has an extensive trail network for cross country skiers and “the biggest tube park around” (that’s tobogganing on big tyre inner tubes). Quite the complete experience.



THE DETAILS Related Article Ski holidays The Aussie former ski instructor now running North America’s No.1 resort STAY + SKI

Big White’s POWDer Card, available in January, offers flexible three‑ to five‑day lift pass options, while season passes are the best value for guests planning to ski more frequently (they sell “a couple of thousand” of these annually to Australians). For a package including lift passes, equipment hire, accommodation and resort transfers, go through Big White Direct Bookings. See bigwhite.com FLY

Air New Zealand (airnewzealand.com.au) flies daily to Vancouver where there are onward connecting flights to Kelowna (about an hour in the air). Big White is a 55-minute drive from Kelowna Airport; there are frequent shuttle connections in winter, hire cars are also available. Go through Big White Direct Bookings for shuttles. The writer flew to Canada as a guest of Air New Zealand and visited Big White as a guest of Destination British Columbia (supernaturalbc.com) and Big White.

World.title: Eliza McCartney finally claims elusive Commonwealth crown
World.content:
After years of injuries that at times left her wondering if she would ever compete again, New Zealand pole vaulter Eliza McCartney has finally added Commonwealth Games gold to her decorated career.

In challenging conditions at Glasgow's Scotstoun Stadium, the 2016 Olympic bronze medallist edged Australia's Nina Kennedy on countback in a tense final. Fellow Kiwi Imogen Ayris clinched bronze, matching her effort in Birmingham four years ago.

McCartney and defending champion Kennedy both cleared 4.65m, but the New Zealander took the title after clearing the height at the first time of asking. Kennedy needed two attempts at 4.65m before both athletes were unable to clear 4.70m.

It is the first Commonwealth Games title for the 29-year-old, who won silver on the Gold Coast in 2018 and has spent much of the past decade battling chronic injuries.

In a competition made difficult by cold conditions and a troublesome crosswind, consistency proved decisive.

While neither McCartney nor Kennedy could find a clearance at 4.70m, McCartney's cleaner card through the earlier heights ultimately made the difference.

Fellow Kiwi Imogen Ayris completed a memorable night for the team, claiming bronze with a clearance of 4.55m to bookend the medal placings for New Zealand.

Olivia McTaggart finished fourth after bowing out at 4.30m.

The 25-year-old was visibly devastated after her third and final miss, remaining on the landing mat for several moments as she composed herself before eventually rising to acknowledge the crowd.

World.title: Commonwealth Games: Eliza McCartney wins gold, Sami Donnelly gets second silver medal
World.content:
Kiwi cyclist Sami Donnelly has claimed a second Commonwealth Games silver medal in as many days.

Donnelly initially was deemed to have won bronze in the Women's 10km Scratch Race Final, but a disqualification bumped her into the silver medal position.

Competing at her first games, the 24-year-old won her first medal as part of the 4000m Team Pursuit on Friday.

A total of three New Zealanders lined up in the Women's Scratch Race final, with Prudence Fowler and Olympic double-medalist Ally Wollaston finishing 16th and 18th respectively.

New Zealand pole vaulter Eliza McCartney has won gold, with team-mate Imogen Ayris clinching bronze.

New Zealand pole vaulter Eliza McCartney has won gold at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Photosport

The 29-year-old held off defending games champion Nina Kennedy, of Australia.

This would be McCartney's first gold at the games, alongside the silver she won on the Gold Coast in 2018.

Para-cyclist Devon Briggs had also won a gold medal for New Zealand, and set a new Commonwealth Games record in the process.

Para-cyclist Devon Briggs has won gold in the 1km C1-3 time trial final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. supplied

Briggs has taken first place in the 1km C1-3 time trial final in Glasgow.

Earlier cyclist Ellese Andrews' was taken out of the medal race in the individual sprint.

The Olympic champion was beaten in consecutive races in a best-of-three quarter final against Welsh rider Emma Finucane.

Ellesse Andrews during the Women's Sprint Qualifying at the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games. Olly Hassell / SWPix / Photosport

Andrews was also part of the New Zealand sprint team that was bundled out during qualifying on Friday.

Rebecca Petch and Olivia King both were unable to get past the round-of-16 stage in their respective sprints.

On the endurance side, Bryony Botha was given a second life in the 4000m individual pursuit following the disqualification of two Australian riders but was beaten by Scotland's Erin Boothman.

AusCycling executive general manager of performance Jesse Korf addresses media after two of his team were disqualified. RNZ / Adam Burns

Botha initially failed to qualify, placing fifth, as did team-mate Emily Shearman, who finished eighth.

However, officials said Australian Felicity Wilson-Haffenden, who originally finished fourth, broke protocols due to strapping on her shoulder that "altered her morphology".

Fellow Australian rider Sophie Edwards was also disqualified due to a non-compliant helmet.

World.title: 'Very controlling' Mother of Marokopa children speaks out about her relationship with Tom Phillips
World.content:
By Mihingarangi Forbes and Annabelle Lee-Mather for Mata Reports.

For most people, the Tom Phillips case began when he first disappeared with his children into the bush in 2021 and ended when he was shot dead by police last year.

But for the children's mother, Cat Christey, the saga stretches back many more years, through a volatile and sometimes violent relationship - and the nightmare she's experienced continues.

In her first interview since her children were recovered from the bush, Cat told Mata Reports: "I would like to see anybody else endure what I have endured for all these years.

"People think that this started … when Thomas abducted the children the first time. This started long before that. This has been going on for a long, long time."

'There was no room for compromise'

As she still deals with agency meetings and the fallout from the dramatic end to Phillips' time on the run, Cat has spoken out about the difficulties of her relationship with him and the toll it has taken.

"He was a good provider but very controlling. It was a very... imbalanced relationship. His views on what a marriage should be were different to my own. We should have been a team. But there was no room for compromise, it was his way or the highway.

"And he liked to be in control, he was a dictator."

For most people, the Tom Phillips case began when he first disappeared with his children into the bush in 2021 and ended when he was shot dead by police last year - not for Cat Christey. RNZ / MATA

Phillips first took the couple's three children into the bush near Marokopa in the western Waikato in September 2021 without telling Cat where he was going. They were separated at the time.

He returned several weeks later, but then, in December 2021, he went bush with the children again.

Phillips remained a fugitive until he was killed in a shoot-out with police following a ram-raid in Piopio.

Cat says that during their relationship, Phillips "wasn't extremely violent" although she described slaps and how he once strangled her.

Tom Phillips’ former partner speaks to Mihingarangi Forbes Morning Report Download MP3 7m

But she was more concerned about his psychological abuse.

"He would control all the finances, he would take vehicle keys away from me … he would control who I saw and when I saw them."

Cat describes a volatile and sometimes violent relationship. RNZ / MATA

A fascination with guns

She says Phillips had a fascination with guns and that at one point, she twice rang 111 to tell the police about it. However, she says, Phillips took the phone off her and hung up both times. "I truly believed police would show up because it was a 111 call … but police did not come."

Phillips ordered her out of the house after that incident. Although he later begged her to come back, Cat says she wouldn't.

A few days later, he began proceedings against her and the situation spiralled over the next few years.

Cat says Tom Phillips had a fascination with guns. RNZ / MATA

Cat found out about the shooting and the discovery of her children after police had first told a Netflix documentary crew - a documentary she says she told the officer in charge, Detective Inspector Andrew Saunders, that she objected to

"I was dead set against it when they first told me. It was very blunt and I said they do not have my permission.

"[Saunders] told me they didn't need my permission, that they were just letting me know."

Cat says she objected to a Netflix documentary about the case. RNZ / MATA

Not a victim

It's one way in which she says she feels like she has been disregarded by police throughout the case.

For instance she says that she only found out through the media about the fact the police had decided not to charge anyone with assisting Phillips while he was on the run and that the case was no longer being actively investigated.

Also, she says, she was declined support for counselling because she was not considered a victim of crime.

"I had reached out to Victim Support … in the hopes that they might be able to assist with some sessions with my psychologist."

Cat feels like she has been disregarded by police throughout the case. RNZ / MATA

Cat says Victim Support spoke to the police about her situation but was told nothing could be done.

"Police refused to do a referral stating that we're not victims of crime." This was because what had happened to her was not considered domestic violence, a point disputed by Auckland University associate professor of law Carrie Leonetti.

"This abduction, I think, was an act of child abuse, but it was also an act of domestic violence against these children's mother," says Leonetti.

"Taking children and saying, 'You will not see them for three years, they will live or die depending on what I decide' is an act of domestic violence."

Cat was told Victim Support spoke to the police about her situation but was told nothing could be done. RNZ / MATA

Even Police Minister Mark Mitchell, who would not comment specifically about police actions, said he personally believed Cat was a victim.

"Any right-minded person would say that a mother, regardless of the circumstances, when they're separated from their children, and they've been through the tragedy that we all saw unfold in front of the country, a lot of people would probably consider her as much a victim in terms of what has happened," Mitchell told Mata.

"But I cannot talk to the police response other than saying, in my experience, police are very, very good at making sure they identify, communicate and support [victims] as much as they can."

Police Minister Mark Mitchell said he personally believed Cat was a victim. RNZ / MATA

Agencies respond

In response to questions from Mata Reports about Cat's treatment and allegations, Detective Inspector Ross McKay said: "A number of the matters you are asking about are subject to the government inquiry into the disappearance of the Phillips children, and it would therefore be inappropriate for us to comment at this time."

A spokesperson for Manaaki Tāngata Victim Support said the organisation could not comment on individual cases, but added: "The Victims Assistance Scheme, which Victim Support administers on behalf of the Ministry of Justice, has specific eligibility criteria.

"Our Support Workers carefully consider each person's circumstances and identify the support available to them."

A public inquiry was tasked with considering whether government agencies took all practicable steps to protect the welfare and safety of the children. RNZ / MATA

A public inquiry into the disappearance of Phillips and his children has been delivered to Attorney-General Chris Bishop.

The inquiry, led by the Honourable Simon Moore KC, was set up under the orders of the previous Attorney-General, Judith Collins, and tasked with considering whether government agencies took all practicable steps to protect the welfare and safety of the children.

Bishop says the report will be presented to Parliament once the government has considered the recommendations and how to deal with suppression orders that are in place in the High Court and Family Court.

World.title: Otago councils want to form unitary authority - without Dunedin
World.content:
By Patrick Manning, Massey University journalism student

A Dunedin city councillor says a proposal to exclude the city from a new Otago unitary authority is "ridiculous", but the mayor behind it says it makes sense.

And Dunedin's mayor says she thinks the city needs its own council - and shouldn't join in to a single Otago council.

Central Otago District and Clutha District councils have both voted in favour of merging together with Queenstown Lakes District Council.

Clutha mayor Jock Martin has proposed three options for the model - one which combines the three district councils into one authority, a second which includes rural parts of Dunedin (Strath Taieri, Taieri Plains and Waihemo) and a third which would add on Gore District.

All options exclude urban Dunedin.

Dunedin city councillor Andrew Simms said the whole of Otago should be encompassed into one unitary authority - including Dunedin.

Dunedin City councillor Andrew Simms. Supplied / Dunedin City Council

"In my view it's just naked self interest and doesn't address the opportunities there are for all of us by actually building a bigger unitary authority for all of Otago.

"It would bring benefits for everybody including Clutha and including Central Otago. I don't understand why people can't see that vision."

He felt it was the government's intention to amlagamate smaller rural councils with larger metro areas.

"To suggest smaller rural councils are going to lop parts off what is the largest city in Otago, I don't know if anybody's taking it too seriously."

Simms said he believed Martin was trying to separate Taieri out from Dunedin due to government criteria for amalgamation.

"They're trying to gain control of those river catchments because that's part of the criteria. So it just so happens that they need those parts of Dunedin to do that. I just don't think anyone's thought it through."

Martin rejected he made the proposals in self-interest.

He said Simms comments were course.

Clutha mayor Jock Martin. Supplied / Clutha District Council

"There's definitely no self interest, I was elected by our district to lead for our people and they are front of mind."

He confirmed his proposal was intended to include all the catchments.

"Everything that happens at the head of the Clutha has an impact on our ratepayers in the lower clutha, so that's why I proposed those bondaries.

"Its nothing against Dunedin, its around catchments and the environment."

When asked why he wanted to exclude urban Dunedin from the unitary authority, he said it was based on public feedback from a survey run by Clutha District Council.

"57 percent of those that completed the survey want to stay rural. It's the rural voice that everyone is concerned about if we are urbanised with the likes of Dunedin.

"It's not about us or them, it's about ... doing right for our people and what're we doing right about our environment."

Martin said he was keeping his councillors up to speed weekly with developments.

"People are telling me there's conversations in the shadows and all sorts but that's just complete nonsense.

"At least by entering the head start we have some control over our destiny."

Queenstown Lakes District Council would meet to consider the proposal on Monday.

Dunedin needs to be its own council or coastal council - mayor

Dunedin Mayor Sophie Barker. Supplied / Frank Film

Dunedin's mayor Sophie Barker said she wasn't in favour of a single council for Otago.

In a Facebook post earlier this week, Barker said the best options were a Dunedin unitary council, or a Dunedin coastal unitary council based around water catchments.

"I am not in favour of a single unitary for Otago.

"We're too big and diverse an area with a very rural/ urban divide - and it looks like most inland Otago residents recognise that and aren't keen for a unitary Otago council either."

Barker said a report by consultants Morrison Low said numbers didn't add up for Dunedin in terms of significant savings.

"We'd double our ratepayers, but have 10 times the land area to manage including areas with significant infrastructure deficits that could crowd out our ability to get stuff done in Dunedin.

"I don't believe mass centralisation will deliver significant benefits for our residents."

But Barker said she didn't agree with having any of Dunedin's Taieri catchment split up, especially the "Pearl of the Plain" Mosgiel.

World.title: Doctors considering weight-loss drugs for detained man to be kept in physical restraints
World.content:
An autistic man who has spent more than 20 years in secure care has become so "obese" his doctors are considering giving him the weight-loss drug Wegovy so physical restraints he has outgrown can again be used on him, the Family Court has heard.

The man, known only as 'J', has been taken on 10 outings in the past year but never been allowed to leave the van transporting him. He has also not seen a psychologist in the last year as she had been on leave, then left her role at Auckland's Mason Clinic where he lived.

A long-awaited Family Court review of whether J should remain detained under the Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care and Rehabilitation) Act began on Friday.

The review was ordered by the Supreme Court in August 2025 after it ruled the previous legal test used to detain J was wrong. It told the Family Court to have another look at his case.

The hearing has been delayed for almost a year due to trouble securing court time and the availability of witnesses.

A specialist assessor told the court the outings were part of efforts to gradually increase J's exposure to, and tolerance of, being in the community, despite him remaining inside the van each time.

"But that does not take away from these experiences. He sees things outside the window," the assessor, a psychiatrist, said.

Clinicians were now considering taking J to a quiet beach and allowing him outside the van for the first time to test how he coped, he said.

"It's hard to know what [his] response will be to that kind of outing, but I think it certainly deserves to be tried."

The court also heard J had begun spending more time outside his private rooms where he lived alone within the Auckland's Mason Clinic to interact with staff and other clients.

While he did not have access to his psychologist for the last year other staff interacted with him in a "psychologically informed manner", the assessor said.

He has recommended J remain in secure care for another three years to give him time to rehabilitate, and for a new home in the community to be found for him.

"I think that's a realistic timeframe."

A February 2026 assessment of J found he continued to make threats and was occasionally violent but some of his behaviours, including an obsession with feet, were not sexual in nature.

The assessor said J had more recently appeared "more cheerful" due to the gradual introduction of "socialisation" activities.

However, he admitted the pace of rehabilitation had been slower than intended due to staff availability.

The court heard J had become severely obese, which meant mechanical restraints could no longer be used on him. This limited the number of staff who felt comfortable accompanying him on outings.

The Mason Clinic was considering treating him with weight-loss drug Wegovy so he could fit restraints again. These restraints were made of soft "leather-like" fabric wrapped around his wrists, attached to a belt, designed to restrict his movement.

Under cross examination by the court-appointed lawyer for J, Andrew Finnie, the assessor said if J was released into the community, he would likely be arrested "in a short space of time" as he was likely to engage in "potentially aggressive...socially embarrassing behaviour".

The lawyer for J's mother, Tony Ellis, argued J's detention was not justified given the original offence of breaking windows would have resulted in only three months' imprisonment. He likened J's detention to being like a "gorilla kept in a cage", saying he was being treated like an animal, not a human being.

Now in his 40s, J has been detained since 2006 after breaking windows in 2004. Repeated assessments have found he was too dangerous to release. For the past five years he has spent almost all his time in seclusion within his "cluster" of two rooms and a bathroom at the Mason Clinic.

World.title: Police officers rescue seal pup wandering through South Auckland suburb
World.content:
Police say a seal pup that was spotted making its way through the South Auckland suburb of Papakura has been taken back to its natural environment.

In a social media post, Counties Manukau police said they received a call from a concerned member of the public and then consulted with the Department of Conservation on the best way to help.

Police consulted DOC about how to help the seal pup. Supplied / Counties Manukau Police

After receiving advice, officers were able to relocate the pup back to a more appropriate place.

"An ex-seal-ent job by everyone involved and a happy ending for this little traveller!" the post said.

World.title: Police officer shot by Tom Phillips returns to work
World.content:
The officer who was shot in the head by Tom Phillips is returning to work.

The officer, who has not been named, was critically injured when Phillips shot him several times last September.

Phillips died shortly after a shootout with another officer, when police were called to reports of a burglary in the early hours of 8 September 2025, after 1358 days in the bush with his children.

It is understood the officer who was shot underwent numerous surgeries at Waikato Hospital, after being hit in his skull and his right shoulder.

Waikato District Commander Scott Gemmell said he had made positive progress in his recovery and was continuing rehabilitation.

World.title: Weekend weather: Snow warnings and strong wind watches as chilly days ahead
World.content:
The country is set to face a chilly weekend as subantarctic winds move up the country, MetService says.

In the South Island, temperatures will start to drop in the south on Friday morning as the southerly pushes through Otago, and then into Canterbury this afternoon, with colder temperatures expected overnight Friday and Saturday.

MetService has road snowfall warnings in place for South Island mountain passes on Friday and the Desert Road on Saturday, with motorists told to avoid travel.

The mountain passes include Crown Range Road, Lindis Pass, Milford Road, Arthur's, Porters and Lewis Pass.

The Civil Defence said just a few centimetres of snow would make driving dangerous on Desert Road, and said to only do so if necessary.

MetService forecasted snow showers lowering to 800 metres and 1 to 2cm of snow could accumulate about the summit.

Meanwhile, the northern Cook Strait and the North Taranaki Bight have experienced thunderstorms.

Strong wind watches are also in place for parts of the South Island.

Coastal Otago's watch is in place from noon to 10pm on Friday, where southwest winds may approach severe gale in exposed places.

A watch for Christchurch, Banks Peninsula and the Canterbury Plains kicks off from 5pm Friday until 1am Saturday.

The watch for coastal Southland and southern Fiordland kicked in late Thursday and continues until 5pm Friday.

All watches have a moderate chance of being upgraded to a warning.

MetService said subantarctic air was being dragged north by southerly winds - resulting in "bitterly cold conditions".

It would make temperatures feel close to -2C in Invercargill on Friday afternoon "and even colder for higher elevations".

The cold weather would move up to the North Island during Saturday, it said, "with the wind chill cooling things to a feels-like temperature of just 1C in Wellington".

For those running or on the sidelines at the Taupō marathon, meteorologist Braydon While suggested dressing warm.

"Those preparing for the marathon, whether competing or cheering on the sidelines, will want to wrap up warm and bring a cosy jacket in case a few showers manage to sneak over the hills."

Sunday would bring clear skies for most of the country, MetService said, and "widespread frosts".

World.title: Infantino's advisor quits as FIFA's World Cup plan triggers backlash
World.content:
A senior advisor to FIFA President Gianni Infantino resigned in protest at plans to sell a stake in the World Cup on Friday, as European football threatened a boycott and regional confederations united in opposition to the controversial proposal.

Carlos Cordeiro resigned with immediate effect, calling the plan "a bad deal for football".

Mr Cordeiro, who was appointed in 2021 by Mr Infantino to help shape FIFA's future, said the soccer body was "mortgaging football's future without any compelling justification".

"It is a bad deal for FIFA's Member Associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game," Mr Cordeiro said in a statement.

A former banker and ex-US Soccer Federation vice president, Mr Cordeiro added that he had no involvement in the proposal and opposed it "unequivocally".

Senior adviser to FIFA president Carlos Cordeiro resigned with immediate effect. (Reuters: Kent Nishimura)

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham also called for Mr Infantino to resign over the plans, labelling them an "outrageous".

"The idea that it could even be brought forward, in my view, shows that the FIFA [president] is the wrong man to lead the organisation," Mr Burnham said.

Despite the mounting opposition, Switzerland-based FIFA said "incorrect media reports" this week had disrupted its planned consultation process but that it would press on with putting the proposal in front of its 211 national football associations.

"We will proceed with this consultation process to ensure that each MA (Member Association) has the ability to express its vote based on facts," it said in a statement issued in the middle of the European night.

FIFA has proposed creating a $US 20-billion subsidiary, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run the World Cup and its other events, with a stake of up to 20 per cent to be offered to external investors.

Thrive Eternal, a fund run by Thrive Capital, founded by Joshua Kushner, was expected to lead the proposed investor group, FIFA said. Joshua is the brother of Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law.

UEFA leads opposition to FIFA World Cup plan

The European football association, UEFA, has led the widespread opposition to the proposal, accusing FIFA of putting the sport's "soul" up for sale.

FIFA equity plan hits strong opposition FIFA boss Gianni Infantino's controversial plan to sell 20 per cent of the organisation's commercial operations to private investors hits trouble, with European nations threatening a World Cup boycott if it goes ahead.

On Thursday, UEFA's 55 member nations voted unanimously to boycott all FIFA tournaments, less than two weeks after Spain were crowned World Cup champions.

"Nobody is selling football. This is not something FIFA would ever entertain," FIFA responded in Friday's statement.

"Everyone has the right to express their opposition and to seek further clarification but no single entity can claim to represent all 211 MAs around the world.

"Each MA should be allowed to review the proposal and have a say in shaping their own future. These are the democratic principles of FIFA."

CONCACAF, the regional federation for North America, Central America and the Caribbean, rejected the proposal during a meeting on Thursday but the 41-member body did not follow UEFA with a boycott threat.

The Asian Football Confederation, comprised of 47 members, issued a statement on Friday saying it "stands in solidarity" with UEFA and CONCACAF, but also stopped short of threatening a boycott.

The AFC, which has not historically been as frequent or vehement a critic of FIFA as its European counterpart UEFA, questioned the viability of the proposal following an overwhelmingly negative response.

It also raised doubts over FIFA's decision-making processes in a thinly-veiled attack on Mr Infantino.

FIFA says process is a democratic one

This week, Mr Infantino said in a letter to all member associations that they would receive $40 million each if they agreed to FIFA's proposal by September 19.

On Friday, FIFA said that it would not go ahead with the plan without the support of the majority of its member associations.

"These principles underpin the FFE proposal: unprecedented development funding, truly global ownership of the commercial opportunities of our sport, and full self-determination through a democratic process for all MAs," FIFA said.

UEFA, CONCACAF and the AFC combined have 143 associations, well over half of FIFA's 211 members.

FIFA boss reveals $US20b plan to sell World Cup FIFA president Gianni Infantino earns more criticism after unveiling a brazen plan to "unleash the commercial potential" of the World Cup.

However, not all individual member nations would be certain to follow their federations' line.

Czech Football Association President David Trunda told Sky Sports that he could see the "positive impact of FIFA's intentions", while the Mexican Football Federation said it would study the proposal before deciding its position, despite CONCACAF's rejection.

Xabi Alonso, a World Cup winner with Spain in 2010, said on Friday that football had to prioritise the people who watch the game, not private interests.

"We have to defend the interests of all the people," the Chelsea coach told reporters in Sydney.

"I think that it's the common feeling of football people that we want something that we keep in the hands of everyone, that it's for all the people. So, hopefully it won't happen."

Reuters

World.title: Freo all but seal minor premiership with hard-fought win over Bulldogs
World.content:
Josh Treacy has broken through the Western Bulldogs' flood in his 100-game milestone as Fremantle all but sealed the minor premiership with a 37-point win at Perth Stadium.

Fremantle's perfect record in Perth this season was under threat in Friday night's blockbuster after the Bulldogs' flooding tactics ensured scores were level at half-time.

(Getty Images)

But spurred on by 53,524 fans, Fremantle kicked seven goals to one in the second half to secure the 11.12 (78) to 5.11 (41) win.

While key forwards Jye Amiss (0.1 from six disposals) and Pat Voss (1.0 from eight disposals) struggled in the flooded forward line, Treacy used his big frame to take some important contested grabs on the way to 3.2 and eight marks to go with 13 disposals.

Treacy's contested mark above three opponents and subsequent goal early in the final quarter gave Fremantle a 19-point buffer, and more importantly finally broke the spirit of the flood.

It sparked a four-goal burst from the Dockers as they extended their record at Perth Stadium to 11-0 this season.

The win guaranteed a top-two berth and two home finals for Fremantle (18-2).

And if Sydney (14-5) lose to St Kilda on Saturday, the Dockers will be crowned minor premiers with three rounds still remaining.

The Bulldogs (12-8) face North Melbourne, Carlton and Melbourne in their final three rounds, and they may need to win all three in order to snare a top-six berth and avoid the wildcard round.

Ed Richards (26 disposals, nine clearances, 752m gained) and Tom Liberatore (28 disposals, six clearances) racked up big numbers for the Bulldogs, while Cooper Hynes kicked two goals from 22 disposals in the absence of Aaron Naughton and Cody Weightman.

Fremantle star Luke Jackson (26 hitouts, five clearances, 16 disposals, two goals) edged Bulldogs big man Tim English (27 hitouts, one clearance, 15 disposals) in an intriguing ruck battle.

AAP

World.title: It's easy to see why Australia brought a psychiatrist to Glasgow
World.content:
When Kiana Elliott finished fourth for the second straight Commonwealth Games, to say the Australian weightlifter was crestfallen would be an understatement.

Over the Birmingham and Glasgow Games, a combined 11 kilograms of weight on the bar kept the gymnast from back-to-back bronze medals.

After faltering on the 118-kilogram clean and jerk that could have secured her third place on the podium, Elliott sat on the Armadillo stage and dropped her head to a depth only permitted by her background as an elite gymnast.

Australian weightlifter Kiana Rose Elliott after missing her last lift at the 2026 Glasgow Commonwealth Games. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The 29-year-old was distraught to have missed the medals just as she did four years ago in Birmingham, graciously speaking to the media in barely a whisper as she tried to maintain her composure.

For a woman who embodies strength and power, her vulnerability was incredibly affecting.

"It's just a moment in time, and you're just hoping that everything will be there," she said.

"Sometimes it is, and sometimes it isn't."

Competition weightlifting is a tricky beast, with athletes having to walk a fine line between lifting the most they can, while also ensuring they can fall into the optimum weight class.

Kiana started weightlifting after an injury. Now, she's a Comm Games athlete Kiana Elliott thought gymnastics would be her pathway to the podium, but turned to weightlifting after an injury forced her to retire.

Elliott was in the 71kg weight class in Birmingham four years ago. At last year's Commonwealth Championships, she won as a 58kg competitor. In Glasgow, she lifted as a 63kg athlete.

She said it was a "really tough decision" to go up to the higher weights where the lifts need to be bigger, but she did it for her mental health.

"In Australia we do sport and we do life, and I needed my brain and my mind for the rest of my life," she said.

"Pushing my body fat down that low was not a sustainable thing for me, so I chose the competitive option.

"Weightlifting is about lifting weights, it's about lifting more weights, it's not about being a smaller person, and I'm proud that I chose the difficult option and fought my hardest.

"This isn't the end of my story. I'm not done yet."

Kiana Elliott is a study in determination while lifting. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

But for this one moment it was. As painful as the result was, she could drop her shoulders and unclench her jaw in an enormous release of emotion.

"So much has gone into this and while I was hoping for a podium result, I think it's just all a culmination of all that's gone into this starting to come out," she said of her reaction after the competition.

"There's so much to process as part of this; there's more stuff to do when I get home. I think I just need to breathe a sigh of relief and move on."

It was five minutes of wholly self-aware introspection, spoken like a woman who has done and will continue to do a lot of work on her brain.

That reflects an emphasis for the entire Australian team, so much so that, for the first time, they have an in-house psychiatrist travelling with the team.

Australian team psychiatrist Adam Deacon. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Adam Deacon is part of a varied team of experts embedded within the team, with one of the floors of the Team Aus HQ effectively transformed into a mini hospital ward.

"We'd be very surprised if any other country has matched the standards that have been established here in the headquarters," Dr Deacon told ABC Sport.

"There's an extraordinary range of talented, experienced people who are able to cater to the broad needs of the athletes.

"It's really just a pop-up sports medicine clinic where all aspects are covered as it would be in a regular clinic."

The margins are fine and tension is high at meets like the Commonwealth Games. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

And while massage therapists, physios, nutritionists and dietitians have been working to keep Australia's 255 Commonwealth Games athletes physically fit over 10 days of intense competition, Dr Deacon is focusing on their minds.

"I think most athletes would argue when they're in a good mental space they're more likely to perform at a high level," he said.

"And you could argue they can't compete at a high level unless their mental health is well. So I think that's a necessary focus."

The team has travelled with sports psychologists before but, after consultation with the athletes, feedback was received that many of them, with their own dedicated psychologists, would like to stick with those programs.

Dr Deacon provides a different, more clinical than therapeutic, service.

"The athletes are people before they're athletes and they can experience everyday issues and concerns and mental health challenges as we all do," he said.

"There are particular things that arise in this environment, in terms of performance or lack of performance or perceived failure, and that can be really, really challenging for the athletes and also the staff.

Failure is a part of sport, but it's still hard to swallow. (Supplied)

"Injuries, illness, these sort of interruptions are not necessarily expected or anticipated, and that can be enormously stressful, and that's where an acute level of crisis response is sometimes necessary."

Unlike footy players who get to take it "one week at a time", for many the Commonwealth Games is the culmination of four or more years of tireless, single-minded work.

Elliott's teammates Chloe Perkins, who missed her 48kg weight, did not even get a chance to compete, and Brenna Kean and Ridge Barredo, both suffered nasty injuries while on stage at the Armadillo.

Dr Deacon, of course, did not reveal any of the people he had spoken to in the team, but the weightlifters like Elliott, Perkins, Kean and Barredo perhaps best exemplify the risky prospect of this high-stakes quadrennial cycle.

Some athletes seek him out, some are referred to him, and for some he attends their competition for a little extra care.

Whatever form it takes, the Australian team is lucky to have him here.

World.title: Live: Kennedy settles for silver, Aussie teen claims race walk gold
World.content:
(Getty)

Sri Lanka has won its first athletics gold medal since 1950, with Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage triumphing in the men's javelin final.

Pathirage seized the gold with a best throw of 89.75m.

He beat a hot field, with India's 2020 Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra taking silver with 85.83m.

World.title: 'We're not going to the finals': Storm set for 16-year first after loss
World.content:
Melbourne Storm coach Craig Bellamy has conceded his side will not be playing finals in 2026, with the club set to miss out for just the fourth time in its history.

The Storm entered the round 22 clash needing to win all five of their remaining games to finish the season on 32 points, which has been needed to make two of the past three finals series.

Missing captain Harry Grant, five-eighth Cameron Munster, and halfback Jahrome Hughes ruled out 90 minutes before kick-off, the Storm threatened a famous upset win when they led 22-16 early in the second half.

But the Bulldogs rallied with the final four tries of the match to record a sixth win in their last seven matches, and leapfrog North Queensland into the NRL top-eight.

The loss ends Melbourne's realistic chance of making the top eight, but Bellamy said he will not be accepting a drop in standards during the final month of the home and away season.

Melbourne Storm coach Craig Bellamy (left) says his side will not be playing finals in 2026. (NRL)

"If anyone wants to go through the motions, if I see that at training and feel that at training, they won't be playing first grade," he said on Friday.

"At the end of the day, every game is important. It's not quite as important as it has been the last few years because we're not going to the finals now.

"But we're out there to play for each other and play for our fans."

The Storm have only missed finals three times since their inaugural season in 1998. The Victorian club missed finals in 2001 and 2002, the two seasons prior to Craig Bellamy becoming head coach.

Roosters put up 82 points for highest NRL score in 91 years The Roosters have scored the third-most points ever seen in Australian rugby league first grade match and beaten the clock against a hapless North Queensland side.

The only time the Storm have not made finals under Bellamy was in 2010, when the club was not allowed to earn premiership points as punishment for salary cap breaches which led to the stripping of the 2007 and 2009 premierships.

The Storm, who have lost the previous two grand finals, have been one of the league's most injury-affected teams in 2026.

Several players have made their NRL debuts this year for the Storm, including playmakers Hayden Watson and Jai Bowden on Friday night.

Bellamy, who is contracted until the end of the 2028 season, said the tough results the club is going through now will hopefully be worth it in coming seasons.

"We haven't got a lot of that experience playing at the moment, with these guys making their debuts or it's their third or fourth game," Bellamy said.

"But next year and the year after, that experience will be really handy for us.

"It's just hard to see past the results at the moment of our games."

Earlier, the Dolphins consolidated fifth place on the NRL ladder with a nervous 28-22 win over the last-placed St George Illawarra Dragons.

Relive all of Friday's NRL action in the blog below.

World.title: Magpies coach throws support behind Bobby Hill as star exits
World.content:
Collingwood's Bobby Hill has exited the club amid support from coach Craig McRae after the premiership hero was racially abused on social media.

Meanwhile Geelong has confirmed its own mutually arranged split with 2022 flag forward Tyson Stengle.

The Magpies have formally split with Hill, cutting short the 26-year-old's bumper contract, which was due to expire at the end of 2030.

"I'm going to take a break from football to keep working on myself and regain my passion for the game," Hill said in a statement released by the Magpies today.

Hill was the star of Collingwood's 2023 premiership under coach Craig McRae, winning the Norm Smith Medal for a four-goal grand final showing against Brisbane.

But having taken stretches of personal leave, he hasn't played at AFL level for almost a year — making just three VFL appearances in 2026.

On Thursday, before the Pies lost to Geelong at the MCG, Hill shared on Instagram a vile direct message from a Collingwood supporter that included a racist slur among other insults.

"You have disappointed this whole club and it's (sic) 100 thousand plus fans what you have done the last 18 months," the account also posted.

"… I hope nothing but the worst for you."

Hill posted a screenshot of the message and captioned it "anyone know this tough guy?"

The Magpies have publicly supported Hill throughout his turbulent period, and McRae again expressed his care for the forward's wellbeing — and disgust at those posting abusive comments on social media.

"Bobby, our thoughts are with you," McRae said after the MCG defeat on Thursday night.

"Not just for Bobby — what's going on? It's a crazy place at times, isn't it?

"I don't do social media, so bear with me, but I did look on a website which had feedback, and the feedback is unbelievable.

"It's just a cesspool for people just to vent. I find it fascinating that's actually something that people would be interested in.

"If Bobby's listening there, I'm sorry to hear that's the case. We'll always love him. It's sad to hear that."

This morning, the Pies' football manager Charlie Gardiner confirmed the end of Hill's contract.

"The club has been working with Bobby over the past 12 months to put support structures in place to help him work through some personal matters," Gardiner said in a statement.

"Despite this, Bobby has unfortunately struggled to meet his commitments to the club consistently this year and agreed that taking a break from football is the best decision for him and his family."

Meanwhile, the Magpies are counting the cost of Thursday night's loss with veteran defender Jeremy Howe suffering a fractured arm.

It is the same arm that he broke horrifically after a nasty landing from an aerial contest, also against Geelong, in 2023.

"The likelihood is he'll probably need an operation," McRae said post-game.

Utility Harry Perryman suffered a left hamstring injury — having strained his right hamstring earlier in the season.

And Brownlow medal favourite Nick Daicos has a bruised right foot, but he played out the game.

Stengle agrees Cats departure

Geelong meanwhile formally cut ties with Stengle, who said he has chosen to step away from AFL football and return home to South Australia after a difficult year.

Stengle, 27, still had three years left on a bumper five-year extension signed in 2024.

Tyson Stengle's last AFL game for Geelong was the 2025 grand final defeat to Brisbane. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

But the Cats confirmed on Friday they had reached a mutual agreement with Stengle and finalised it with his management and the AFL Players' Association.

The forward played only one VFL game this season amid off-field issues, and last played at the top level in Geelong's 2025 AFL grand final loss.

"Geelong Football Club gave me another chance to play at the highest level and achieve a lot of highs and lows and to win a premiership and All Australian in 2022 will forever be my greatest achievements I would have never thought I would have done," Stengle said in a post on Instagram.

"But after a tough year or so I have made the decision to step away from AFL football and move home and be with family where I feel more comfortable. It was a tough decision but it was the best decision for me mentally.

"I will always be grateful for playing at the top level and playing in the biggest games of them all, it was always fun and exciting.

"Thank you to everyone who has supported along the way."

AAP

World.title: How a classification change ended Korey's Commonwealth Games hopes
World.content:
As the track cycling competition at the 2026 Commonwealth Games gets underway, Australians expecting to see Paralympic champion Korey Boddington in action will be left disappointed.

The popular para cyclist, who won the kilometre C4-5 time trial in Paris, has joined swimmer Alexa Leary as another high-profile para athlete removed from the Glasgow Games after a reclassification of his disability.

Leary, the reigning S9 100m world record holder, was to make her Commonwealth Games debut in Scotland but was reclassified as an S10 athlete earlier this year.

Partly due to the stripped-down nature of these Games, there are no sprint freestyle events for S10 swimmers at the Tollcross pool, with the only event in that category being the 200-metre individual medley, which Leary does not compete in.

Boddington, the reigning Sir Hubert Opperman Trophy winner and 2025 Australian cyclist of the year, was also reclassified, twice in the space of a year, first becoming eligible to compete, and then ineligible.

Boddington's year as a C3 athlete

Korey Boddington is the world record holder in the kilo at C3 and C4 classifications. (Supplied: Cycling New Zealand)

Classification for para athletes has long been a contentious and complicated issue.

The process exists in para sport to enable athletes with different impairment types — not necessarily the same disabilities — the chance to compete on a relatively level playing field.

"International classification is conducted by a panel comprising medical classifiers and technical classifiers before a competition, after which they will be informed which class they are in and why," AusCycling told ABC Sport in a statement.

"Their role is to assess whether an athlete has an eligible impairment that meets the minimum impairment criteria for Para cycling, assess the extent to which the athlete is able to execute the specific tasks and activities fundamental to Para cycling, and, where required, undertake observation in competition assessment."

Within the classification framework imposed by the sport's governing body, the UCI, Boddington — who won two Paralympic medals as a C4 athlete — was, briefly, reclassified as a C3 athlete in 2025.

This indicates a higher level of impairment than under which he competed in Paris. In cycling, the scale is from 1-5, where 1 is the most severe impairment and 5 the least.

This is not uncommon.

Boddington only made his first national team appearance in the Paralympic year of 2024.

He endeared himself to the Australian public with his love of burritos, enjoying up to four of them a day: "You know how many carbs are in the wrap, and you can specifically portion out all your protein that are on them," he told AusCycling in 2025 by way of explanation.

It earned him the affectionate nickname the Flying Burrito.

Korey Boddington was a breakout star of the Paris Paralympics. (Getty Images: PA Images/Andrew Matthews)

For an athlete like Boddington, who lives with an acquired brain injury and had not spent all that long in the sport, it is understandable that his classification level was still being sorted out.

But having been reclassified, Boddington promptly won four world championship gold medals as a C3 athlete at the 2025 world championships in Rio, winning the men's sprint, 1,000-metre (kilo) time trial and elimination race before helping Australia clinch victory in the mixed C1-5 team sprint.

The 30-year-old Queenslander, the world record holder for the C4 flying 200m sprint time trial, also broke world records in the C3 flying 200m sprint and the C3 kilo at the Oceania Championships in Cambridge, New Zealand in February this year.

He won four gold medals in total at those championships: the kilo, sprint, individual pursuit and mixed C1-5 team sprint, as well as winning silver medals in the elimination and scratch races.

All signs were pointing towards Boddington competing in the C1-3 3,000m individual pursuit and 1,000m time trial events at the Games in Glasgow.

However, upon his return from New Zealand, Boddington was reclassified a C4 athlete and competed in that category at the TrackNats in Brisbane in late March.

Boddington still won gold in the sprint, elimination, scratch, kilo and C1-C5 team sprint at the Anna Meares Velodrome.

However, there are only four men's para cycling events set to be contested on the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome in Glasgow; none of which C4 athletes are eligible for — the sprint and 1,000m time trial in the tandem B category, and the 3,000m individual pursuit and 1,000m time trial events in the C1-3 classification.

Classification can be 'tough'

Korey Boddington won gold in the men's C4 1,000m time trial at the 2024 Paralympic Games in Paris. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

Being rubbed out of a major competition like the Commonwealth Games, the only multi-sport event where able-bodied and para athletes compete on the same program, through no fault of their own, is a bitter pill for the athletes to swallow.

And classification can be a very sensitive and personal process.

A Four Corners investigation in 2023 found that some Paralympic athletes were deliberately exaggerating their impairments in a bid to win medals and that the system itself was ripe for manipulation.

Australians embroiled in Paralympics scandal Former athletes and officials tell Four Corners the system of Paralympic classification is flawed and easily manipulated.

AusCycling said it took care to ensure that its athletes are educated about classification throughout their time in the sport.

That takes the form of education about the classification system itself, guidance from classification experts, discussion of possible classification outcomes, and planning for different scenarios.

"The focus is on ensuring athletes understand the UCI Classification Rules, including eligible impairments, sport class profiles and assessment methods, while continuing to focus on their development and performance goals," the statement read.

The statement also noted that "not all classification outcomes can be anticipated, particularly for more complex impairment profiles".

Classification for para athletes can take place over the course of an athlete's career to ensure they are in their correct category for competition.

They may also have to be tested if the criteria for their classification change or if the governing body changes its tests. In cycling, that falls under the UCI's jurisdiction.

When a classification panel allocates a sport class to an athlete, it also assigns a status to that status: confirmed, review at the next available opportunity, review with a fixed review date or expired.

Needless to say, most athletes have to go through the process multiple times during their career.

Double world champion Tara Neyland detailed the process of classification. (Supplied: AusCycling)

Two-time world champion on the road and three-time track world champion Tara Neyland, who is also competing in the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome at these Games, said in a detailed Instagram video in May that classification days can be incredibly tough.

Neyland lives with facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy, a genetic disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness, which means her level of impairment is likely to change over time.

"Being a progressive degenerative condition, they need to keep reassessing as my body will keep changing," Neyland said in her Instagram video.

AusCycling noted that in instances such as Neyland's, athletes can request a medical review, but it is not imposed by AusCycling out of competition if it is against the athlete's wishes.

Regardless, the process is clearly incredibly emotionally draining for the athletes involved.

"Classification day is a tough one," Neyland said.

"Essentially you're being assessed, being graded, for your level of impairment of your condition, disability, injury, whatever it may be, however you define it.

"It can bring up a lot of emotions.

"It's a necessary part of para sport so that we can be as fairly graded as possible, but it's still quite challenging.

"For me, until coming into para sport, I've tried to view myself as someone who's incredibly capable, and then to flip the mindset and have to prove your level of impairment and speak to all your challenges and struggles and areas that, for me, weaken, struggle to do the same things that an able body can do is hard."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

AusCycling said it was committed to helping athletes with any issues that arose from classification changes.

"Ultimately, classification exists to protect the integrity and fairness of Para sport," AusCycling's statement read.

"While the prospect of reclassification can be challenging, particularly given its potential impact on competitive opportunities and performance goals, AusCycling remains committed to prioritising athlete wellbeing and supporting athletes' continued performance throughout the entire process.

"Athlete wellbeing remains a key priority throughout any classification review process, whether anticipated or unexpected.

"Appropriate support is identified both on the ground and remotely to ensure athletes are well supported throughout the process."

World.title: 'It was weird': De Minaur beats Hewitt in Aussie tussle
World.content:
Alex de Minaur has cast aside sentiment to end Cruz Hewitt's breakout run and storm into the Washington Open quarter-finals.

The top seed and defending champion produced a clinical display to defeat the 17-year-old Hewitt, son of former world number one Lleyton, 6-2, 6-3 in just 61 minutes.

De Minaur shared a warm embrace with Hewitt at the net as Lleyton looked on from the stands at Stadium Court.

"It was definitely weird," de Minaur said.

"I knew I was going to play him on the tour some day, but I didn't actually expect it to be this week. It was an amazing feeling."

Cruz Hewitt has breakthrough Tour win Cruz Hewitt wins for the first time at ATP Tour level, his Washington upset of former world number 37 Marcus Giron set to rocket him up the tennis rankings.

A Wimbledon boys' finalist this month, Hewitt idolised de Minaur while growing up around the Davis Cup team captained by his father.

"Even [with] all the lead-up, seeing all the incredible pictures that we have together and how we've grown up, I'm glad I managed to get through," de Minaur said.

"But I'm sure we're going to have many battles in the years to come."

Australia's world number six charged to the net with authority and displayed great hands en route to improving his win-loss record to 29-14 this season.

Despite his defeat, Hewitt is set to soar some 252 spots in the rankings to a fresh career high of about world number 360 after qualifying in Washington and then winning his maiden ATP match.

Competing for the first time since marrying British WTA star Katie Boulter this month, de Minaur next faces American Brandon Nakashima, who ousted seventh-seed Jakub Mensik 7-6 (5), 3-6, 6-4 to reach his second consecutive Washington quarter-final.

Nakashima holds a 2-1 edge over the Australian, with de Minaur's lone win against the American also coming in last year's quarter-finals before he went on to lift the title.

AAP

Tech.title: Apple’s new AirTags are back down to their best price
Tech.content:
We spotted a great deal on Tile trackers earlier this week that’s still live, but if you’re an iPhone owner, we ultimately recommend Apple’s latest AirTag. Right now, you can pick up a four-pack for $89 ($10 off) at Amazon and Target, matching the bundle’s all-time low price. If you’re a member, Costco also has a deal that throws in a fifth AirTag for free.

A growing number of Bluetooth trackers can tap into Apple’s Find My network these days, but none combine that with Apple’s latest ultra wideband (UWB) chip, which powers even better Precision Finding than before. Precision Finding uses on-screen arrows and distance indicators in the Find My app to guide you directly to a misplaced item, while the second-generation AirTag’s upgraded chip and extended Bluetooth range make it faster and more reliable to locate tags, even in multistory homes. You can also use Precision Finding to find lost items on an Apple Watch, provided you have a Series 9 or later. And if all else fails, the built-in speaker is noticeably louder than before, making it easier to track down an AirTag by sound.

Plus, like its predecessor, the second-generation AirTag comes with a handful of features that are especially useful if you’re traveling this summer. AirTag sharing lets up to five people keep track of the same item, while Apple’s Share Item Location feature allows you to temporarily share an AirTag’s location with participating airlines, including United, Delta, and American Airlines. It’s still a shame Apple doesn’t include a built-in lanyard hole, meaning you’ll need to buy a separate loop or holder, but the tracker continues to use a replaceable CR2032 battery, so you won’t have to replace the entire device when it eventually runs out of power. And at $89 for a four-pack, it’s also a little easier on your wallet today.

Tech.title: Google Earth’s AI deepfake tool only lasted one day
Tech.content:
Google has shut down Google Earth feature it launched Thursday that allowed users to edit satellite images with text prompts using AI. The tool essentially let users create AI deepfakes of the real world using text prompts; Digital Digging’s Henk van Ess, for example, intentionally generated images adding things like refugees near the Mexican border and a bomb crater by a hospital in Gaza. On Thursday, Google’s initial response to van Ess noted that images generated with Nano Banana 2 in Google Earth included a digital watermark and that the company prevented “image creation on harmful topics.”

One day later, Google’s new statement says that “We know that people uniquely trust Google Earth for a reliable view of the world. We’ve seen geospatial professionals using this feature for a range of useful purposes, however we’ve also seen people sharing screenshots of generated imagery that appear to violate our policies. So we’re rolling back this feature in Google Earth while we work on implementing stronger guardrails. It’s important to note that generated images didn’t appear in the main Google Earth experience for others to see and were watermarked as AI generated.”

van Ess pointed out that he was able to fool Hive’s AI detection tool with a video generated in Google Earth, showing how the generated media could spread despite the watermarks, and said in his testing, “Nothing was refused, nothing was softened, and nothing suggested I try a different prompt.”

Tech.title: The NHTSA is investigating 1.2 million Tesla vehicles over suspension failure reports
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) is probing nearly 1.2 million Tesla vehicles after receiving complaints about a suspension failure that could cause “a loss of vehicle directional control,” as reported earlier by Reuters. The preliminary investigation includes the 2018-2020 Model 3 and 2021-2023 Model Y, according to a filing from the NHTSA’s Office of Defects Investigation.

The NHTSA says it received 156 complaints about the issue, which “involves the detachment of the front lower lateral link.” In most cases reviewed by the NHTSA, failure occurred with “no advance warning,” but some “cite noises occurring prior to failure.” The NHTSA hasn’t recorded any crashes, injuries, or fatalities related to the potential issue.

This isn’t the first time Tesla dealt with suspension issues. In 2021, Tesla recalled 2,791 Model Y and Model 3 vehicles over a potential suspension defect. It later recalled another round of Model 3 vehicles after the NHTSA found that a “loose fastener could cause the lateral link to separate from the sub-frame.” The NHTSA says the complaints linked to its current investigation don’t appear to be related to these issues.

Tech.title: The ban on robot vacuums won’t make them safer, only worse
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

All the smart home news, reviews, and gadgets you need to know about

No other gadget knows as much about your home as a robot vacuum. They map your space, learn your routines, and many now carry a camera and microphone into every room in your house. As AI gives them a better understanding of what they see, the privacy and security risks these autonomous robots pose are only growing.

That’s why greater scrutiny makes sense, but the ban on foreign-made mobile robots issued by the Federal Communications Commission earlier this week — implemented to address “unacceptable risks to the national security of the United States or the safety and security of United States persons” — doesn’t actually judge products by how secure they are, just where they’re built. It effectively means no new robot vacuums from major companies can enter the US market unless they are built here. And spoiler alert: none are.

This ban means Americans will see fewer new models, slower innovation, and more expensive robot vacuums.

Cybersecurity and manufacturing are not the same thing. If the goal is safer robot vacuums (and robot lawnmowers, companion bots, humanoids, and all the other robots this ban sweeps up), this policy misses the mark. A meaningful security standard for robots would require encrypted map storage, security audits, vulnerability disclosures, and clear data retention policies.

Instead, this ban means Americans will see fewer new models, slower innovation, and more expensive robot vacuums. In short, we’ll get worse vacuums than those we have today.

The Matic robot vacuum is the only model currently assembled in the US, but it doesn’t use enough US-made parts to be considered American made. Photo by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Those failures don’t point toward regulating manufacturing, but toward the need for stronger cybersecurity requirements, like those defined by the government’s Cyber Trust Mark program. But that program doesn’t exist yet, and if it ever does, it will be entirely voluntary.

This manufacturing ban applies to any foreign-made robot, but footnotes in the FCC’s public notice indicate that China is a particular concern, warning that foreign governments could use vulnerabilities found in advanced robotics to access sensitive data. China’s commerce ministry has already called the policy “discriminatory and suppressive against Chinese companies and products.”

A robot vacuum made in Massachusetts isn’t automatically more secure than one made in Shenzhen.

There are real security advantages to domestic robot production. Mehul Nariyawala, president and co-founder of Matic, the only robot vacuum currently assembled in the US (although with too many foreign parts to be considered US-made), points out that domestic manufacturing makes it easier to ensure there are no hardware backdoors and to hold companies accountable for any failures.

But a robot vacuum made in Massachusetts isn’t automatically more secure than one made in Shenzhen. And the FCC’s ban doesn’t actually take steps to ensure they will be.

The robot ban is a carbon copy of those the FCC has issued to Wi-Fi routers and drones over the last few months. So far, it has already granted several waivers to router companies that don’t appear to be moving their manufacturing to the US, which the waivers require. This raises questions about how consistently and fairly the new rules will be enforced and whether they can actually achieve their intended effect.

Today, the practical consequences won’t be better security — the millions of robot vacuums already in American homes remain unaffected, as do any currently sold models. If these really are a risk, and we’ve seen plenty of evidence they can be, why leave the largest source of that risk exactly where it is?

In an optimistic future, the ban could spur American manufacturing. Nariyawala believes it “creates the conditions for American startups to design, engineer, and build all manner of trustworthy robots at scale.” He adds that consumer robots are where robotics manufacturing reaches scale, and the supply chains they require are the same ones defense, industrial, and healthcare robots will depend on. “Get it right, educate customers to demand it, and that domestic supply chain stops being an aspiration and becomes an industry,” he says.

But even if he’s right, and he has more incentive than most to hope he is, that transition will take years. Today’s Matic relies heavily on imported parts, and its price is going up to $1,495 in September, showing how far building these products in the US is from replacing the $300 robot vacuum you can buy at Walmart. Meanwhile, restricting the import of new products means US households will miss out on the next wave of innovations in a fast-moving category.

This was iRobot’s first combination mopping robot, which arrived in 2022. iRobot’s reluctance to adopt lidar and to offer mopping on its robot vacuums hurt it, leading to the company being swallowed up by its Chinese competition. Photo by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Chinese manufacturers may have started out as fast followers, but they have transformed the robot vacuum industry over the past decade. Fierce competition brought better navigation, improved obstacle avoidance, self-emptying docks, and much better mopping systems. That competition also squeezed American manufacturers out of business; iRobot, the American pioneer in this space, filed for bankruptcy last year and is now owned by its Chinese manufacturing partner.

“We see this as part of a broader moment for US robotics, one where the opportunity lies in building domestic leadership.” — Colin Angle

Without that competitive pressure, progress in the US market will slow, and prices will rise. But the competition I would most like to see isn’t who can build the wildest appendages or produce the highest suction power — it’s competing on privacy; I want a robot vacuum that doesn’t require an internet connection to clean my house, maps that stay on the device instead of the cloud; object recognition that runs locally instead of on remote servers; and clear explanations of what data leaves my house and why.

Matic does much of this today, which is one reason it’s my top pick of the many robot vacuums I’ve tested, but it’s a high price to pay for what should be easy features to deliver.

It feels too late to save the American robot vacuum industry. But iRobot co-founder and former CEO Colin Angle, whose startup Familiar Machines & Magic is developing a robotic companion that could fall under this ban, supports the ban’s stated goals. “We see this as part of a broader moment for US robotics, one where the opportunity lies in building domestic leadership,” he told me. “That means continued investment in domestic manufacturing, R&D, and talent, and we’re committed to being part of that effort as the category grows.”

If that is the goal, it may well succeed, but only because it shuts out the competition — which is the same thing Angle argues the Chinese government did to help its burgeoning robot vacuum market a decade ago. But if the goal is making robots more secure, we’re still floundering.

Dreame’s latest X60 robot vacuum could be one of the last the Chinese manufacturer releases in the US. So much for its dream of a huge US expansion. Photo by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Meanwhile, Chinese robot vacuum makers and their US-based users are in limbo. Current products will continue to work and be sold, but the path forward is murky at best. One bright spot is that current products can continue to get security updates; the FCC doesn’t regulate software patches unless they change the radio characteristics of a device.

Kristen Marion, global PR brand lead at Eufy, owned by Anker, told me that they plan to continue to sell, support, and update existing products, adding that “Like others across the industry, we are seeking further clarity on how the rule will be applied to future products, and we will keep our customers informed.” Narwal was more bullish. Yunlin Kong, president of Narwal Overseas Business, told me, “We’re not going anywhere. The US is one of our most important markets, and our commitment here is unchanged.” I reached out to several other Chinese manufacturers who either said much the same thing as Eufy or politely declined to comment.

The concerns driving the ban are legitimate. Robot vacuums deserve more scrutiny than they’ve received, especially as AI expands their capabilities far beyond the original purpose of cleaning our floors. But a broad manufacturing ban that ignores what’s already in your house and can’t tell a secure product from an insecure one isn’t solving that problem. It’s just slowing down the only thing that’s actually worked in our favor: competition. If the government wants safer robot vacuums, don’t regulate where they’re made; regulate how securely they work.

Tech.title: Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream is a quirky life sim that’s worth buying at this discount

Brad Bourque is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Looking to start your own island paradise full of Miis based on family, friends, and celebrities, but don’t feel like paying full fare?
